Based on population projections, elderly consumer willingness, and potential changes in their consumption habits, please produce a market size analysis report for the elderly demographic.
without_scope.answer:
# China Elderly Market Size Analysis Report

## 1) Scope and headline conclusion

Assuming you mean **China’s elderly / “silver economy” market**, the addressable market is already very large and set to expand sharply. <cite id="S14">At the end of 2024, the population aged 60 and over was 310.31 million, accounting for 22.0 percent of the national population; the population aged 65 and over was 220.23 million, accounting for 15.6 percent.</cite> By 2035, <cite id="S83">China's population aged 60 and above is expected to exceed 400 million, accounting for over 30 percent of the total</cite>, while <cite id="S41">the scale of China's silver economy is roughly 7 trillion yuan at present, accounting for about 6 percent of GDP, and is expected to reach 30 trillion yuan by 2035</cite>.  

**Bottom line:** on official top-down estimates, the elderly market expands from roughly **¥7T now to ¥30T by 2035**; that implies about a **4.3x** increase in market value, far faster than the increase in elderly headcount alone (author calculation from the cited figures). <cite id="S14,S41,S83">Current 60+ population is 310.31 million; the silver economy is about 7 trillion yuan now; by 2035 the 60+ population is expected to exceed 400 million and the silver economy to reach 30 trillion yuan.</cite>

## 2) Why the market can grow faster than population

The official “silver economy” is broad, not just pensions or healthcare: <cite id="S90">The silver economy covers a wide range of goods and services aimed at the elderly and the aging process, from daily necessities and assistive devices to healthcare, elderly care, culture, entertainment and beyond.</cite> Demand-side willingness also looks strong. <cite id="S85">Approximately 90 percent of respondents are willing to spend more on products and services such as smart devices, health management, cultural entertainment and travel.</cite>  

Digital adoption is accelerating, which matters because it expands access and lifts spending efficiency. <cite id="S75">The proportion of Chinese internet users aged 60 and above grew rapidly to 52.0 percent by June 2024 from 43.2 percent in December 2023</cite>, and <cite id="S78">elderly consumers' average daily online shopping time has exceeded 65 minutes... Their top search interests include clothing, food and groceries, transportation, and medication and supplements.</cite> Academic evidence is consistent with this channel: <cite id="P4">The elderly's internet use can increase the total consumption level and promote the optimization of the consumption structure, specifically, increasing developmental and enjoyment consumption while reducing survival consumption.</cite>

## 3) Likely changes in elderly consumption habits

The near-term elderly wallet is still anchored in essentials, especially food. <cite id="S88">Compared to other generations, senior consumers favor spending on food and groceries, as the category makes up 35% of their total expenditures.</cite> At the same time, aging tends to reduce some traditional categories: <cite id="P2">age has a positive impact on the share of healthcare expenditure and a negative effect on spending on work-related items such as clothes and transportation.</cite> Another study similarly finds that <cite id="P3">the share of food expenditure rises... while the shares of ... transportation and communication decrease significantly</cite>.  

That said, the mix is not simply “less spending”; it is **reallocated spending**. Seniors show strong willingness to spend more on travel, entertainment, health management, and smart devices, <cite id="S85">approximately 90 percent of respondents are willing to spend more on products and services such as smart devices, health management, cultural entertainment and travel</cite> and there is visible housing-related upgrade potential because <cite id="S43">21.1% are willing to purchase smart home devices... Currently, only 4.8% of the 60+ urban population own or use smart home devices, indicating a large untapped market.</cite>

## 4) Market sizing methodology

Because the retrieved official totals describe a **broad silver economy** rather than a published category-by-category retail breakdown, the splits below are **top-down scenario estimates**, not official category statistics. I use two anchors:

1. **Official total elderly market size:** <cite id="S41">roughly 7 trillion yuan at present ... expected to reach 30 trillion yuan by 2035</cite>  
2. **China’s 2024 household spending mix as baseline proxy:** <cite id="S59">the per capita expenditure on food, tobacco and liquor was 8,411 yuan, clothing 1,521 yuan, housing 6,951 yuan... transportation and communications 3,975 yuan</cite> out of <cite id="S59">the nationwide per capita consumption expenditure was 28,227 yuan</cite>  

That baseline implies approximate category shares of **food 29.8%**, **clothing 5.4%**, **housing 24.6%**, and **transport/communication 14.1%** (author calculation from the cited NBS figures). I then compare those baseline shares with elderly-specific evidence showing **higher food weight** and **lower clothing/transport weight**. <cite id="S88">Senior consumers favor spending on food and groceries, as the category makes up 35% of their total expenditures.</cite> <cite id="P2,P3">Age has a negative effect on spending on clothes and transportation; transportation and communication shares decrease significantly as aging rises.</cite>

## 5) Category-by-category market size estimates

### Food
Using the national-spending baseline, food would be about **¥2.09T now** and **¥8.94T by 2035** (29.8% of ¥7T and ¥30T). Using the elderly-specific evidence that food/grocery is **35% of senior expenditures**, food rises to about **¥2.45T now** and **¥10.5T by 2035**. <cite id="S41,S59">The silver economy is roughly 7 trillion yuan now and expected to reach 30 trillion yuan by 2035; 2024 per-capita food spending was 8,411 yuan out of 28,227 yuan total.</cite> <cite id="S88">Senior consumers favor spending on food and groceries, as the category makes up 35% of their total expenditures.</cite>  

**Interpretation:** food is likely the **largest immediate everyday-spending pool** in the elderly market.

### Clothing
Applying the national baseline gives roughly **¥0.38T now** and **¥1.62T by 2035**. But elderly-specific research suggests clothing’s share should be lower than the all-population average, so a more realistic range is roughly **¥0.2T–¥0.4T now** and **¥0.9T–¥1.6T by 2035**. <cite id="S41,S59">Current and 2035 silver-economy totals are about 7 trillion and 30 trillion yuan; 2024 clothing spending was 1,521 yuan out of 28,227 yuan total.</cite> <cite id="P2">Age has ... a negative effect on spending on work-related items such as clothes</cite>.  

**Interpretation:** clothing is not the biggest elderly wallet share, but it still supports a meaningful market, especially for **comfort, health, easy-wear, adaptive, and outdoor-function apparel**.

### Housing
Using the national-spending baseline, housing-related consumption is about **¥1.72T now** and **¥7.39T by 2035**. <cite id="S41,S59">Current and 2035 silver-economy totals are about 7 trillion and 30 trillion yuan; 2024 housing spending was 6,951 yuan out of 28,227 yuan total.</cite> The adjacent upside is likely larger than that core figure suggests, because housing for seniors increasingly includes retrofits, assistive devices, and smart-home products, and <cite id="S43">only 4.8% of the 60+ urban population own or use smart home devices</cite> even though <cite id="S43">21.1% are willing to purchase smart home devices</cite>.  

**Interpretation:** housing is a **large absolute market** today, and “aging in place” upgrades could make it one of the fastest-growing subsegments.

### Transportation
Using the national baseline, transport/communication is about **¥0.99T now** and **¥4.22T by 2035**. Because seniors tend to spend less on work-related transport than the average adult, a more conservative elderly-specific range is about **¥0.7T–¥1.0T now** and **¥3.0T–¥4.2T by 2035**. <cite id="S41,S59">Current and 2035 silver-economy totals are about 7 trillion and 30 trillion yuan; 2024 transportation and communications spending was 3,975 yuan out of 28,227 yuan total.</cite> <cite id="P2,P3">Age has a negative effect on transportation spending; transportation and communication shares decrease significantly as population aging rises.</cite>  

But transport’s quality mix is changing, not disappearing. <cite id="S85">Approximately 90 percent of respondents are willing to spend more on ... travel</cite>, and <cite id="S50">China's senior travelers aged over 50 now make up 37.8% of the total domestic tourism market</cite>.  

**Interpretation:** routine transport share may be lower, but **tourism, assisted mobility, and premium senior-friendly travel** are important growth areas.

## 6) Implied per-capita spending power

Using the official aggregate figures, current silver-economy value of **¥7T** spread across **310.31M** people aged 60+ implies roughly **¥22.6k per elderly person per year** today. By 2035, **¥30T** over **400M+** elderly people implies at least **~¥75k per person per year** if the official projection is realized (author calculation from the cited figures). <cite id="S14,S41,S83">Current 60+ population is 310.31 million; the silver economy is about 7 trillion yuan now; by 2035 the 60+ population is expected to exceed 400 million and the silver economy to reach 30 trillion yuan.</cite>  

This means the elderly market story is not just about more seniors; it is also about a much bigger **wallet per senior**, supported by digital adoption, product upgrading, and service expansion. <cite id="S75,P4,S85">Internet use among the elderly is rising rapidly; internet use increases total consumption and upgrades consumption structure; about 90 percent are willing to spend more on smart devices, health management, entertainment, and travel.</cite>

## 7) Executive summary

  - **Clothing:** about **¥0.2T–¥0.4T now**, **¥0.9T–¥1.6T by 2035**, best positioned in comfort/health/function segments rather than fashion-only positioning. <cite id="S41,S59,P2">Derived from the 7T/30T totals, clothing's 2024 spending share, and evidence that aging reduces clothing spend share.</cite>

What is their consumption potential across various aspects such as clothing, food, housing, and transportation? Based on population projections, elderly consumer willingness, and potential changes in their consumption habits, please produce a market size analysis report for the elderly demographic.
without_term.answer:
**Assumption:** because the question does not name a country, I treat it as **China**, using Chinese official statistics and recent China-focused research.

### 1) Elderly population outlook (2020–2050)

On a **strict 65+ definition**, <cite id="703cc292-3,20b00fcc-1">China’s elderly population is estimated to rise from **172 million in 2020** to **366 million in 2050**, more than doubling, while its share of the total population rises from **12.0%** to **26.0%**.</cite> On the broader **60+ definition** commonly used in China, <cite id="96438c8f-3">the population was **296.97 million in 2023** (including **216.76 million aged 65+**)</cite>, <cite id="96438c8f-2">**310.31 million in 2024** (including **220.23 million aged 65+**)</cite>, and <cite id="96438c8f-1">**323.38 million in 2025** (including **223.65 million aged 65+**).</cite> Looking forward, <cite id="20b00fcc-0">by **2035**, China is forecast to have **more than 450 million people aged above 60**, or **32.7%** of the population.</cite>

### 2) Benchmark market size: how much consumption spending could this population support?

Using China’s official household data as a benchmark, <cite id="45c3a894-0,d4713f1e-0">the **national per-capita consumption expenditure in 2024 was 28,227 yuan**</cite>; in 2025, <cite id="45c3a894-1">it rose to **29,476 yuan**.</cite> If we multiply that benchmark basket by the elderly headcount, the **comparable consumption pool** for the elderly is about:

- **2020 (65+ basis):** **¥4.86 trillion** = 172m × ¥28,227 <cite id="703cc292-3,45c3a894-0">[inputs]</cite>  
- **2024 (65+ basis):** **¥6.22 trillion** = 220.23m × ¥28,227 <cite id="96438c8f-2,45c3a894-0">[inputs]</cite>  
- **2025 (65+ basis):** **¥6.59 trillion** = 223.65m × ¥29,476 <cite id="96438c8f-1,45c3a894-1">[inputs]</cite>  
- **2035 (60+ basis, broad elderly market):** **more than ¥12.70 trillion** = 450m × ¥28,227 <cite id="20b00fcc-0,45c3a894-0">[inputs]</cite>  
- **2050 (65+ basis):** **¥10.33 trillion** = 366m × ¥28,227 <cite id="703cc292-3,45c3a894-0">[inputs]</cite>  

These are **benchmark spending-potential estimates**, not exact realized spending forecasts. That distinction matters because <cite id="a20adc21-6">a UNDP-linked aging report notes that older people in China show **relatively low consumption willingness**</cite>, and <cite id="e3c2c136-1">a 2024 study finds that consumption declines with age, with older adults spending less on **appearance-related categories** and entertainment, though **not on dining**.</cite>

### 3) Cross-check with China’s “silver economy” projections

A broader industry view is even larger than the pure household-consumption benchmark. <cite id="543bdd52-3">China’s silver economy is projected to exceed **¥30 trillion by 2035**, roughly **10% of GDP**.</cite> Another source places the present scale at about <cite id="543bdd52-2">**¥7 trillion in 2025**, rising to **¥30 trillion by 2035**.</cite> This broader number is bigger than the simple consumer-basket estimate because <cite id="543bdd52-7">the silver economy is described as a **comprehensive lifecycle initiative** spanning both pre-retirement preparation and actual aging phases</cite>, and <cite id="543bdd52-4">China’s elderly-care service sector is said to have **vast growth potential**.</cite>

### 4) “Clothing, food, housing, transportation” market view

#### Food
<cite id="896bdd8b-0">In 2024, China’s per-capita spending on **food, tobacco and liquor** was **¥8,411**, accounting for **29.8%** of total consumption.</cite> Applied to the 2024 **65+ population**, that implies a benchmark elderly **food market** of roughly **¥1.85 trillion** = 220.23m × ¥8,411 <cite id="96438c8f-2,896bdd8b-0">[inputs]</cite>. Food should remain the most resilient elderly category because <cite id="e3c2c136-1">older consumers do **not** appear to cut **dining** spending the way they cut appearance-related purchases</cite>, and <cite id="a20adc21-5">a 2023 Mintel-based summary says **72% of consumers aged 55+ shop for groceries offline at least three days per week**.</cite>

#### Clothing
<cite id="96d60ec2-0">In 2024, per-capita spending on **clothing** was **¥1,521**, or **5.4%** of total consumption.</cite> On the same 2024 **65+ population** base, that gives a benchmark elderly **clothing market** of about **¥0.335 trillion** = 220.23m × ¥1,521 <cite id="96438c8f-2,96d60ec2-0">[inputs]</cite>. But this category likely underperforms the national average because <cite id="e3c2c136-1">older adults spend **significantly less on appearance-related categories**</cite>; the offset is that <cite id="da1a4b04-0">seniors are increasingly buying **daily necessities, clothes, and food online**, alongside electronics and smart products.</cite>

#### Housing / at-home consumption
A precise national **housing/residence** point estimate was not retrievable from the search results here, so I would treat this as a **high-opportunity but not yet point-sized** segment in this report. Qualitatively, <cite id="da1a4b04-2">many elderly Chinese spend much of their time **at home** and often **look after grandchildren**</cite>, which supports demand for aging-in-place upgrades, household services, community care, and home-use products. That direction is consistent with the broader policy and industry view that <cite id="543bdd52-4">elderly-care services in China have **vast growth potential**</cite> and that <cite id="543bdd52-3">the silver economy as a whole could surpass **¥30 trillion by 2035**.</cite>

#### Transportation / travel
For transport, the retrieved official category value was incomplete, but a secondary China data series reports that <cite id="d4713f1e-1">China’s per-capita spending on **transport and communication** was **¥4,306 in 2025**.</cite> If applied to the 2025 **65+ population**, that implies a rough elderly **transport/communication benchmark** of about **¥0.96 trillion** = 223.65m × ¥4,306 <cite id="96438c8f-1,d4713f1e-1">[inputs]</cite>. Demand may strengthen over time because <cite id="a20adc21-2">one survey found elderly people in China took **almost eight short trips** and **at least one overseas trip a year**</cite>, while <cite id="a20adc21-1">the number of Chinese internet users aged over 60 has been **increasing**</cite>, supporting digital ticketing, mobility apps, and travel-commerce adoption.

### 5) What changes in elderly consumption habits imply for market size

The main structural shift is not just “more elderly people,” but a different mix of spending. <cite id="a20adc21-6">Consumption willingness is still relatively low among many older Chinese</cite>, so the market will not scale linearly with headcount in every category. At the same time, the mix is moving toward <cite id="e3c2c136-1">food and daily-living resilience rather than fashion-heavy spending</cite>, plus <cite id="da1a4b04-0,a20adc21-1">rising online adoption for necessities, clothes, food, smart products, and services</cite>, and <cite id="a20adc21-2">meaningful travel demand</cite>. In practice, that means the biggest winners are likely to be **food**, **home-based care and household services**, **mobility/travel**, and **digitally enabled senior products**, while **fashion/apparel** should grow more slowly.

### 6) Bottom line

On a narrow **65+** basis, China’s elderly population grows from <cite id="703cc292-3">**172 million in 2020** to **366 million in 2050**</cite>, and on a simple national-consumption benchmark that lifts the elderly consumption pool from roughly **¥4.86 trillion** to **¥10.33 trillion** <cite id="703cc292-3,45c3a894-0">[inputs]</cite>. On the broader **60+** basis, China already had <cite id="96438c8f-2">**310.31 million** older people in 2024</cite> and is expected to exceed <cite id="20b00fcc-0">**450 million by 2035**</cite>, implying a very large addressable market even before allowing for income growth. The strongest evidence points to a silver-economy market that is moving from today’s roughly <cite id="543bdd52-2">**¥7 trillion**</cite> toward more than <cite id="543bdd52-3">**¥30 trillion by 2035**</cite>, with **food** the most defensible mass-market category, **clothing** comparatively weaker, and **housing-at-home services** plus **transport/travel** the major structural growth opportunities.

If you want, I can turn this into a **full consulting-style report with tables, scenario assumptions (conservative/base/aggressive), and 2020/2030/2035/2040/2050 market forecasts by category**.

without_preference.text: From 2020 to 2050, how many elderly people will there be in Japan? What is their consumption potential across clothing, food, housing, and transportation? Based on population projections, elderly consumer willingness, and potential changes in their consumption habits, please produce a market size analysis report for the elderly demographic.
without_preference.answer:
# Japan Elderly Market Size Analysis (2020–2050)

## 1) How many elderly people will there be?

Using the standard Japanese definition of elderly as age 65+, <cite id="9c33950a-4">the population aged 65 and over was 36,325 thousand</cite> in 2020.  
For 2050, an IPSS projection estimated <cite id="46155c50-1">an elderly population of 35.86 million in 2050</cite>, and another IPSS source stated that <cite id="46155c50-4">the proportion aged 65 and over will expand from 14.6% in 1995 to 32.3% in 2050</cite>.

**Bottom line:** Japan’s elderly market is likely to stay at roughly **36 million people** from 2020 to 2050—<cite id="9c33950a-4">36.325 million in 2020</cite> versus <cite id="46155c50-1">35.86 million projected in 2050</cite>—so the headcount is broadly flat, but its weight in the economy rises because the elderly share of the population keeps increasing. As longer-run context, the latest IPSS revision says <cite id="46155c50-0">the population aged 65 and over [is projected] to make up about 40% of the population by 2070</cite>.

## 2) The key structural shift: more elderly living alone

The most important change for market sizing is household structure, not just headcount. Reuters reported that <cite id="cd3db8f9-0">The number of senior citizens living alone in Japan will likely jump 47% by 2050</cite>; another report summarized the same projection as <cite id="cd3db8f9-7">By 2050, 10.8 million elderly people will be living alone, making up 20.6 percent of all households</cite>. At the same time, <cite id="cd3db8f9-4">The number of single-person households is expected to reach 23.3 million in 2050, accounting for 44.3 percent of total households</cite>, and <cite id="cd3db8f9-1">senior citizens aged 65 or older will likely represent 46.5% in 2050, compared with 34.9% in 2020</cite> of one-person households.

**Implication:** even if the elderly population is roughly flat, the **elderly-consumption market becomes more fragmented, smaller-basket, and service-heavy** by 2050.

## 3) Consumption potential by category

### Food: the strongest and most defensive category

Evidence on spending patterns shows that older Japanese consumers are more necessity-oriented than younger groups. A Europe-Japan Centre report states <cite id="ce528982-0">Elderly Japanese spend less on housing, clothing and footwear, and transportation expenses than younger Japanese consumers.</cite> A similar summary says <cite id="ce528982-2">Of their consumption expenditures, the elderly devote smaller shares for housing, clothing and footwear, and transportation expenses.</cite> In the broader Japanese household basket, <cite id="6c8ad071-5">food accounted for. 27.1%</cite> while <cite id="6c8ad071-5">transportation and communication [accounted] for 16.4%</cite>.

**Market-size view:** Food is the **largest and most resilient** opportunity within the elderly market. The combination of a roughly <cite id="9c33950a-4">36,325 thousand</cite>-person elderly base in 2020, a still-roughly-<cite id="46155c50-1">35.86 million</cite>-person base in 2050, and a sharp rise in solo elderly households <cite id="cd3db8f9-0">living alone</cite> points to growing demand for **smaller portions, prepared meals, delivery, nutrition-focused products, and easy-to-cook staples**.

### Housing: moderate in routine spending, large in adaptation/services

The same evidence indicates that elderly consumers devote relatively less of their spending to housing than younger consumers: <cite id="ce528982-0">Elderly Japanese spend less on housing</cite>, and <cite id="ce528982-2">the elderly devote smaller shares for housing</cite>. However, housing opportunity should not be read as weak; instead, it is likely to shift away from standard household formation spending and toward **age-in-place, home modification, assisted living, monitoring, and senior-friendly rentals** because <cite id="cd3db8f9-7">10.8 million elderly people will be living alone</cite> by 2050.

**Market-size view:** routine housing consumption may be comparatively subdued, but **housing-related services and retrofit demand** should expand strongly as the elderly increasingly live alone and as the country ages further.

### Transportation: smaller budget share, but strong accessibility demand

Older consumers also devote relatively smaller shares to transport: <cite id="ce528982-0">Elderly Japanese spend less on ... transportation expenses than younger Japanese consumers.</cite> Still, mobility remains strategically important because Japan <cite id="ce528982-3">first enacted the Transportation. Accessibility Improvement Law in 2000, aiming to promote easy access to public transportation for older adults</cite>.

**Market-size view:** this is likely a **service and accessibility market**, not a volume market. The growth areas are less about conventional mass transport spending and more about **barrier-free transit, assisted mobility, community transport, ride services, and last-mile solutions** for a much older and more solo-living population.

### Clothing: the weakest of the four for volume growth

Among the four categories asked about, clothing looks weakest in structural terms. The evidence is direct: <cite id="ce528982-0">Elderly Japanese spend less on ... clothing and footwear</cite>, and <cite id="ce528982-2">the elderly devote smaller shares for ... clothing and footwear</cite>.

**Market-size view:** clothing remains a large market in absolute consumer count because the elderly base stays near **36 million**, but category growth is likely to be concentrated in **functional apparel, easy-wear garments, temperature regulation, comfort, and health-support products**, rather than fashion-led expansion.

## 4) Overall market ranking and outlook

Based on the available evidence, the elderly market opportunity across the four categories is best ranked as:

1. **Food** — biggest and most stable  
2. **Housing-related services/adaptation** — structurally important because of solo aging  
3. **Transportation/mobility services** — moderate spend, but strong accessibility need  
4. **Clothing** — smallest relative growth potential

The core reason is that Japan will still have about **36 million elderly consumers** in 2050 <cite id="46155c50-1">35.86 million in 2050</cite>, but they will be living in far more single-person households <cite id="cd3db8f9-7">10.8 million elderly people will be living alone</cite>. That means the elderly market should become **more necessity-driven, more convenience-driven, and more accessibility-driven** over time.

## 5) Practical conclusion

Japan’s elderly market is not mainly a story of more elderly people in absolute numbers; it is a story of a **persistent ~36 million-person customer base** becoming a **larger share of a shrinking country** and a **much larger share of one-person households**. In business terms, the strongest opportunities are the categories that serve daily living and independence: **food first, then housing adaptation and mobility support, with clothing more niche and functional**.

**Headline answer:** <cite id="9c33950a-4">the population aged 65 and over was 36,325 thousand</cite> in 2020, and an IPSS projection estimated <cite id="46155c50-1">an elderly population of 35.86 million in 2050</cite>. The addressable elderly market therefore remains roughly **36 million people** through 2050, with the best consumption potential in **food**, then **housing-related services**, then **transportation/mobility**, and lastly **clothing**.

### Note on precision
A fully yen-denominated TAM/SAM/SOM by category would require the underlying e-Stat table cells for 65+ household spending by category. The retrieved snippets support a strong demographic and directional market analysis, but not a defensible exact yen total for each category.

questions.original_query: What are the investment philosophies of Duan Yongping, Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger?

query.text: What are the investment philosophies of Duan Yongping, Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger?
query.answer: Duan Yongping’s philosophy is to <cite id="b43d0123-0">“do not short sell, do not use Margin Trading, and do not” touch investments you do not understand</cite>; he also frames <cite id="181453e2-7">“margin of safety” as how well you understand the company, not simply whether it looks cheap</cite>. Warren Buffett’s philosophy centers on <cite id="6eaa84b9-0">staying within your “circle of competence” and knowing its boundaries</cite>, <cite id="5b0172c0-0">thinking like a long-term part owner of a business rather than trading “a piece of paper whose price wiggles around daily”</cite>, and <cite id="32a30357-0">buying “wonderful businesses purchased at fair prices”</cite>. Charlie Munger’s philosophy emphasizes <cite id="33fa7a1b-2">buying “a great business at a fair price” rather than a mediocre one just because it is cheap</cite> and <cite id="3ea01a2e-6">avoiding stupidity and bad decisions instead of constantly chasing brilliance</cite>.

query.answer: In practice, many of the world’s wealthiest governments invest through <cite id="fa209e88-2">sovereign wealth funds, which are government-owned investment funds</cite> that are <cite id="fa209e88-2">commonly funded by the transfer of foreign exchange assets</cite> and often use that capital <cite id="fa209e88-1">to invest export revenues in foreign financial assets such as equities, private and government debt, and currencies</cite>. fully_underspecified.answer:
Across the three tasks, the model families tend to differ by what they are optimized to do. For <cite id="9a214b6f-2">volatility forecasting, GARCH-family models are probably the most commonly used methods</cite>, while newer ML methods can deliver <cite id="2f6bc423-1">significant clear improvement in volatility forecasting in both in-sample and out-of-sample accuracy</cite>; some evidence also suggests <cite id="2f6bc423-3">deep learning models outperform traditional machine learning models in forecasting stock return volatility</cite>. For instance, the Mean-Variance model assumes asset returns follow a normal distribution, which often doesn't align with actual market conditions. The Black-Litterman model relies on subjective view inputs, introducing a degree of subjectivity. Although deep learning models can handle complex non-linear relationships, they suffer from poor interpretability. So, what are the core differences between these various models in terms of risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation? And is it possible to combine their strengths to build a more general-purpose and effective modeling framework?
without_scope.answer:
## A useful way to compare the models

At a high level, these models differ most in <cite id="04722f36-3,04722f36-4">what they treat as “risk,” what information they use to form return expectations, and how they translate those expectations into portfolio weights.</cite> <cite id="04722f36-3">Markowitz mean-variance optimization formalizes risk as portfolio variance</cite>, <cite id="862d0e66-0">Black-Litterman starts from market-equilibrium returns and then blends in analyst views with explicit uncertainty</cite>, and <cite id="c7707502-0,ec158d01-4">deep learning and deep reinforcement learning models are built to learn nonlinear, time-dependent patterns and to allocate dynamically in complex markets.</cite>

## 1) Mean-Variance: simple, transparent, but fragile

In the Markowitz framework, <cite id="04722f36-1,04722f36-3">asset allocation is posed as a trade-off between expected return and variance, with variance used as the explicit risk measure.</cite> Its attraction is that <cite id="04722f36-4">the problem is reduced to two statistics—the mean and the variance/covariance structure—so the optimization is analytically clean and easy to interpret.</cite>

Its main weakness is that <cite id="c54bb2ec-5,c54bb2ec-4">mean-variance optimality is classically justified when returns are normally distributed or investor preferences can be represented by quadratic utility.</cite> In real markets, those conditions are often violated, and <cite id="cf417487-9">the optimization is particularly sensitive to estimation errors in expected returns, so small changes in sample means can produce large changes in portfolio weights.</cite> A second conceptual limitation is that <cite id="04722f36-3">variance treats all volatility as risk</cite>; in practice, that means upside and downside variation are not distinguished.

## 2) Black-Litterman: Bayesian blending of structure and views

Black-Litterman keeps the mean-variance allocation logic, but changes how expected returns are formed. <cite id="41d2a6d8-5,41d2a6d8-4">It uses an equilibrium prior for returns and a Bayesian mechanism to combine that prior with investor or analyst views.</cite> In implementation terms, <cite id="862d0e66-0">the model “allows investment analysts to incorporate subjective views … into market equilibrium returns,” and the required inputs include the view matrix, view returns, view uncertainty, equilibrium returns, and prior uncertainty.</cite>

So the core improvement over plain Markowitz is not a new allocator, but <cite id="862d0e66-0">a more structured return-estimation layer that blends analyst views and equilibrium returns instead of relying only on historical asset returns.</cite> The trade-off is that <cite id="41d2a6d8-2,862d0e66-0">the model depends on subjective views and on how much confidence is assigned to them</cite>, so model output can still be highly influenced by human judgment. Put differently, <cite id="41d2a6d8-4">Black-Litterman is more disciplined than ad hoc forecasting, but it does not eliminate subjectivity; it formalizes it.</cite>

## 3) Deep learning / deep reinforcement learning: flexible, nonlinear, and dynamic

Deep learning-based portfolio models differ most sharply from the two classical models on the prediction side. <cite id="c7707502-0">Deep learning architectures can capture temporal dependencies and nonlinear relationships</cite>, which is valuable because financial signals are often regime-dependent, cross-sectional, and nonstationary. Rather than assuming the world can be summarized well by a static mean vector and covariance matrix, <cite id="c7707502-0,ec158d01-0">these models are aimed at learning complex market dynamics directly from data.</cite>

Deep reinforcement learning goes one step further by changing the allocation mechanism itself. Instead of solving a one-shot efficient-frontier problem, <cite id="ec158d01-4">it can construct portfolio strategies in dynamic, complex, large-dimensional markets</cite> and <cite id="ec158d01-5">dynamically allocate funds across assets according to investor objectives.</cite> Because the reward can be designed, <cite id="ec158d01-2">the optimization can target log returns, differential Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, or a unified policy combining several objectives</cite>; <cite id="ec158d01-4">risk aversion and transaction costs can also be embedded directly in the reward.</cite>

The cost of this flexibility is interpretability. <cite id="0e040b10-0">Deep learning methods in finance are widely regarded as black boxes</cite>, which makes it harder to explain why the model prefers certain assets or exposures. That is why <cite id="c7707502-5,0e040b10-0">explainable-AI approaches are now being developed specifically to interpret deep portfolio-management actions and predictions.</cite>

## Core differences across the three dimensions you asked about

### Risk measurement
- <cite id="04722f36-1,04722f36-3">Mean-Variance measures risk primarily as variance.</cite>
- <cite id="862d0e66-0">Black-Litterman typically still feeds into a mean-variance-style optimizer, so its downstream risk measure is often still variance/covariance, even though its return estimates are Bayesian.</cite>
- <cite id="ec158d01-2,ec158d01-4">Deep learning/DRL can optimize against broader risk definitions through the loss or reward function, including Sharpe-like objectives, drawdown, transaction costs, and investor risk aversion.</cite>

### Return prediction
- <cite id="04722f36-4">Mean-Variance usually relies on exogenous estimates of expected returns and covariance.</cite>
- <cite id="41d2a6d8-4,862d0e66-0">Black-Litterman predicts returns by combining equilibrium returns with subjective views and their confidence levels in a Bayesian update.</cite>
- <cite id="c7707502-0">Deep learning estimates returns or allocation signals from data directly, exploiting nonlinear and temporal structure.</cite>

### Asset allocation mechanism
- <cite id="04722f36-1">Mean-Variance allocates by solving a static optimization problem on the efficient frontier.</cite>
- <cite id="862d0e66-0">Black-Litterman also typically allocates through portfolio optimization, but after replacing raw return estimates with blended posterior returns.</cite>
- <cite id="ec158d01-4,ec158d01-5">Deep RL allocates sequentially and dynamically, learning policies that adapt over time rather than solving only a static cross-sectional optimization.</cite>

## Can their strengths be combined?

<cite id="734b6d51-4">Yes—recent work explicitly combines hybrid forecasting with Black-Litterman and reports better return/risk behavior for the resulting portfolios.</cite> More broadly, <cite id="cf417487-2">there are studies that integrate advanced deep learning architectures with traditional financial models to improve portfolio optimization</cite>, and <cite id="c7707502-2,af1e47f3-0">systematic machine-learning portfolio systems are increasingly built by combining recognized analytical techniques rather than relying on a single model family.</cite>

## A practical general-purpose framework

A strong “best-of-all-worlds” framework would usually separate the problem into layers:

### 1. Structural prior
Use a <cite id="41d2a6d8-5,862d0e66-0">Black-Litterman-style equilibrium prior with explicit uncertainty and optional expert views</cite> so the model starts from an economically coherent baseline rather than noisy sample means alone.

### 2. Data-driven predictive overlay
Use <cite id="c7707502-0">deep learning to learn nonlinear and temporal signals</cite> and convert those signals into either return views or tilts. In other words, the neural model need not replace Black-Litterman; it can <cite id="734b6d51-4,cf417487-2">supply the “views” or forecasts that are then regularized by a classical Bayesian portfolio layer.</cite>

### 3. Risk-aware allocator
Use either a <cite id="04722f36-1">mean-variance optimizer when simplicity and transparency matter</cite> or a <cite id="ec158d01-2,ec158d01-4">deep reinforcement learning policy when the problem is dynamic and must account for drawdown, transaction costs, and changing market states.</cite>

### 4. Explainability and controls
Because <cite id="0e040b10-0">deep learning is often black-box</cite>, attach <cite id="c7707502-5,0e040b10-0">XAI tools to explain predictions and portfolio actions</cite>, and keep classical constraints and risk budgets in the optimization layer.

## Bottom line

The models are not simply “old versus new”; they solve different parts of the problem well. <cite id="04722f36-1,04722f36-3">Mean-Variance is transparent and elegant but depends on variance risk and fragile parameter estimates.</cite> <cite id="41d2a6d8-4,862d0e66-0">Black-Litterman improves the return-estimation step by blending equilibrium structure with views, but it still depends on subjective inputs.</cite> <cite id="c7707502-0,0e040b10-0,ec158d01-4">Deep learning and DRL are better at nonlinear prediction and dynamic allocation, but they are harder to interpret and govern.</cite> 

So the most promising general-purpose approach is usually <cite id="734b6d51-4,cf417487-2">hybrid rather than monolithic</cite>: <cite id="41d2a6d8-5,862d0e66-0">use Bayesian structure for priors and uncertainty</cite>, <cite id="c7707502-0">use deep models for forecasting complex patterns</cite>, and <cite id="ec158d01-2,ec158d01-4">use a risk-aware optimization or reinforcement-learning layer for actual allocation under real trading objectives.</cite>

without_preference.text: In the field of FinTech, machine learning algorithms are now widely applied to asset allocation and investment decisions. Examples include classic models like Mean-Variance and Black-Litterman, as well as emerging deep learning models. While these models have shown certain advantages under different market conditions, each also has its limitations. For instance, the Mean-Variance model assumes asset returns follow a normal distribution, which often doesn't align with actual market conditions. The Black-Litterman model relies on subjective view inputs, introducing a degree of subjectivity. Although deep learning models can handle complex non-linear relationships, they suffer from poor interpretability. What are the core differences between these various models in terms of risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation? Is it possible to combine their strengths to build a more general-purpose and effective modeling framework?
without_preference.answer:
## Short answer

<cite id="S21,S11,S31,S34">Mean-Variance, Black-Litterman, and deep-learning portfolio models differ mainly in how they define risk, how they form return expectations, and how directly they map information into portfolio weights.</cite> <cite id="S30,S39,S54">There is unlikely to be one model that dominates in all market regimes, because returns and covariance structures change over time and ML performance is often regime-dependent.</cite>

## 1) Core differences

### Mean-Variance (MV)
<cite id="S21,S27">Mean-Variance optimization chooses portfolios on the efficient frontier by maximizing expected return for a given variance, or minimizing variance for a target expected return.</cite> <cite id="S22,S25">Its core risk measure is variance, so it is exact under normally distributed returns or quadratic utility; otherwise it penalizes upside and downside volatility symmetrically and can miss tail risk and asymmetry.</cite> <cite id="S23,S24,S30">Its main weakness is that expected returns are hard to estimate, sample-mean errors can make optimal weights unstable and concentrated, and static inputs can become suboptimal when markets are time-varying.</cite>

### Black-Litterman (BL)
<cite id="S59,S64">Black-Litterman is best viewed as a Bayesian improvement to the inputs of Markowitz optimization rather than a wholly different allocation objective.</cite> <cite id="S11,S12,S60,S61">It starts from market-implied equilibrium returns, updates them with investor or model views and associated confidence levels, and then typically feeds the posterior returns into a standard variance-covariance quadratic optimizer.</cite> <cite id="S13,S18">This usually produces more diversified portfolios and reduces sensitivity to estimation noise relative to naive Mean-Variance optimization.</cite> <cite id="S8,S16,S19,S63">Its limitations are that posterior returns depend materially on the specified views, their confidence calibration, and the quality of the covariance input.</cite>

### Deep learning / end-to-end ML
<cite id="S31,S32">Deep models can learn nonlinear relationships and temporal patterns from technical, fundamental, alternative, and textual data, often using architectures such as LSTMs and Transformers.</cite> <cite id="S33,S34">They can be used in a two-stage pipeline that predicts returns, volatilities, or scores before optimization, or in an end-to-end way where a network or reinforcement-learning policy outputs portfolio weights directly.</cite> <cite id="S38">Their risk handling is flexible and is usually imposed through the loss or reward function, for example with volatility penalties, drawdown limits, or CVaR-aware objectives.</cite> <cite id="S35,S36,S37,S39">Their main drawbacks are poor interpretability, high data requirements, overfitting risk, sensitivity to nonstationarity, and the gap between backtest and live performance when costs and liquidity are ignored.</cite>

## 2) Difference by dimension

### Risk measurement
<cite id="S22,S25,S26">MV uses variance as the canonical risk measure, though many practical extensions replace or augment it with semivariance, CVaR, or lower partial moments in non-Gaussian markets.</cite> <cite id="S61,S63">Canonical BL usually inherits the same variance-covariance risk model as MV, so its main contribution is not a new definition of risk but a better way to form expected-return inputs.</cite> <cite id="S6,S38">Deep models are more flexible because they can optimize directly against volatility, drawdown, VaR/CVaR, or custom utility-based rewards.</cite>

### Return prediction
<cite id="S23,S24">MV normally relies on externally estimated expected returns, and errors in those estimates are a major source of instability.</cite> <cite id="S11,S12,S62">BL shrinks return estimates toward market equilibrium and then tilts them with views weighted by confidence, which acts as Bayesian regularization.</cite> <cite id="S31,S42">Deep learning can generate richer forecasts from complex and heterogeneous data, and Bayesian deep learning or ensembles can also provide uncertainty estimates.</cite>

### Asset allocation
<cite id="S21,S27">MV allocates assets through a transparent efficient-frontier optimization.</cite> <cite id="S13,S60">BL typically uses the same optimization machinery after replacing naive expected returns with posterior returns, which helps reduce corner solutions.</cite> <cite id="S33,S34">Deep approaches either pass predictions into a classical optimizer or learn the allocation policy directly.</cite> <cite id="S47">Compared with monolithic end-to-end reinforcement learning, modular pipelines are easier to audit, stress test, and align with institutional constraints.</cite>

## 3) Can their strengths be combined?

<cite id="S5,S43,S46">Yes. Recent research explicitly advocates hybrid, modular portfolio systems that use machine learning for signal extraction and classical Bayesian or optimization layers for final allocation.</cite> <cite id="S17,S44">A particularly natural combination is to let ML generate alpha signals or relative views and convert forecast uncertainty into Black-Litterman confidence levels.</cite> <cite id="S45,S48">Those posterior returns can then be passed into a constrained Mean-Variance, CVaR, or distributionally robust optimizer to control turnover, transaction costs, and model risk.</cite> <cite id="S40,S50">Interpretability and governance can be strengthened further by using factor structures, attention or attribution methods, and multi-objective optimization that balances return, risk, turnover, and explainability.</cite>

## 4) A practical general-purpose framework

<cite id="S46">A strong general-purpose design is a layered architecture with separate prediction, uncertainty, risk, and optimization modules.</cite> <cite id="S31,S32,S33">In the prediction layer, combine linear factor signals with deep models to estimate expected returns, volatility, or relative rankings.</cite> <cite id="S42,S44,S49">In the uncertainty layer, use ensembles or Bayesian deep learning to estimate forecast dispersion and translate it into calibrated Black-Litterman confidence levels, while avoiding overconfident views.</cite> <cite id="S11,S17,S43">In the prior/posterior layer, anchor the system with market-implied equilibrium returns and blend them with ML-generated views through Black-Litterman.</cite> <cite id="S6,S45,S48">In the allocation layer, optimize under variance and tail-risk controls such as CVaR, with explicit transaction-cost, liquidity, and turnover constraints, ideally using robust or distributionally robust optimization.</cite> <cite id="S51,S52,S53,S58">For robustness, add regime-aware logic or mixture-of-experts switching and stress-test the framework across crises, because both expected returns and covariance structures are time-varying.</cite>

## 5) Bottom line

<cite id="S2,S4,S41">A hybrid system can be more stable than plain Mean-Variance, more disciplined than purely subjective Black-Litterman, and more robust than a pure end-to-end deep model because it combines market priors, uncertainty-aware forecasts, and explicit constrained optimization.</cite> <cite id="S39,S49,S57">But it still will not be universally optimal: confidence can be miscalibrated, regime changes can be abrupt, and all adaptive systems remain exposed to model risk.</cite>

<cite id="S46,S47">So the most effective answer is usually not to choose one model family exclusively, but to build a modular framework</cite> <cite id="S17,S43,S45">that uses ML for return/view generation, Black-Litterman for Bayesian blending, and robust or tail-aware optimization for final asset allocation.</cite>

query.answer: Yes. A practical way to do this is to define a <cite id="e7a8b0ae-0,b8ffe1d2-0">standardized backtesting/evaluation pipeline</cite> and score every strategy on four layers: <cite id="2c04a86b-0,2c04a86b-3">statistically adjusted performance</cite>, <cite id="b8ffe1d2-5,b8ffe1d2-1">implementation realism</cite>, <cite id="40a0aed8-0,7cb362e8-6">out-of-sample robustness via walk-forward testing</cite>, and <cite id="40a0aed8-6,3bf2c2c7-9">adaptability across market regimes</cite>. Concretely, the framework should require a common data universe and identical execution assumptions; report net returns together with costs, spreads, slippage, and turnover because <cite id="b8ffe1d2-5">transaction costs and slippage can significantly affect strategy performance</cite> and <cite id="b8ffe1d2-1">costs, spreads, slippage, or turnover should be explicitly modeled or reported</cite>. For headline performance, use Sharpe but adjust it with the <cite id="2c04a86b-0,2c04a86b-3">Deflated Sharpe Ratio, which corrects for non-normality, selection effects, and backtest overfitting</cite>. Validation should be based on <cite id="40a0aed8-0,7cb362e8-6,f63adf98-0">walk-forward / out-of-sample testing</cite> because it <cite id="40a0aed8-0">is designed to mitigate overfitting and lookahead bias</cite>. Finally, since <cite id="40a0aed8-6,3bf2c2c7-9">financial markets are non-stationary and can abruptly change behavior across regimes</cite>, each strategy should be broken out by bull/bear, high/low volatility, and crisis/recovery subperiods, then compared on stability rather than only average return. In short, the benchmark can be built as a reproducible “quant strategy card” combining net performance, risk-adjusted significance, execution frictions, walk-forward robustness, and regime-specific stability into one common reporting standard.

fully_underspecified.text: Could we develop a general evaluation framework to compare different strategies across multiple dimensions?
fully_underspecified.answer: Yes. <cite id="P1">Multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) is specifically designed to compare alternatives across multiple criteria and to aggregate criterion-level data into indicators of overall option performance.</cite> A general framework would be: <cite id="P4,P26">define the decision context and stakeholders, identify the strategies/options, choose the evaluation criteria, measure each option’s performance on those criteria, assign criterion weights that reflect stakeholder preferences, combine scores and weights to produce an overall assessment, and then examine the results with sensitivity analysis.</cite> The criteria set should be <cite id="P9">exhaustive, cohesive, non-redundant, and measurable</cite>, and the dimensions can be tailored to the problem—for example <cite id="P37,P38">cost, effectiveness, equity, organizational impact, and evidence uncertainty</cite>. For scoring, <cite id="P16">a weighted-sum model is a simple default because it multiplies each criterion score by a normalized weight and sums the results</cite>, but <cite id="P22,P45">other MCDA methods such as TOPSIS may be preferable depending on the decision context, data quality, and desired output, since there is no single universally optimal method</cite>. Finally, <cite id="P30,P36">robustness should be checked with sensitivity analysis because uncertainty in criteria weights, option performance, and method parameters can change rankings</cite>.

## Overall picture

Across the leading global consulting firms, AI activity has shifted from pure advisory into <cite id="S171">named, reusable enterprise platforms</cite>, <cite id="S136">embedded service capabilities</cite>, and <cite id="S42">AI-assisted delivery engines for consultants</cite>. The common pattern is an alliance-led model: <cite id="S174">Accenture is building new business groups with NVIDIA around process reinvention, simulation, sovereign AI and agentic architecture</cite>; <cite id="S178">Deloitte is scaling alliances with NVIDIA, AWS, Google Cloud, IBM, Microsoft, Oracle and Salesforce</cite>; <cite id="S182">EY is expanding AI services on solutions from Dell Technologies, Microsoft, SAP, ServiceNow and Thomson Reuters</cite>; <cite id="S21">KPMG and Microsoft announced a $2 billion investment in AI and cloud services</cite>; and <cite id="S126">Capgemini and Mistral AI are collaborating to define strategy, identify use cases, and implement and scale generative AI</cite>.

A second shared theme is workforce scaling. <cite id="S11">PwC tied its US$1 billion program to upskilling its entire global workforce of 364,000</cite>; <cite id="S64">Deloitte’s GenAI academy is set to train 120,000+ professionals</cite>; <cite id="S24">KPMG and Microsoft said they would train KPMG’s global workforce of more than 265,000 in foundational and advanced AI skills</cite>; <cite id="S43">IBM is upskilling 160,000 consultants in AI and planned to add 1,000 specialized AI consultants</cite>; <cite id="S46">Capgemini aims to train 50,000 employees in generative AI</cite>; and <cite id="S31">BCG says it has trained over 30,000 consultants and enabling teams</cite>.

## Firm-by-firm summary

### Accenture

<cite id="S1">Accenture plans to invest $3 billion in its Data & AI practice over three years</cite>, and <cite id="S2">it announced plans to double its AI talent to 80,000 people through hiring, acquisitions and training</cite>. On the product side, <cite id="S171">Accenture AI Refinery is designed to help organizations turn AI ambition into action at speed and scale</cite>; <cite id="S172">it is built on NVIDIA AI foundry and includes AI agent foundation models, architecture models and industry models that can be customized with company data</cite>; and <cite id="S173">organizations can use it to rapidly create 12 industry agent solutions</cite>.  

Accenture also continues to industrialize delivery: <cite id="S175">it says it is building on 1,450 patents and pending patent applications related to AI, plus hundreds of client solutions spanning marketing, customer service, software engineering, digital manufacturing and life sciences R&D</cite>. In client work, <cite id="S51">S&P Global and Accenture launched a procurement and supply-chain GenAI solution that has already delivered more than a 10% reduction in overall supplier costs, more than a 25% increase in user adoption, and about a 70% reduction in onboarding cycle time</cite>; <cite id="S52">Marriott International is using a GenAI tool with Accenture and Salesforce to improve customer service</cite>; and <cite id="S55">PUMA used GenWizard to create copy and images in less than an hour instead of the eight weeks it previously took</cite>.

### Deloitte

<cite id="S61">Deloitte announced plans to invest more than $1.4 billion globally over three years in technology, training and alliances to expand its GenAI capabilities</cite>. Its current direction is strongly platform and alliance driven: <cite id="S178">the firm is scaling strategic alliances with major technology organizations including NVIDIA, AWS, Google Cloud, IBM, Microsoft, Oracle and Salesforce</cite>, while <cite id="S65">also advancing market-ready assets for broad client use</cite>.  

On outputs, <cite id="S136">Deloitte’s globally available generative AI capabilities, Zora AI, are embedded throughout its services, software and infrastructure</cite>; <cite id="S137">Zora AI provides ready-to-deploy AI agents that can perceive, reason and act</cite>; and <cite id="S140">its initial suites target finance, human capital, supply chain, procurement, sales and marketing, and customer service</cite>. Deloitte also highlights practical delivery examples: <cite id="S56">it reports an AI-powered contact-center transformation that deployed more than 50 virtual experts to assist agents in real time with next-best-action guidance and generative call summaries</cite>. On talent, <cite id="S64">Deloitte’s GenAI academy, supported by its alliances, will train more than 120,000 professionals</cite>.

### PwC

<cite id="S12">PwC announced a US$1 billion investment over three years in generative AI</cite> to <cite id="S69">transform how it works, deliver value to clients, and scale new AI-powered products and services</cite>. The workforce element is unusually broad: <cite id="S11">PwC says the program is tied to upskilling its entire global workforce of 364,000 partners and staff</cite>, <cite id="S14">with AI training for all staff and specialized modules by role</cite>; <cite id="S15">it reports having trained more than 95% of US employees on responsible GenAI and more than 291,000 people globally on AI fundamentals</cite>.  

Its internal and external tooling is also becoming productized. <cite id="S142">ChatPwC is a US-market GenAI tool that uses GPT-4o plus PwC’s proprietary tax, audit and assurance methodologies and secure internal firm data</cite>, and <cite id="S141">nearly 70,000 US employees have access to it</cite>. For clients, <cite id="S143">PwC says enterprise clients are using its secure and scalable GenAI toolkit</cite>; <cite id="S67">there are already more than 150 client pilots and deployments underway</cite>; and <cite id="S144">these include software development, product innovation, customer operations and business-process efficiency</cite>, with <cite id="S68">use cases such as draft-content generation, document summarization, data analysis and workflow automation</cite>. Operationally, <cite id="S145">PwC is also creating GenAI pods that pair AI/data specialists with industry and functional experts</cite>.

### EY

<cite id="S17">EY announced a US$1.4 billion investment in AI and launched the EY.ai platform</cite>. The program combines platforms, governance and capability building: <cite id="S16">the investment included the launch of EY.ai EYQ, a secure large language model, and the EY Fabric data intelligence solution</cite>; <cite id="S20">EY says the effort centers on four focus areas—client value creation, equipping EY people with AI skills and mindsets, EY’s own AI-powered transformation, and managing AI risk</cite>; and <cite id="S18">it includes a comprehensive learning program with prompt-engineering training, plus new EY Badges and curricula developed with Microsoft and learning institutions</cite>.  

In service delivery, <cite id="S185">EY.ai lets organizations combine AI models and capabilities including Microsoft Azure OpenAI Service and EY Q</cite>, while <cite id="S19">EY Fabric gives teams and clients access to trillions of data signals in a secure integrated environment</cite>. EY also emphasizes trust and front-office use cases: <cite id="S183">EY.ai Confidence embeds governance, risk management and compliance from strategy through execution</cite>; <cite id="S181">the EY–Microsoft alliance is applying AI to personalized customer care, sales growth and employee experience</cite>; and <cite id="S72">EY says its human-centered AI solutions are already deployed in life sciences, consumer products, retail and financial services</cite>. Internally, <cite id="S73">EYQ is intended to support more than 400,000 EY people</cite>.

### KPMG

<cite id="S21">KPMG and Microsoft announced a $2 billion investment in artificial intelligence and cloud services</cite>, with <cite id="S22">incremental investment in technology, people and processes to accelerate AI transformation for KPMG and its clients</cite>. Client-facing priorities are practical and domain-specific: <cite id="S23">KPMG says its professionals will help clients modernize cloud environments and create domain-specific AI solutions</cite>; <cite id="S187">KPMG firms can quickly develop and deploy generative-AI solutions using Microsoft Azure OpenAI Service and Azure AI</cite>; and <cite id="S188">targeted applications include digital assistants, AI-powered virtual experts, search, knowledge management and workflow automation</cite>.  

KPMG’s distinctive emphasis is AI assurance. <cite id="S134">Its Trusted AI framework is positioned as a cornerstone of KPMG’s services and solutions</cite>, helping ensure <cite id="S186">AI systems are reliable, accountable and compliant with evolving regulations</cite>. This was extended when <cite id="S131">KPMG launched a suite of AI trust services</cite>, including <cite id="S132">AI management system, AI model validation and AI controls validation offerings</cite>. On talent, <cite id="S24">KPMG and Microsoft said they would train KPMG’s global workforce of more than 265,000 in foundational and advanced AI skills</cite>.

### McKinsey / QuantumBlack

McKinsey’s AI work is concentrated in QuantumBlack. <cite id="S26">QuantumBlack says McKinsey has helped clients with AI since 2009 and now has 7,000 practitioners spanning data engineering, architecture, data science, product development, machine-learning engineering, AI strategy and risk</cite>. Its delivery model is both advisory and build oriented: <cite id="S149">it offers end-to-end services covering AI strategy, technical use cases and AI governance</cite>, <cite id="S81">scales solutions through a discover-design-develop-deliver “4D” approach</cite>, and <cite id="S30">works with a partner ecosystem of more than 100 strategic technology and data partners</cite>.  

The firm also has notable internal AI productization. <cite id="S29">Lilli is a GenAI solution developed by McKinsey and rolled out firmwide to 45,000 colleagues</cite>, and <cite id="S147">it now sits within a broader suite of GenAI tools and human/digital capabilities</cite>. For application scenarios, <cite id="S82">QuantumBlack highlights work across consumer, energy, financial services, healthcare, industrials, private equity, public sector, technology, telecom and travel/logistics</cite>. On talent development, <cite id="S148">McKinsey promotes a Data and AI Academy for practical, experiential learning</cite>.

### BCG

<cite id="S31">Since 2020, BCG says it has invested over $2 billion in AI, built a team of more than 7,000 experts, and trained over 30,000 consultants and enabling teams</cite>. The strategic direction is to treat AI as a staged transformation: <cite id="S92">BCG supports implementation from data and digital transformation, to AI at scale, and ultimately GenAI</cite>, while <cite id="S151">helping clients identify where AI and GenAI can create competitive edge and how to put new leadership and operating models in place</cite>. Productization happens largely through <cite id="S116">a portfolio of AI products and services powered by BCG X</cite>.  

BCG also showcases varied application scenarios and client outputs. <cite id="S156">For Indigo Ag, GenAI is simplifying field analysis and helping farmers quickly access agronomic information</cite>; <cite id="S157">BCG partnered with Blue Yonder to create a generative-AI demand-planning solution for supply chain</cite>; <cite id="S158">Xylem uses AI to help customers optimize water use and conserve resources</cite>; and <cite id="S159">NASA’s Air Traffic Management Exploration project is using AI in a decade-long collaboration with BCG to unlock benefits for air travelers</cite>. On governance and ecosystem leadership, <cite id="S160">BCG says it leads the World Economic Forum’s AI Governance Alliance involving 600+ members</cite>.

### Bain & Company

Bain’s recent AI activity is centered on deep partnership with OpenAI. <cite id="S38">Bain launched an OpenAI Center of Excellence in February 2024</cite>; <cite id="S39">the center is co-located with OpenAI in San Francisco and includes strategy experts, AI technologists, and specialists in content creation, design and software engineering</cite>; and <cite id="S113">it is already set up to serve customers from top global retailers, consumer goods companies and financial institutions</cite>. Bain describes the alliance as helping clients in three dimensions: <cite id="S112">embedding and deploying AI system-wide, reimagining workflows and processes, and exploring new growth opportunities enabled by AI advances</cite>.  

In terms of application scenarios, <cite id="S97">Bain highlights customer service, sales and marketing, software coding and internal knowledge management as active GenAI use cases</cite>. It also points to measurable outputs: <cite id="S163">Bain cites up to a 20% increase in coding productivity, a 35% reduction in customer-service operating costs, and a 25% improvement in issue resolution</cite>. For talent and change management, <cite id="S164">one Bain-supported cross-functional team trained more than 3,000 frontline, managerial and back-office employees on AI and advanced analytics</cite>.

### IBM Consulting

IBM’s AI consulting push is anchored in watsonx and AI-assisted delivery. <cite id="S42">IBM announced a Consulting Advantage center powered by watsonx that combines specialized AI assistants, methods and tools for consultants</cite>, and <cite id="S121">says the platform will use IBM’s full technology stack to improve delivery speed, productivity and consistency</cite>. The offering is meant to be reusable and multi-model: <cite id="S122">it will include purpose-built AI assistants on IBM Granite models and partner models for delivery, sales and solutions</cite>, while <cite id="S123">watsonx itself is IBM’s portfolio of AI products for accelerating the impact of generative AI in core workflows</cite>.  

IBM also provides clearer commercial output metrics than many peers. <cite id="S41">IBM said that since launching watsonx in July 2023, it had signed more than $500 million in bookings for watsonx business over the fourth quarter</cite>, and <cite id="S124">IBM Consulting estimates the Consulting Advantage platform can produce 50% productivity gains on common services such as application modernization</cite>. On people, <cite id="S43">IBM is upskilling 160,000 consultants in AI and planned to add 1,000 specialized AI consultants before the end of 2024</cite>. Example application scenarios include <cite id="S167">a generative AI assistant for WPP</cite>, <cite id="S168">NatWest’s AI virtual assistant for customer service</cite>, and <cite id="S170">Bouygues Telecom’s digital factory to transform customer experience</cite>.
