fully_underspecified.answer:
## Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: how common is it, and why does it matter?

In eukaryotes, horizontal gene transfer (HGT)—the movement of genes between species outside ordinary parent-to-offspring inheritance—is <cite id="S1">generally viewed as uncommon in multicellular eukaryotes compared with prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes</cite>. Even so, it is now clear that <cite id="S41">both eukaryote-to-eukaryote and prokaryote-to-eukaryote HGT are indisputable</cite>, and conservative genome surveys suggest that <cite id="S110">roughly 0.3%–0.8% of genes in eukaryotic genomes may derive from HGT</cite>, although <cite id="S111">such percentages are highly sensitive to sampling, contamination filters, hidden paralogy, and differential gene loss</cite>. The safest summary is that HGT is usually a <cite id="S118">small but evolutionarily meaningful signal in eukaryotes</cite>, not a dominant force on the scale seen in bacteria.

A crucial exception is endosymbiotic gene transfer. The origin of plastids and mitochondria involved <cite id="S64">extensive transfer of genes from those bacterial endosymbionts to the host nucleus</cite>, and <cite id="S4">plastid acquisition in particular involved large-scale endosymbiotic gene transfer</cite>. In that sense, the largest bacterial contribution to many eukaryotic genomes may come not from routine HGT between free-living species, but from <cite id="S68">massive gene transfer associated with organelle evolution</cite>.

## Why is HGT rarer in eukaryotes than in prokaryotes?

The main reason is that successful eukaryotic HGT faces more barriers. For a transferred gene to shape the evolution of a multicellular eukaryote, it must <cite id="S11">enter the relevant hereditary cells, evade genome-defense mechanisms and drift, and eventually become fixed in the population</cite>. In animals especially, <cite id="W1">DNA entering a somatic cell is not enough; to affect species evolution, the foreign material must enter a germ cell and be inherited</cite>.

There are also molecular barriers after DNA arrival. A foreign gene must be domesticated into a eukaryotic genome, and that often requires <cite id="S13">compatible promoters, intron processing, codon usage, and appropriate subcellular targeting</cite>. The genes that persist are therefore biased toward <cite id="S12">“operational” functions rather than deeply networked informational functions</cite>, and many retained cases involve <cite id="S20">metabolism, stress responses, and interactions with the environment</cite>.

A further reason HGT in eukaryotes often seems rarer than initially claimed is methodological. <cite id="S14">Contamination, hidden paralogy, and differential gene loss can mimic HGT</cite>, and <cite id="S16">some early claims of extensive HGT in animals were revised downward after better assemblies and contamination filtering</cite>. That is why the strongest cases today are those supported not just by sequence similarity, but by phylogeny, genomic context, expression, and phenotype.

## When does eukaryotic HGT happen most often?

The clearest pattern is ecological opportunity plus selective payoff. <cite id="S17">Endosymbiotic and parasitic intimate associations recurrently increase opportunities for DNA transfer</cite>, while <cite id="S35">phagotrophic protists that engulf prey appear especially prone to acquiring foreign genes</cite>. In microbial eukaryotes, <cite id="S97">the lack of a segregated germline and often large effective population sizes may make adaptive foreign genes easier to spread</cite>.

That helps explain why the strongest evidence comes from lineages living in microbe-rich, stressful, or highly intimate biological settings. <cite id="S39">Anaerobic protists and fungi often show elevated numbers of bacterial-derived metabolic genes</cite>, <cite id="S137">extreme habitats may increase both exposure to microbial donors and selection for stress-tolerance functions</cite>, and <cite id="S103">in anaerobic gut fungi, most donors are bacteria sharing the same gut habitat</cite>. Put simply, eukaryotic HGT seems most likely when species are in close physical contact with donor DNA and when the acquired genes solve an immediate ecological problem.

## Best-studied examples where transferred genes appear beneficial

### 1) Microbial eukaryotes and extremophiles

Among microbial eukaryotes, evidence for HGT is especially strong. <cite id="S31">Comparative genomics finds the strongest evidence in microbial eukaryotes and fungi, often linked to metabolic innovation</cite>, and in protists <cite id="S94">acquired genes commonly support central and specialized metabolism</cite>. In anaerobic protists, HGT has repeatedly added <cite id="S95">genes involved in fermentation, hydrogen production, and oxygen-stress defense</cite>.

A well-known case is the red algal lineage *Galdieria* (within the Cyanidiales). Genome analyses indicate that it carries <cite id="S24">numerous bacterial- and archaeal-derived genes contributing to heavy-metal detoxification and heterotrophic growth</cite>, and these genes are thought to have <cite id="S135">helped polyextremophilic red algae colonize hot, acidic, metal-rich environments</cite>. Even though <cite id="S136">the absolute number of HGTs in Galdieria is debated</cite>, a smaller core of adaptive transfers appears robust.

### 2) Fungi, especially anaerobic gut fungi

Fungi are one of the best-supported eukaryotic groups for recurrent, adaptive HGT. A kingdom-wide analysis showed that fungal HGT-derived genes are <cite id="W2">enriched in peptidases, carbohydrate metabolism, and xenobiotic metabolism</cite>, and that <cite id="W2">ecological habitats and fungal lifestyles shape fungal HGT patterns</cite>. More broadly, fungal transfers can confer <cite id="W2">host adaptation, nutrient assimilation, and pathogenicity</cite>.

Anaerobic gut fungi (*Neocallimastigomycota*) may be the clearest non-endosymbiotic case of extensive adaptive HGT in eukaryotes. In these fungi, HGT supplied <cite id="S102">numerous enzymes and metabolic traits required for survival in the herbivore gut</cite>, including <cite id="S104">functions in polysaccharide breakdown, fermentation, detoxification, and adaptation to anoxia</cite>. Because many of these events appear to predate diversification of modern genera, <cite id="S105">transfer may have facilitated a major habitat transition early in the lineage</cite>.

### 3) Plant-parasitic nematodes

Among animals, plant-parasitic nematodes provide one of the strongest adaptive HGT examples. They have repeatedly acquired <cite id="S22">microbial genes encoding plant cell wall-degrading enzymes</cite>, and these genes are <cite id="S81">central to the origin of plant parasitism because they enable cell wall modification, tissue invasion, and feeding-site establishment</cite>. Many such genes show <cite id="S82">duplication and diversification within nematode genomes</cite>, implying long-term retention and refinement after acquisition.

This case is significant because it links HGT to a major ecological transition. The repeated recruitment of such genes in different nematode clades <cite id="S83">illustrates how HGT can trigger major niche shifts in animals</cite>. It is also one of the better functionally supported systems, since <cite id="S84">expression studies and RNA interference support the role of some acquired genes in parasitism</cite>.

### 4) Aphids

The aphid carotenoid pathway is a classic example of a functional animal HGT. Aphids possess <cite id="S21">carotenoid biosynthesis genes of fungal origin</cite>, and these genes are <cite id="S27">expressed by the insect and underlie endogenous carotenoid production</cite>, which is unusual among animals. Their expression contributes to <cite id="S89">pigmentation differences that may affect interactions with predators, parasitoids, and environmental stress</cite>.

This case matters because it shows that foreign genes can do more than sit passively in a genome. In aphids they became <cite id="S90">integrated, expressed, and phenotypically important</cite>. Still, even this famous case should be viewed as <cite id="S93">exceptional rather than typical for animals</cite>.

### 5) Coffee berry borer

Another animal example with a direct ecological link is the coffee berry borer. It carries <cite id="S23">a bacterial mannanase acquired by HGT that allows digestion of galactomannan-rich coffee beans and is highly expressed in the gut</cite>. This is a strong illustration of how one acquired gene can help exploit a specialized food source.

### 6) Bdelloid rotifers

Bdelloid rotifers remain one of the most discussed animal lineages for HGT. They appear to harbor <cite id="S76">substantial horizontally acquired gene content</cite>, and many foreign genes are <cite id="S73">expressed and enriched in carbohydrate metabolism, stress response, and antioxidant defense</cite>. Proposed explanations include <cite id="S75">asexual reproduction and repeated exposure to environmental DNA</cite>, while <cite id="S74">desiccation-linked DNA repair has been proposed but does not fully explain the pattern</cite>.

This is an important but still debated system. The basic point—that bdelloids have unusually many non-metazoan-like genes—is fairly secure, but <cite id="S72">estimates vary with methods and assembly quality</cite>. So bdelloids are best treated as a compelling lineage for elevated HGT, not as a simple universal model for how animal HGT works.

## Systems that are less clear, less frequent, or less well studied

Evidence is much weaker in vertebrates. Reviews conclude that <cite id="S32">well-supported examples in vertebrates are extremely rare</cite>, and the human case is a cautionary tale: <cite id="W1">a claim that 145 human genes came from prokaryotic HGT was later argued to reflect methodological artifacts, with no evidence supporting HGT in the human genome</cite>. So in vertebrates, rarity may be real, but it is also reinforced by the high evidentiary bar needed to exclude error.

Plants occupy an intermediate position. On the one hand, <cite id="S56">plant HGT is most convincingly documented in mitochondrial genomes</cite>, and <cite id="S58">natural grafting and haustorial connections can create bridges that facilitate DNA movement</cite>. On the other hand, <cite id="S57">clearly functional host-derived nuclear genes in parasitic plants are modest in number</cite>, and <cite id="S62">stringent phylogenomic surveys of land plants recover only a small number of robust HGT candidates</cite>.

There are also special mechanistic plant cases. <cite id="S128">Several plant species carry Agrobacterium T-DNA sequences in their nuclear genomes</cite>, showing that bacterial-to-plant transfer can happen naturally, and <cite id="S130">Agrobacterium provides a mechanistically well-understood route for DNA delivery into plant nuclei</cite>. But these examples remain <cite id="S131">exceptions rather than evidence of frequent routine nuclear HGT across land plants</cite>.

## Do transferred genes usually confer benefits?

The best answer is: sometimes clearly, but not usually by default. Reviews emphasize that <cite id="W1">many transferred non-mobile protein-coding genes are likely neutral or detrimental</cite>, while only some are linked to functions such as <cite id="W1">immunity, metabolism, and anti-microbial or anti-pathogen responses</cite>. More generally, <cite id="S126">foreign genes may begin as neutral or weakly deleterious, with only a small fraction later co-opted for beneficial roles</cite>.

The strongest adaptive claims are those backed by both evolutionary and functional evidence. <cite id="S121">Adaptive interpretations are strongest when foreign genes are integrated into eukaryotic expression, expressed in relevant tissues or conditions, and associated with fitness-related phenotypes</cite>. At present, though, <cite id="S120">only a subset of reported eukaryotic HGTs have direct functional evidence</cite>, and <cite id="S122">for many candidates the proposed benefit remains plausible rather than proven</cite>.

## Overall assessment

A balanced conclusion is that HGT in eukaryotes is real, important, and highly uneven. It is <cite id="S40">a small but non-negligible component of many eukaryotic genomes</cite>, but it becomes much more prominent in certain lineages—especially <cite id="S31">microbial eukaryotes and fungi</cite>, and in special animal cases such as <cite id="S81">plant-parasitic nematodes</cite> or <cite id="S90">aphids</cite>. Its rarity in many multicellular eukaryotes is likely explained by <cite id="S11">heredity barriers, genome defense, and fixation hurdles</cite> together with <cite id="S13">the difficulty of integrating foreign genes into complex eukaryotic regulation</cite>.

So the “interesting reason” behind eukaryotic HGT is probably not one single adaptation, but a combination of opportunity and filtering. DNA transfer opportunities are increased by <cite id="S17">symbiosis, parasitism, and intimate ecological contact</cite>, while long-term retention favors genes that <cite id="S119">mediate environmental interaction or metabolism</cite>. In that sense, HGT in eukaryotes is uncommon not because it never happens, but because most transfers fail—and the few that persist are the ones that solve a real ecological problem.

citations.fact: The occurrence of HGTs and their evolutionary significance in eukaryotes has only recently started to be considered, and HGT in eukaryotes is far less common than in bacteria and varies between groups.

Within eukaryotes, protists and fungi are more prone to gaining genes by HGT than metazoans, so HGT appears to be a small but significant player rather than a dominant force in microbial eukaryote evolution.

That said, the best-supported cases show real evolutionary importance: across the green lineage, recently sequenced plant genomes have revealed hundreds of HGTs, including widespread microbe–plant and plant–plant transfers, with impacts on plant adaptation and functional diversification.

So the interesting evolutionary story is not that eukaryotes never exchange genes, but that successful transfers are rare because they must overcome substantial mechanistic and regulatory barriers; when they do succeed, they can open new niches or accelerate adaptation.

A likely reason it is rarer in eukaryotes is that transferred genes face extra barriers to becoming functional, including spliceosomal introns, the need to work within more connected cellular networks, and—in practice—limited opportunity for stable transfer.

In fungi, the ToxA virulence gene was horizontally transferred among three wheat pathogens, and this transfer has a direct negative impact on global wheat yields, showing that single transferred genes can rapidly reshape ecological interactions.

In animals, bdelloid rotifers are a classic exception: they carry an unusually high proportion of horizontally transferred non-metazoan genes, including genes linked to toxin degradation, antioxidant biosynthesis, and metabolism, suggesting clear functional benefits.

Overall, the current picture is that eukaryotic HGT is genuine, unevenly distributed, and most consequential when it supplies ready-made functions—especially metabolic, stress-tolerance, pathogenicity, or host-interaction traits—that would be difficult to evolve quickly from scratch.

without_preference.text: Exploring Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT) in Plants and Animals (Non-Microbial Systems)
without_preference.answer:
## Overview

<cite id="016103e5-7">Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is the non-sexual movement of genetic information between genomes.</cite> In multicellular eukaryotes, <cite id="603ceb78-0">HGT was long considered a rare, anecdotal phenomenon that was unlikely to be a major evolutionary force</cite>, but <cite id="603ceb78-0">recent genomic work has shown that HGT does occur in plants</cite> and <cite id="3aeb14ee-0">is increasingly described between bacteria and animals as well</cite>.

## HGT in plants

The case for HGT is especially strong in plants. <cite id="53e9952f-5">A recent plant review describes the widespread occurrence of both microbe–plant HGT and plant–plant HGT</cite>, and <cite id="a69d7435-9">the strongest evidence for plant-to-plant HGT is between parasitic plants and their hosts</cite>. A likely reason is biological intimacy: <cite id="60cdf60a-0">parasitic plants form vascular connections with hosts through a haustorium that enables transfer of water, nutrients, proteins, and mRNAs</cite>, and <cite id="53e9952f-1">these direct host–parasite connections provide excellent examples of how transfers are facilitated by intimate association</cite>.

A classic plant example involves bacteria. <cite id="53e9952f-3">A remarkable and well-studied example of HGT is the interaction between the soil bacterium *Agrobacterium tumefaciens* and plants</cite>. The best-known natural case is sweet potato: <cite id="d32f79f3-1">the genome of cultivated sweet potato contains *Agrobacterium* T-DNAs with expressed genes</cite>, making it <cite id="d32f79f3-1">an example of a naturally transgenic food crop</cite>.

## HGT in animals

In animals, the evidence is real but generally narrower and more uneven than in plants. <cite id="3aeb14ee-0">Horizontally inherited transfers between bacteria and animals have the potential to influence animal evolution</cite>, and <cite id="3aeb14ee-0">many reported cases occur in intimate symbioses, especially between endosymbionts and invertebrate hosts such as insects and nematodes</cite>. Reviews of arthropods further suggest that <cite id="d71eb3f9-5">horizontally acquired genes often functionally diversify in arthropod recipients, enabling colonization of more host plant species</cite>.

A striking recent example is the whitefly. <cite id="35003aa7-0">Researchers reported the first known case of horizontal gene transfer between a plant and an animal in the whitefly (*Bemisia tabaci*)</cite>. Functionally, <cite id="35003aa7-3">the transferred BtPMaT1 protein detoxifies plant phenolic glucosides that plants normally use for defense against insect herbivores</cite>, showing that some transferred genes are not just present but adaptive.

## How common is it, really?

The current picture is nuanced. On one hand, <cite id="a69d7435-5">HGT is now widely accepted as occurring in eukaryotes, including plants</cite>, and <cite id="a69d7435-0">it is increasingly described between bacteria and animals</cite>. On the other hand, <cite id="a69d7435-3">HGT events in eukaryotes are still considered rare, particularly in mammals</cite>, and <cite id="a69d7435-1">contaminating sequences from other species are a major source of false positives</cite>. 

## Bottom line

<cite id="603ceb78-0">HGT in non-microbial systems is no longer viewed as impossible or merely anecdotal</cite>. The strongest, cleanest evidence is in plants—especially <cite id="a69d7435-9">parasitic plant–host systems</cite> and <cite id="d32f79f3-1">natural *Agrobacterium* transfers such as those in sweet potato</cite>—while in animals the best-supported cases are concentrated in <cite id="3aeb14ee-0">invertebrates with intimate microbial associations</cite> and a few remarkable exceptions such as <cite id="35003aa7-0">plant-to-insect transfer in whitefly</cite>. Overall, HGT in plants and animals appears to be <cite id="a69d7435-3">real but far less pervasive than in microbes</cite>, and its study requires careful filtering of <cite id="a69d7435-1">contamination and other false positives</cite>.

questions.original_query: In ecology, how do birds achieve precise location and direction navigation during migration? What cues and disturbances influence this process?

query.text: In ecology, how do birds achieve precise location and direction navigation during migration? What cues and disturbances influence this process?
query.answer: \boxed{<cite id="48eab178-0,3988fa9c-1">Migrating birds achieve precise navigation by combining a compass with a map-like system: they are capable of “true navigation” from unfamiliar places, and a mental map used together with a stellar or magnetic compass lets them orient toward the goal.</cite> <cite id="48eab178-2,098bd4ab-3">For direction, birds use multiple cues, including the Sun, stars, patterns of polarized light, and the Earth’s magnetic field.</cite> <cite id="48eab178-6,48eab178-8,3988fa9c-3">For location, they can extract positional information from magnetic inclination and declination, and they also use landmarks, olfactory cues, and remembered spatial cues along the route.</cite> <cite id="9b9996d5-0,9b9996d5-1">This navigation system is influenced or disrupted by geomagnetic disturbances (“space weather”), which are associated with fewer birds migrating and with greater difficulty maintaining course, including more wind drift.</cite> <cite id="9b9996d5-5,9b9996d5-9">It can also be disturbed by anthropogenic electromagnetic/radiofrequency noise, which can disrupt the magnetic compass of migratory birds.</cite>}

citations.fact: Migrating birds achieve precise navigation by combining a compass with a map-like system: they are capable of “true navigation” from unfamiliar places, and a mental map used together with a stellar or magnetic compass lets them orient toward the goal.

fully_underspecified.text: How do animals navigate during migration, and what affects this process?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="4b24b8e2-0">Many migratory species use cues from the sun, stars, landmarks, olfaction and the Earth’s magnetic field</cite>, and <cite id="03950dd7-4">migratory birds use multiple sources of compass information for orientation, including the geomagnetic field, the sun, skylight polarization patterns and star patterns</cite>. In some groups, these cues are integrated: <cite id="03950dd7-2">monarch butterflies and bogong moths combine skylight and magnetic compasses to find their way</cite>, and <cite id="03950dd7-3">reed warblers can use a combination of cues derived from the Earth’s magnetic field to detect a displacement and adjust their migratory direction accordingly</cite>. query.text: How to conduct comprehensive and accurate situational awareness of space targets in the cislunar space, and support the effectiveness of short-term cislunar space tracking and monitoring tasks?
query.answer:
To achieve comprehensive and accurate situational awareness in cislunar space, start with a <cite id="20802462-0,2612ac12-0">three-body Earth–Moon tracking model</cite>, because <cite id="20802462-0">the region is governed by both Earth’s and Moon’s gravity</cite> and <cite id="20802462-0">traditional two-body (Keplerian) dynamics are insufficient</cite>; cislunar trajectories are <cite id="20802462-0">complex, non-planar, chaotic, often non-repeating, and significantly perturbed</cite>. The sensing architecture should be <cite id="137e0ef1-0,2612ac12-0">distributed across Earth orbits, Moon orbits, and Earth–Moon L1/L2 orbits</cite>, and sensor placement should be designed with <cite id="137e0ef1-0">observability metrics that explicitly account for occultation and lighting conditions</cite>, since cislunar tracking suffers from <cite id="137e0ef1-0,2612ac12-0">large ranges and limited viewing geometries</cite>. 

To support effective short-term tracking and monitoring, use <cite id="5b828e90-1">sensor-tasking algorithms for constellations of optical observers</cite> and plan for both <cite id="5b828e90-5">stable observation demands and unanticipated detection/tracking demands</cite>. The orbit-determination pipeline should <cite id="0b826f22-0">fuse multiple sensors’ short-arc angles-only measurements into a single solution</cite>, and should add range data whenever available, because <cite id="f703b637-0">the best-performing architectures combined Moon-based and space-based angles and range observations</cite>. In one cislunar study, <cite id="f703b637-0">four Moon-based narrow-field-of-view angles-only observers maintained 100% track custody with average position RSS error below 1 km</cite>, and <cite id="f703b637-0">adding a single space-based angles-only observer reduced average position estimation RSS error by a factor of five</cite>. In practice, the most effective near-term approach is therefore <cite id="f703b637-0,0b826f22-0,5b828e90-1">a mixed Moon/space/ground sensing network, observability-driven sensor placement, continuous sensor retasking, and multi-sensor orbit determination that fuses angles-only and range measurements</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How to do situational awareness of targets in space and support tracking and monitoring tasks?
fully_underspecified.answer:
To do situational awareness of targets in space, build a workflow that <cite id="b9e82485-7">tracks space objects and their operational environment</cite> and <cite id="00ce6880-0">knows what is in orbit and what it is doing</cite>. In practice, that means first using a sensor network—especially <cite id="b9e82485-8">optical and radar sensors, which enable the surveillance and tracking of space objects, are the most important technical components of SSA systems</cite>—because <cite id="b9e82485-6">radar and sensor systems are essential for effective SSA</cite> and are used <cite id="b9e82485-6">to detect, track and characterize resident space objects</cite>. 

For sensing, combine modalities: <cite id="b9e82485-0">optical telescopes are highly effective in tracking space objects and are indispensable for the space situational awareness ecosystem</cite>, while <cite id="f178e30a-2">sensor data from both radar and optical sensors is critical</cite>. This is valuable because <cite id="b9e82485-4">optical and radar observations provide disparate yet complimentary orbit track update information</cite>, and <cite id="b9e82485-4">optical sensors are likely to reduce in-track error</cite>. 

To support tracking and monitoring tasks, turn those observations into state estimates: <cite id="f178e30a-0">orbital determination and tracking are important sections of target monitoring</cite>. Then fuse multi-sensor measurements—for example, <cite id="f178e30a-7">a fused result combining optical and radar measurements for all sensors within the UKF orbit determination computation</cite>—and use the resulting catalog and estimates for operations such as <cite id="00ce6880-2">conjunction assessment and sensor tasking optimization</cite>. The operational output is timely warning and monitoring, because <cite id="00ce6880-4">SSA data is used to predict conjunctions between objects and warn space operators of potentially dangerous close approaches to enable collision avoidance</cite>.

query.text: Research on the price dynamics of chub mackerel in major aquatic markets of Pacific Rim countries, and its interannual variations in weight/length. Combined with oceanographic theory, these research findings can further establish direct correlations between high-quality marine biological resources, aquatic markets, fishery economics, and the marine environment.
query.answer:
## Chub mackerel in Pacific Rim markets

Chub mackerel is <cite id="f34cd1af-6">a commercially important species in the Northwest Pacific Ocean</cite>, and its fishery is clearly transboundary: <cite id="78e94168-9">Pacific chub mackerel is a transboundary and straddling species</cite>, while <cite id="78e94168-7">Japan’s fishery for chub mackerel occurs inside its EEZ and is mostly conducted by large purse seiners</cite>. In the western North Pacific, the stock is economically relevant across multiple countries because <cite id="78e94168-2">potential spawning grounds extend from the southern East China Sea to the Korea Strait</cite> and <cite id="47839866-2">Korean and Japanese purse seiners harvest chub mackerel mainly in the East China Sea, Tsushima Strait, and the Sea of Japan</cite>.

Available market evidence shows that price dynamics are tightly linked to fish size, supply composition, and export demand. In Korea, <cite id="47839866-0">the market channel for chub mackerel is determined by size: fish above about 30 cm go to the domestic food trade, while fish below about 30 cm are directed elsewhere</cite>. Busan auction data for 2014–2025 show that <cite id="c689076a-0">Grades 3–4 together made up 92–100% of landed weight throughout</cite>, and within the small-fish segment <cite id="c689076a-0">Grade 4 rose from 77% to 97% of landed weight</cite>. Economically, this mattered because <cite id="c689076a-0">Grade 4’s share of chub mackerel revenue rose from 47% to 89% without any gain in its price relative to the largest grade</cite>, implying that revenue shifts were driven mainly by composition and volume rather than a premium on small fish. The same paper also links this market shift to trade, noting that it <cite id="c689076a-0">coincided with an African export market for small mackerel (exports US$28 M → US$200 M) and a weakening won</cite>. Consistent with a firming regional market, a trade source reports that <cite id="34ed6685-9">South Korea’s yearly average wholesale prices were 1.79 USD/kg in 2021, 2.24 in 2022, 2.56 in 2023, and 2.40 in 2024</cite>.

For Japan, direct open-access price detail is thinner, but the literature confirms that <cite id="04a4e56e-0">a 2022 study on Japan’s purse-seine fishery explicitly analyzed price changes associated with mackerel</cite>. Together with the Korean evidence, the pattern suggests that Pacific-Rim chub mackerel prices are shaped by a combination of stock status, fleet behavior, trade outlets, and size composition rather than by catch volume alone.

## Interannual variation in weight and length

Research also documents clear interannual variation in body size. A recent population study found that <cite id="15677f0a-2">the asymptotic fork length of chub mackerel varied from 36.2 cm in 2019 to 41.3 cm in 2020</cite>, demonstrating measurable year-to-year shifts in growth outcomes. Longer-run work has specifically focused on <cite id="26892ca9-8">interannual variation in length-at-age of chub mackerel in the Kuroshio-Oyashio area</cite>, and the NPFC species summary confirms that this line of research examined the <cite id="15677f0a-6">effects of density dependence and sea surface temperature on inter-annual variation in length-at-age</cite>.

Mechanistically, body condition and growth vary with stock density and competitive environment. Kamimura et al. reported that <cite id="cbf53831-0">annual changes in body condition, habitat temperature, and cohort-specific growth were investigated in the western North Pacific</cite>, and found that <cite id="cbf53831-0">body condition, habitat temperature, and growth all decreased with increasing conspecific and heterospecific abundance</cite>. They also showed that <cite id="cbf53831-0">mean annual growth rates were positively correlated with body condition</cite>. This is important economically because shorter fish and poorer body condition can alter the proportion of fish that enter higher-value domestic fresh markets versus lower-value export or reduction channels.

## Oceanographic theory and the biology–market–economy linkage

Oceanographic theory helps explain why these biological and economic variables are connected. Chub mackerel distribution and abundance respond to large-scale marine physical forcing: recent work explicitly examines the <cite id="15677f0a-0">effects of western boundary currents and sea surface temperature anomalies on interannual variability of chub mackerel abundance in the Northwest Pacific</cite>. Climate-suitability studies likewise show that <cite id="15677f0a-1">chub mackerel is divided into Tsushima Warm Current and Pacific stocks based on different distribution, migration, and life history</cite>, and that the species is <cite id="78e94168-1">economically important and extensively distributed in the East China Sea, Yellow Sea, and Sea of Japan</cite>.

Warming-driven range and spawning shifts provide a direct pathway from marine environment to fishery economics. Recent projections indicate that <cite id="78e94168-0">spawning grounds are shifting northward due to ocean warming driven by climate change</cite>, while another study finds that <cite id="78e94168-2">potential spawning grounds extend from southern East China Sea waters to the Korea Strait</cite>. In Korea’s purse-seine fishery, the 2025 market event also had a spatial signature: <cite id="c689076a-0">the fishery concentrated abruptly in the southern East Sea and fished much closer to home port</cite>, and <cite id="c689076a-0">the southern East Sea catch was the smaller one</cite>. This fits standard fisheries-oceanography logic: changes in temperature, current structure, spawning habitat, and prey fields alter where fish aggregate and how fast they grow; fleets then respond by reallocating effort; markets finally register the biological outcome through size grades, channel choice, and price realization.

## Overall conclusion

The combined evidence supports a direct environment-to-market chain. Chub mackerel is <cite id="f34cd1af-6">commercially important</cite> and <cite id="78e94168-9">transboundary</cite> in Pacific-Rim fisheries. Its <cite id="15677f0a-2">length varies interannually</cite>, and both <cite id="15677f0a-6">sea surface temperature</cite> and <cite id="cbf53831-0">density-dependent competition</cite> affect growth and condition. Markets then translate those biological changes into economics because <cite id="47839866-0">size determines market channel</cite>, and composition shifts can dramatically alter revenue even <cite id="c689076a-0">without an increase in relative price</cite>. In short, the literature does support building direct correlations among high-quality marine biological resources, aquatic markets, fishery economics, and the marine environment—though the strongest evidence currently comes from the Northwest Pacific, especially Japan–Korea–China linked fisheries, rather than from every Pacific Rim country equally.

## Pacific fish markets: what the research already shows

Research on Pacific-rim fisheries already supports a coherent environment-to-biology-to-market chain. In the Western and Central Pacific Ocean (WCPO), <cite id="d188eae8-0">the tuna fishery is the largest in the world, with 2,627,696 t caught in 2013, representing 82% of the Pacific Ocean tuna catch and 58% of the global tuna catch</cite>. That catch <cite id="d188eae8-0">supplies fresh and frozen tuna markets for local consumption, export, and canning industries in the Pacific Islands and abroad</cite>, and <cite id="d188eae8-0">the value of the tuna catch in the WCPO was estimated at U.S.$6.2 billion in 2013</cite>. This makes Pacific fish markets large enough that biological and oceanographic variability can plausibly propagate into measurable economic outcomes.

Price dynamics are also visible in regional case studies. In Alaska salmon markets, <cite id="d8aec4ac-0">harvests have been strong over the past decade</cite>, while <cite id="d8aec4ac-0">the frozen share of pink salmon production increased dramatically</cite>. At the same time, <cite id="d8aec4ac-0">the shares exported to Japan declined dramatically, while the shares consumed in U.S. domestic markets and exported to the EU and China increased</cite>. The same source frames these shifts as part of <cite id="d8aec4ac-0">the dramatic recovery in Alaska salmon prices over the past decade</cite>, indicating that price dynamics are tied not just to catch levels but also to product form, destination markets, and trade geography.

At a broader seafood-market level, recent trade reporting suggests demand conditions matter too. <cite id="01eb3288-6">In February 2024, the FAO Fish Price Index remained stable at 119 points</cite>, with <cite id="01eb3288-6">elevated prices for capture fisheries products and lower average prices for aquaculture products</cite>. That pattern is consistent with Pacific capture fisheries being exposed to both environmental supply shocks and substitution effects in protein markets.

## Year-to-year variation in fish length and weight

The biological side of the link is also well established. For Pacific yellowfin tuna, <cite id="0a5ec5d4-5">the relationship between length and weight is far from constant</cite>, which means size-based biomass and value estimates can shift even when fish numbers do not. Growth itself can vary between years: <cite id="0a5ec5d4-3">one study describes inter-annual variation in growth rates of yellowfin tuna from waters south of Guam in the Pacific Ocean</cite>. This is important because year-to-year changes in growth alter harvestable size distributions, processing yields, and often market category.

Small pelagics show similar environmental sensitivity. A recent sardine study found that <cite id="b946d0bc-0">habitat temperature, early life growth rates, energy expenditure, metabolically optimal temperature, and the relationship between growth rate and temperature are remarkably different between western and eastern North Pacific subpopulations</cite>. The authors further conclude that <cite id="b946d0bc-0">varying metabolic responses to environmental changes partly explain the contrasting growth responses</cite>. In short, interannual or decadal temperature variability can translate directly into changes in fish growth trajectories, and therefore into average length and weight entering markets.

## Oceanographic theory linking the marine environment to fish biology

Oceanographic theory provides the mechanism for those biological shifts. Classic climate-fisheries work emphasizes that <cite id="43c7709a-0">interannual temperature variations are important elements of this way of thinking about population variation</cite>. For tuna specifically, <cite id="43c7709a-5">population dynamics of tuna in the tropical Pacific Ocean are strongly influenced by ENSO</cite>. A newer yellowfin tuna study goes further, showing that <cite id="05f0d067-0">productivity varies over time in response to environmental variability</cite> and that <cite id="05f0d067-0">large-scale climate variability and ocean conditions, particularly the Pacific Decadal Oscillation and mixed layer thickness, were positively associated with tuna productivity</cite>.

The ENSO connection is especially useful for building direct correlations across the Pacific. NOAA notes that <cite id="7c5284fb-0">you cannot tell the story of El Niño without mentioning its impacts on the anchovy fishery off the coast of Peru</cite>, and also states that <cite id="7c5284fb-0">ENSO does affect salmon</cite>. That means a common climate mode can influence very different Pacific fisheries through changes in temperature, stratification, currents, prey fields, and habitat suitability.

## A practical synthesis: direct correlations that can be tested

Taken together, the literature supports a testable chain:

<cite id="05f0d067-0,43c7709a-5,7c5284fb-0">climate variability such as ENSO or the PDO changes ocean conditions</cite> → <cite id="b946d0bc-0,0a5ec5d4-3,0a5ec5d4-5">fish growth, size structure, productivity, and length-weight relationships change from year to year</cite> → <cite id="d8aec4ac-0,d188eae8-0">harvest composition, trade flows, and market value change</cite>.

So yes: these findings can help establish direct correlations between marine biological resources, markets, economics, and the marine environment. The strongest empirical design would combine annual oceanographic indices (ENSO, PDO, mixed-layer depth, SST, upwelling), stock-level biological indicators (growth, mean length, weight-at-length, productivity), and market variables (landings, export destination, product form, dockside price, wholesale price). The available research already shows that each link in that chain exists; the next step is integrated panel analysis across Pacific countries and species to quantify the strength and timing of those links.

Research already supports a coherent ocean–biology–market pathway for chub mackerel. On the market side, fish price studies show that <cite id="783d4616-0">fish market prices are strongly positively related to maximum fish length, while landings amount alone is not a significant single predictor</cite>; the same study concludes that <cite id="783d4616-0">market prices may reveal ecosystem variations as well as socioeconomic drivers</cite>. For chub mackerel specifically, Korean evidence shows that <cite id="42bb2d83-0">the market channel is size-based</cite>: <cite id="3ac85e38-0">fish above about 30 cm go to the domestic food trade, fish below about 30 cm are exported or canned, and fish below about 200 g go to feed</cite>. This means interannual variation in body size is not just biological—it directly changes product destination, quality class, and revenue structure. In the Korean purse-seine fishery, <cite id="42bb2d83-0">small fish chronically dominated landings</cite>, and <cite id="42bb2d83-0">Grade 4’s share of chub mackerel revenue rose from 47% to 89%</cite>, showing how shifts in size composition can reconfigure fishery earnings even <cite id="42bb2d83-0">without any gain in its price relative to the largest grade</cite>.

On the biological side, interannual variation in length/weight-related traits is strongly linked to density dependence and thermal habitat. A long-term study in the Kuroshio–Oyashio region specifically examined <cite id="6e14db1d-0">interannual variation in length-at-age of chub mackerel during 1970–1997</cite> and attributed it to <cite id="6e14db1d-0">density-dependence and sea surface temperature</cite>. More recent work found that <cite id="b1f4b9e9-1">chub mackerel body condition, habitat temperature, and growth all decreased with increasing conspecific and heterospecific abundance</cite>. That result is important because poorer body condition typically implies lower weight at a given length and potentially lower commercial quality.

Oceanographic theory provides the mechanism tying these findings together. Chub mackerel spawning habitat is temperature-sensitive: <cite id="d2ec1712-0">the suitable spawning SST ranges from 15°C to 22°C</cite>. The species also shows <cite id="d2ec1712-0">obvious interannual to decadal variability in abundance</cite>, and the <cite id="d2ec1712-0">spatio-temporal variation in spawning temperature suitability may have had an important impact on stock recovery</cite>. Moreover, <cite id="d2ec1712-0">the relationship between abundance and temperature suitability is non-stationary and driven by climate variabilities such as the Siberian High and the Aleutian Low</cite>. Consistent with this, recent work concludes that <cite id="8694c80c-6">the spatio-temporal distribution of chub mackerel is strongly susceptible to climate variability</cite>, and another study directly targets <cite id="8694c80c-1">the effects of western boundary currents and sea surface temperature anomalies on interannual variability of chub mackerel abundance</cite>.

Taken together, the evidence supports a direct correlation chain: climate variability and ocean conditions alter spawning suitability, distribution, and stock abundance; those changes affect growth, body condition, and length-at-age; and because chub mackerel markets are explicitly size-graded, the biological changes transmit into market prices, product channels, and fishery revenue. In short, <cite id="783d4616-0">size is a core economic signal in fish markets</cite>, <cite id="42bb2d83-0">size composition changes revenue composition in chub mackerel fisheries</cite>, and <cite id="6e14db1d-0">temperature and density affect interannual length-at-age</cite>. This is exactly the basis needed to link high-quality marine biological resources, aquatic markets, fishery economics, and the marine environment in a single analytical framework.

questions.original_query: What are the most effective approaches to scaling ion trap quantum computing from small-scale demonstration projects to large-scale systems capable of solving real-world problems? This research should investigate the various proposed scaling strategies, assess their feasibility, and evaluate which approaches are most likely to succeed based on current technological advancements and practical implementation challenges.

query.text: What are the most effective approaches to scaling ion trap quantum computing from small-scale demonstration projects to large-scale systems capable of solving real-world problems? This research should investigate the various proposed scaling strategies, assess their feasibility, and evaluate which approaches are most likely to succeed based on current technological advancements and practical implementation challenges.
query.answer:
## Bottom line

<cite id="9ecc42ab-0">Trapped-ion platforms are a strong foundation for quantum computing because qubits encoded in trapped ions offer very high gate fidelities and long coherence times.</cite> <cite id="50971cde-9">The central unsolved engineering problem is scaling from today’s devices to hundreds or thousands of qubits and beyond.</cite> <cite id="50971cde-2,50971cde-7">A single ever-longer ion chain is unlikely to be the winning strategy, because adding ions slows two-qubit gates through a denser vibrational-mode spectrum and long chains also suffer fidelity problems from residual heating driven by noisy electric fields.</cite>

<cite id="391f187b-1,9ecc42ab-0">Based on current evidence, the most credible route to large-scale trapped-ion computing is a modular architecture built from QCCD-style local processors, combined first with high-fidelity ion shuttling or matter-links between nearby modules and then with photonic links for longer-range interconnects.</cite> <cite id="430f07f0-5,430f07f0-0">Newer proposals based on large ion crystals with dynamically operated optical potentials and tightly focused optical tweezers are scientifically promising, but in the evidence retrieved here they are still at the proposal stage rather than system-level demonstrations.</cite>

## 1) The main scaling strategies

### Monolithic long chains

<cite id="50971cde-2">The basic appeal of a single long chain is simplicity and native Coulomb-mediated interactions, but its main drawback is that two-qubit gates slow down as the chain grows because the motional spectrum becomes harder to control.</cite> <cite id="50971cde-7">Experimental and theoretical work on long chains also identifies residual electric-field-noise heating as a mechanism that degrades gate fidelity.</cite> <cite id="50971cde-2,50971cde-7">That makes pure monolithic scaling technically possible in principle, but increasingly unattractive as the path to utility-scale machines.</cite>

### QCCD: many small trapping zones with ion shuttling

<cite id="391f187b-1">QCCD architectures divide the processor into multiple traps and have already been studied in detail for 50–100 qubit systems.</cite> <cite id="86346947-8,7d944355-8">Their key idea is to keep only a small number of ions in each trap so gates remain reliable and then use ion shuttling to bring qubits together for entangling gates across zones.</cite> <cite id="391f187b-5">A long-standing assessment from the ion-trap community is that QCCD could plausibly support roughly 50–1,000 qubits on a processor before still-larger systems require stronger modularization.</cite>

### Modular processors linked by moving ions between chips

<cite id="9ecc42ab-0">A major recent advance is the demonstration of a quantum matter-link between adjacent ion-trap microchip modules, motivated by the fact that a single module is ultimately limited by chip size.</cite> <cite id="9ecc42ab-0">In that experiment, ion transport between adjacent modules was achieved at 2424 s−1 with transport infidelity from ion loss below 7 × 10−8, and the transfer did not measurably harm qubit phase coherence.</cite> <cite id="9ecc42ab-0">The authors explicitly describe this matter-link as a practical mechanism for interconnecting QCCD devices and as a step toward fault-tolerant, utility-scale trapped-ion computing.</cite>

### Modular processors linked by photons

<cite id="87fc4e64-0">Photonic interconnects are the other major modular strategy, and one reported trapped-ion realization achieved entanglement at 182 s−1 with 94% fidelity.</cite> <cite id="87fc4e64-7">Earlier architectural analysis described typical inter-module photonic connection rates of about 100 Hz, while also noting that these rates could be improved substantially.</cite> <cite id="22102536-3">A 2024 integrated-photonics analysis concluded that integrated photonic structures can support scalable trapped-ion systems that distribute quantum information through photon-mediated entanglement.</cite>

### Large ion crystals with local optical control

<cite id="430f07f0-5">A newer 2024 proposal argues that large ion crystals can be made scalable by dynamically operated optical potentials.</cite> <cite id="430f07f0-0">Its central mechanism is to use tightly focused optical tweezers to create additional local trapping for selected ions along a chain.</cite> <cite id="430f07f0-5">Because this approach is presented as a proposed architecture intended to overcome current scaling issues, it looks like an important research direction but not yet the most implementation-ready path.</cite>

## 2) Feasibility and practical implementation challenges

<cite id="edceeb80-7">Large-scale trapped-ion systems are not limited only by qubit physics; they also require several tunable laser systems and substantial optical infrastructure.</cite> <cite id="22102536-3">That is why integrated photonics matters: it promises to compress and stabilize the optical layer needed for scalable interconnects.</cite> <cite id="391f187b-3">Control delivery is also a recognized scaling issue, often called the “wiring problem,” because each qubit or trap zone must receive precise signals.</cite>

<cite id="391f187b-1,86346947-8">QCCD is feasible because it preserves the best part of trapped ions—high-quality local gates in small ion sets—while using transport operations to recover connectivity across a larger chip.</cite> <cite id="9ecc42ab-0">Its next challenge is not whether ions can be moved between zones or even between neighboring modules, since that has now been shown with very low loss, but whether all of that transport can be orchestrated with acceptable overhead in a fault-tolerant machine.</cite> <cite id="edceeb80-7">This makes QCCD a systems-engineering problem more than a basic-physics problem.</cite>

<cite id="87fc4e64-0,22102536-3">Photonic networking is feasible and almost certainly necessary for truly distributed trapped-ion computers, but today’s demonstrated link performance is still far below the quality of local trapped-ion operations, so it is the less mature part of the stack.</cite> <cite id="87fc4e64-0">A 94% entanglement fidelity at 182 s−1 is a real milestone, but it still implies substantial purification, heralding, or error-correction overhead compared with near-perfect local transport and gate operations.</cite> <cite id="22102536-3">Integrated photonics improves the outlook, yet the main practical hurdle remains boosting link rate, collection efficiency, and fidelity simultaneously.</cite>

<cite id="430f07f0-0,430f07f0-5">The optical-tweezer/large-crystal approach could, if validated experimentally, reduce some of the shuttling overhead by creating more local control inside a bigger crystal.</cite> <cite id="430f07f0-5">However, the evidence retrieved here shows it as a recent architectural proposal rather than a mature hardware platform, so its feasibility is still more prospective than demonstrated.</cite>

## 3) Which approaches are most likely to succeed?

### Most likely near-term winner: QCCD on a chip

<cite id="391f187b-1,86346947-8">For the next scaling step—from small demonstrations to useful processors with tens to low hundreds of qubits—the best bet is QCCD, because it directly addresses the long-chain bottleneck while staying close to already-practiced trapped-ion control methods.</cite> <cite id="391f187b-1">It is also the approach for which explicit application-driven architectural studies already exist in the 50–100 qubit regime.</cite>

### Most likely medium-term extension: QCCD plus matter-links between neighboring modules

<cite id="9ecc42ab-0">The strongest recent result supporting modular growth is the matter-link experiment, which showed fast inter-module ion transfer with negligible loss and no measurable coherence penalty.</cite> <cite id="9ecc42ab-0">Because this mechanism directly interconnects QCCD devices, it looks like the most practical way to extend beyond the size limits of one chip while preserving trapped ions’ strongest performance characteristics.</cite>

### Most likely long-term necessity: photonic interconnects

<cite id="22102536-3,87fc4e64-0">For very large, distributed, or data-center-scale machines, photonic links are likely unavoidable, and current work on integrated photonics makes that vision technically plausible.</cite> <cite id="87fc4e64-0">But based on present demonstrations, photonic links are not yet strong enough to be the primary scaling mechanism if the goal is near-term real-world problem solving.</cite>

### Most promising but least proven: large-crystal optical-tweezer architectures

<cite id="430f07f0-5,430f07f0-0">These architectures may eventually become highly competitive because they try to preserve the advantages of larger ion crystals while regaining local controllability through optical tweezers.</cite> <cite id="430f07f0-5">Still, with the current evidence limited to recent proposals, they rank behind QCCD-based modular strategies in implementation readiness.</cite>

## Final assessment

<cite id="50971cde-2,391f187b-1,9ecc42ab-0,22102536-3">The most effective overall scaling roadmap is therefore hierarchical: avoid relying on a single long chain, build high-fidelity local QCCD processors, connect nearby modules with ion-transport or matter-links where possible, and reserve photonic interconnects for longer-range modular networking.</cite> <cite id="9ecc42ab-0,87fc4e64-0">Among the competing approaches, QCCD plus modular interconnects has the strongest combination of demonstrated hardware, architectural analysis, and a credible path to fault-tolerant utility-scale systems.</cite> <cite id="430f07f0-5">Optical-tweezer large-crystal schemes are important to watch, but today they look more like next-generation contenders than the leading path to scalable implementation.</cite>

citations.fact: Trapped-ion platforms are a strong foundation for quantum computing because qubits encoded in trapped ions offer very high gate fidelities and long coherence times.
A major recent advance is the demonstration of a quantum matter-link between adjacent ion-trap microchip modules, motivated by the fact that a single module is ultimately limited by chip size.

In that experiment, ion transport between adjacent modules was achieved at 2424 s−1 with transport infidelity from ion loss below 7 × 10−8, and the transfer did not measurably harm qubit phase coherence.
The authors explicitly describe this matter-link as a practical mechanism for interconnecting QCCD devices and as a step toward fault-tolerant, utility-scale trapped-ion computing.
Photonic interconnects are the other major modular strategy, and one reported trapped-ion realization achieved entanglement at 182 s−1 with 94% fidelity.

Its next challenge is not whether ions can be moved between zones or even between neighboring modules, since that has now been shown with very low loss, but whether all of that transport can be orchestrated with acceptable overhead in a fault-tolerant machine.

Photonic networking is feasible and almost certainly necessary for truly distributed trapped-ion computers, but today’s demonstrated link performance is still far below the quality of local trapped-ion operations, so it is the less mature part of the stack.

A 94% entanglement fidelity at 182 s−1 is a real milestone, but it still implies substantial purification, heralding, or error-correction overhead compared with near-perfect local transport and gate operations.
The strongest recent result supporting modular growth is the matter-link experiment, which showed fast inter-module ion transfer with negligible loss and no measurable coherence penalty.

Because this mechanism directly interconnects QCCD devices, it looks like the most practical way to extend beyond the size limits of one chip while preserving trapped ions’ strongest performance characteristics.
But based on present demonstrations, photonic links are not yet strong enough to be the primary scaling mechanism if the goal is near-term real-world problem solving.

Among the competing approaches, QCCD plus modular interconnects has the strongest combination of demonstrated hardware, architectural analysis, and a credible path to fault-tolerant utility-scale systems.
The central unsolved engineering problem is scaling from today’s devices to hundreds or thousands of qubits and beyond.

A single ever-longer ion chain is unlikely to be the winning strategy, because adding ions slows two-qubit gates through a denser vibrational-mode spectrum and long chains also suffer fidelity problems from residual heating driven by noisy electric fields.

The basic appeal of a single long chain is simplicity and native Coulomb-mediated interactions, but its main drawback is that two-qubit gates slow down as the chain grows because the motional spectrum becomes harder to control.
That makes pure monolithic scaling technically possible in principle, but increasingly unattractive as the path to utility-scale machines.

The most effective overall scaling roadmap is therefore hierarchical: avoid relying on a single long chain, build high-fidelity local QCCD processors, connect nearby modules with ion-transport or matter-links where possible, and reserve photonic interconnects for longer-range modular networking.

Based on current evidence, the most credible route to large-scale trapped-ion computing is a modular architecture built from QCCD-style local processors, combined first with high-fidelity ion shuttling or matter-links between nearby modules and then with photonic links for longer-range interconnects.
QCCD architectures divide the processor into multiple traps and have already been studied in detail for 50–100 qubit systems.
QCCD is feasible because it preserves the best part of trapped ions—high-quality local gates in small ion sets—while using transport operations to recover connectivity across a larger chip.

For the next scaling step—from small demonstrations to useful processors with tens to low hundreds of qubits—the best bet is QCCD, because it directly addresses the long-chain bottleneck while staying close to already-practiced trapped-ion control methods.
It is also the approach for which explicit application-driven architectural studies already exist in the 50–100 qubit regime.

Newer proposals based on large ion crystals with dynamically operated optical potentials and tightly focused optical tweezers are scientifically promising, but in the evidence retrieved here they are still at the proposal stage rather than system-level demonstrations.
A newer 2024 proposal argues that large ion crystals can be made scalable by dynamically operated optical potentials.

Because this approach is presented as a proposed architecture intended to overcome current scaling issues, it looks like an important research direction but not yet the most implementation-ready path.
However, the evidence retrieved here shows it as a recent architectural proposal rather than a mature hardware platform, so its feasibility is still more prospective than demonstrated.
These architectures may eventually become highly competitive because they try to preserve the advantages of larger ion crystals while regaining local controllability through optical tweezers.
Still, with the current evidence limited to recent proposals, they rank behind QCCD-based modular strategies in implementation readiness.
Optical-tweezer large-crystal schemes are important to watch, but today they look more like next-generation contenders than the leading path to scalable implementation.
Experimental and theoretical work on long chains also identifies residual electric-field-noise heating as a mechanism that degrades gate fidelity.
Their key idea is to keep only a small number of ions in each trap so gates remain reliable and then use ion shuttling to bring qubits together for entangling gates across zones.
A long-standing assessment from the ion-trap community is that QCCD could plausibly support roughly 50–1,000 qubits on a processor before still-larger systems require stronger modularization.
Earlier architectural analysis described typical inter-module photonic connection rates of about 100 Hz, while also noting that these rates could be improved substantially.
Large-scale trapped-ion systems are not limited only by qubit physics; they also require several tunable laser systems and substantial optical infrastructure.
This makes QCCD a systems-engineering problem more than a basic-physics problem.
A 2024 integrated-photonics analysis concluded that integrated photonic structures can support scalable trapped-ion systems that distribute quantum information through photon-mediated entanglement.
That is why integrated photonics matters: it promises to compress and stabilize the optical layer needed for scalable interconnects.
Integrated photonics improves the outlook, yet the main practical hurdle remains boosting link rate, collection efficiency, and fidelity simultaneously.
For very large, distributed, or data-center-scale machines, photonic links are likely unavoidable, and current work on integrated photonics makes that vision technically plausible.
Its central mechanism is to use tightly focused optical tweezers to create additional local trapping for selected ions along a chain.
The optical-tweezer/large-crystal approach could, if validated experimentally, reduce some of the shuttling overhead by creating more local control inside a bigger crystal.
Control delivery is also a recognized scaling issue, often called the “wiring problem,” because each qubit or trap zone must receive precise signals.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the best ways to scale quantum computing from small demonstrations to large systems?
fully_underspecified.answer: The best path from small demonstrations to large quantum computers is to combine <cite id="b22e3f61-0">quantum error correction</cite>—whose <cite id="b22e3f61-0">purpose ... is to enable large-scale quantum algorithms</cite>—with hardware and software that can run it efficiently, since <cite id="b22e3f61-5">quantum error correction offers a path to algorithmically relevant error rates by encoding logical qubits within many physical qubits</cite> and <cite id="b22e3f61-7">the accumulation of physical errors prevents the execution of large-scale algorithms in current quantum computers</cite>. A second key strategy is <cite id="a4d2e65b-0">error-corrected modular quantum computers</cite>, which <cite id="a4d2e65b-0">offer a promising route to overcome the noise and scalability challenges of large-scale</cite> systems by linking smaller processors instead of building one monolithic chip. Finally, scaling requires major investment in the classical side: <cite id="ff828d4f-8">scaling superconducting quantum computers to the fault-tolerant regime calls for a commensurate scaling of the classical control and readout stack</cite>, while <cite id="ff828d4f-0">ensuring high connectivity and minimizing unwanted interactions are essential for scaling up quantum computers</cite>; architectures that <cite id="ff828d4f-9">embed multiplexing subsystems at cryogenic</cite> temperatures are one concrete way to reduce wiring and control bottlenecks. In practice, that means the “best ways” are: build better logical qubits with QEC, adopt modular/networked architectures, and co-design scalable control/readout/packaging infrastructure around the chosen qubit technology.

without_term.text: What are the most effective approaches to scaling quantum computing from small-scale demonstration projects to large-scale systems capable of solving real-world problems? This research should investigate the various proposed scaling strategies, assess their feasibility, and evaluate which approaches are most likely to succeed based on current technological advancements and practical implementation challenges.
without_term.answer:
## Executive summary

The scaling strategy with the strongest evidence today is a **three-part stack**: <cite id="278f3d73-0,278f3d73-1">fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC), which turns many physical qubits into lower-error logical qubits</cite>; <cite id="d804db95-0,71198a24-6">modular architectures, which avoid the prohibitive complexity of a single monolithic machine and can connect separate error-corrected regions fault-tolerantly</cite>; and <cite id="d804db95-1,3e1a2f60-0">classical/cryogenic control co-design, because wiring, I/O, cooling power, and readout/control hardware are now system-level scaling constraints</cite>. Based on current demonstrations, <cite id="0a0032b2-0,419b9705-1">superconducting qubits lead in near-term scalability and manufacturing momentum</cite>, while <cite id="0c501c82-0,71198a24-7,278f3d73-3">neutral atoms have become the strongest challenger because they already support large reconfigurable arrays and recent logical/fault-tolerant demonstrations</cite>. <cite id="e72356ab-6,e72356ab-1,e72356ab-4">Photonics looks especially important as the networking layer for modular or distributed systems and may also become a useful compute platform if current fault-tolerance roadmaps succeed</cite>, whereas <cite id="71198a24-0,e72356ab-0">trapped ions remain a credible modular route</cite> and <cite id="419b9705-2,419b9705-4,419b9705-8">silicon spin qubits remain a high-upside long-term bet if variability and large-scale control can be tamed</cite>.

## What “scaling” actually requires

The central technical fact is that <cite id="278f3d73-0">practical quantum computing requires QEC that combines multiple physical qubits into a logical qubit</cite>. More specifically, <cite id="278f3d73-1">QEC offers a path to algorithmically relevant error rates by encoding logical qubits within many physical qubits</cite>, and <cite id="278f3d73-6">fault-tolerant protocols work only when the hardware error rates are below threshold</cite>. That is why recent progress on <cite id="278f3d73-1,278f3d73-5">surface-code scaling and other logical-qubit demonstrations</cite> matters more for real-world utility than raw physical-qubit counts alone.

A second requirement is architectural: <cite id="d804db95-0,d804db95-3">building a monolithic fault-tolerant machine with millions of qubits can be prohibitively complex and expensive</cite>. The main alternative is <cite id="d804db95-0,71198a24-1">a modular quantum computer made from smaller quantum processing units</cite>, and this idea is no longer platform-specific because <cite id="71198a24-1">modular architectures have been proposed for superconducting qubits, neutral atoms, and other hardware</cite>. Recent work also shows that <cite id="71198a24-6">distinct surface-code patches can be connected in a fault-tolerant manner</cite>, which is a key sign that modularity is technically plausible rather than just conceptually attractive.

The third requirement is systems engineering. <cite id="278f3d73-7">QEC produces a continuous stream of syndrome data that must be decoded</cite>, and <cite id="278f3d73-8">researchers are now building learned decoders for the surface code, still the leading QEC code</cite>. At the hardware level, <cite id="d804db95-1">wiring scalability, I/O limits, cooling-power budgets, and constraints across temperature stages</cite> are already recognized as major barriers, so <cite id="3e1a2f60-0">scalable cryogenic control/readout platforms are essential for large-scale systems</cite>.

## The major proposed scaling strategies

The most mature strategy is **fault-tolerant scaling through QEC**, especially with surface-code-style approaches. The evidence is strong that <cite id="278f3d73-1">scaling a surface code can suppress errors toward algorithmically relevant rates</cite>, and recent theory also suggests that <cite id="278f3d73-2">high-threshold, lower-overhead fault-tolerant schemes may eventually compete with the surface code while retaining thresholds around 0.7%</cite>. In practice, this means the winning architecture probably will not be the one with the most raw qubits, but the one that can most efficiently produce and operate many logical qubits.

The next key strategy is **modularity and distribution**. <cite id="71198a24-6,0c501c82-8">Multiple groups now describe modularity as one of the most promising routes to scalable quantum computing</cite>, because it lets engineers scale by linking smaller, more controllable units rather than enlarging a single fragile device. This is reinforced by the fact that <cite id="e72356ab-4">photonic-network connectivity and reconfigurability provide a scalable approach for other hardware platforms too</cite>, suggesting that future large systems may look more like distributed computers than giant monolithic chips.

A third strategy is **classical-quantum co-design**. For example, <cite id="419b9705-6">superconducting processors still often rely on microwave signals delivered from room-temperature electronics into the cryogenic environment</cite>, which does not scale cleanly. Similarly, <cite id="3e1a2f60-7">shared control has only recently been demonstrated as a first step toward sustainable operation of larger semiconductor processors</cite>. This makes co-design of qubits, packaging, electronics, decoding, and networking a practical necessity rather than an optimization.

## Assessment by hardware platform

### Superconducting qubits

Superconducting qubits currently look strongest for **near-term large-scale engineering**. Reviews and summaries state that <cite id="0a0032b2-0">superconducting qubits lead in scalability and near-term applicability</cite>, and recent manufacturing work argues that <cite id="419b9705-1">superconducting-qubit technology has shown great potential for constructing practical quantum computers</cite>. This platform also benefits from visible progress on industrial fabrication, including <cite id="419b9705-1">advanced CMOS manufacturing of superconducting qubits</cite>.

Their biggest risks are system-level rather than conceptual. <cite id="419b9705-6">Per-qubit microwave wiring from room temperature into cryogenic hardware</cite> is a clear scalability bottleneck, and dedicated reviews emphasize <cite id="d804db95-1">wiring and I/O scalability, cooling-power budgets, and multi-stage cryogenic constraints</cite>. The most likely path to success here is therefore <cite id="278f3d73-1,71198a24-6,3e1a2f60-0">error-corrected superconducting modules paired with aggressive cryogenic-control integration</cite>.

### Neutral atoms

Neutral atoms have moved from “promising” to “serious contender.” Nature papers now describe <cite id="0c501c82-0">optical-tweezer atom arrays as increasingly recognized as a promising platform for scalable quantum computing</cite>, and related work says <cite id="0c501c82-2">neutral-atom arrays have emerged as a leading platform for quantum information processing and simulation</cite>. Their scaling appeal comes from naturally large, reconfigurable arrays and the ability to rearrange qubits geometrically.

The strongest reason to take neutral atoms seriously is recent fault-tolerance progress. Researchers reported <cite id="71198a24-7">a programmable logical quantum processor operating with up to 280 physical qubits</cite>, and later work used <cite id="d804db95-6">reconfigurable arrays of up to 448 neutral atoms to implement and combine key elements of a universal fault-tolerant architecture</cite>. Even more importantly, <cite id="278f3d73-3">surface-code experiments on a neutral-atom architecture demonstrated repeated QEC with 2.14(13)× below-threshold performance over four rounds</cite>. On current evidence, this makes neutral atoms one of the most plausible routes to large fault-tolerant machines.

### Trapped ions

Trapped ions remain one of the most credible routes for **high-quality modular quantum computing**. Nature’s long-running trapped-ion roadmap states that <cite id="e72356ab-0,0c501c82-1">trapped atomic ions are a leading platform for first-generation quantum computers and are fundamentally scalable to more powerful systems</cite>. The platform’s clearest scaling vision is modular: <cite id="71198a24-0">a modular quantum computer with thousands or more qubits can be engineered from ion crystals</cite>.

The main reason trapped ions are still relevant to the scaling debate is that they align naturally with distributed designs. <cite id="d804db95-0">Modular QPUs can simplify engineering and reduce costs relative to a monolithic machine</cite>, and trapped ions have long been developed around precisely that architecture. My assessment is that trapped ions remain highly feasible technically, but their path to very large systems is likely to depend heavily on successful photonic interconnects and systems integration rather than simply enlarging single devices.

### Photonic quantum computing

Photonics is especially attractive because its scaling advantages are architectural. Recent work states that <cite id="e72356ab-6">photonic quantum computing offers low decoherence, modest cryogenic requirements, and native networking</cite>. That combination makes photonics unusually well matched to modular and distributed quantum computing.

The recent outlook is also stronger than it was a few years ago. A Nature paper reports that <cite id="e72356ab-1">current work lays out a path to cross the fault-tolerant threshold and scale photonic quantum computers to the point of addressing useful problems</cite>. Even if photonics does not win as the dominant compute substrate, <cite id="e72356ab-4">photonic-network connectivity and reconfigurability provide a scalable approach for other quantum-computing platforms</cite>, so photonics is likely to be central as the interconnect fabric of any large distributed machine.

### Silicon spin qubits

Silicon spin qubits have the strongest **long-term density argument**. Nature materials state that <cite id="419b9705-2">semiconductor spin qubits provide a promising foundation for scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computing</cite>, and recent work emphasizes that <cite id="419b9705-4">their sub-micron footprint could allow a single silicon chip to host the millions of qubits needed for useful algorithms</cite>. That is an exceptional scaling proposition if it can be realized.

What keeps spin qubits from the top tier today is not the vision but the engineering maturity. There is real progress—<cite id="419b9705-0">a silicon CMOS architecture has been proposed for parallel addressing and repetitive error correction</cite>, and <cite id="3e1a2f60-7">shared control of a 16-quantum-dot device was presented as a first step toward sustainable control of large processors</cite>. But the platform still faces fundamental manufacturability questions because <cite id="419b9705-8">quantifying device variability is necessary to develop a sensible scalable architecture</cite>. So spin qubits look more like a high-upside medium- to long-term bet than the most likely first path to real-world fault-tolerant computing.

## Which approaches are most likely to succeed?

The **most likely successful scaling recipe** is a hybrid one: <cite id="278f3d73-0,278f3d73-1">logical-qubit-first scaling via QEC</cite> combined with <cite id="d804db95-0,71198a24-6">modular or distributed architecture</cite> and backed by <cite id="d804db95-1,3e1a2f60-0">deep investment in control electronics, packaging, decoding, and cryogenic infrastructure</cite>. Put differently, the evidence does not support a “just build more qubits” strategy; it supports building **more logical capability per unit engineering complexity**.

Among hardware choices, the best-supported near-term leaders are **superconducting qubits and neutral atoms**. <cite id="0a0032b2-0,419b9705-1">Superconducting qubits currently have the clearest industrialization and manufacturing momentum</cite>, while <cite id="71198a24-7,278f3d73-3">neutral atoms have some of the most compelling recent logical and below-threshold demonstrations</cite>. <cite id="e72356ab-1,e72356ab-4">Photonics is the strongest complementary technology for networking and distribution</cite>, and it may itself become a leading compute platform if its threshold-crossing roadmap is borne out. <cite id="71198a24-0">Trapped ions remain a technically coherent modular path</cite>, while <cite id="419b9705-4,419b9705-8">spin qubits remain a plausible long-term winner if density advantages can be translated into controllable, low-variability large-scale systems</cite>.

## Bottom line

If the question is “what will actually get quantum computing from demos to real-world machines,” the best current answer is: <cite id="278f3d73-1">scale logical qubits, not just physical qubits</cite>; <cite id="d804db95-0,71198a24-1">use modular architectures instead of trying to build one enormous monolithic processor</cite>; and <cite id="d804db95-1,278f3d73-7">treat decoding, wiring, cooling, and control as first-class scaling problems</cite>. On present evidence, <cite id="0a0032b2-0,419b9705-1">superconducting systems are the most likely near-term workhorse</cite>, <cite id="71198a24-7,278f3d73-3">neutral atoms are the most credible rising challenger for fault-tolerant scale</cite>, and <cite id="e72356ab-4">photonic networking is likely to be essential to whatever ultimately wins</cite>.

questions.original_query:
(working on LN-based nonlinear photonics):
Possible ways to mitigate the material damage of LN after plasma etching?

query.text:
(working on LN-based nonlinear photonics):
Possible ways to mitigate the material damage of LN after plasma etching?
query.answer:
Possible approaches are:

- <cite id="1301ab2a-6,56adf1ef-4">Use a post-etch wet chemical clean to remove LiF redeposition and other residues, because fluorine-based etching can leave LiF on the surface/sidewalls, and wet cleaning can remove redeposition/contaminants and reduce sidewall roughness.</cite>
- <cite id="56adf1ef-0,4a52d0e6-4,1301ab2a-1,1301ab2a-2">Reduce damage in-process by moving to redeposition-free ICP conditions and optimizing bias/pressure/gas flow for minimal sidewall and surface roughness.</cite>
- <cite id="56adf1ef-5,f574daf8-1">Add a post-etch CMP step, since CMP on LNOI can reduce waveguide sidewall roughness after etching and improve optical performance/power transmission.</cite>
- <cite id="4a52d0e6-1,f574daf8-8">If your stack allows it, try high-temperature annealing as a defect-recovery step; in LN thin films it has been used to restore lattice damage and substantially improve resonator Q, although the retrieved evidence here is for implantation-induced damage rather than plasma-specific damage.</cite>

So, in practice, the most evidence-backed flow is <cite id="56adf1ef-4,56adf1ef-5,1301ab2a-1">optimized low-redeposition etching + wet post-clean + CMP</cite>, with <cite id="4a52d0e6-1">annealing as an additional recovery option when thermally compatible</cite>.
