# A New Paradigm of Holistic Empowerment in Elementary English Education and Teaching

## Abstract

<cite id="7563db54-0">The surge of globalisation and the recognition of English as a lingua franca have propelled the worldwide advancement of English as a foreign language (EFL) education.</cite> In elementary settings, however, language growth alone is too narrow a goal. <cite id="e8ebacf5-0">Social and emotional learning (SEL) programs are a low-cost, evidence-based educational intervention that improves outcomes for all students</cite>, and <cite id="81483ff5-6">participation in an SEL program significantly improved student academic achievement, school functioning, social and emotional skills, attitudes, behaviors</cite>. This paper argues that elementary English education should move toward a holistic empowerment paradigm that integrates language development, emotional security, cultural responsiveness, multimodal literacy, formative assessment, and family partnership. Drawing on current research, the paper proposes a practice-oriented framework and discusses how classroom teaching can translate these principles into daily instruction for young learners.

**Keywords:** holistic empowerment; elementary English education; whole-child education; social and emotional learning; formative assessment; culturally responsive teaching; multimodality; family engagement; young learners; EFL pedagogy

## 1. Introduction

<cite id="7563db54-0">The surge of globalisation and the recognition of English as a lingua franca have propelled the worldwide advancement of English as a foreign language (EFL) education.</cite> Yet for children in elementary school, English learning is inseparable from identity formation, emotional development, play, interaction, and belonging. A purely exam-centered model cannot fully address these needs, especially when young learners differ in readiness, confidence, home language, and access to support.

A more adequate response is holistic empowerment. In broad educational research, <cite id="e8ebacf5-6">whole-child education</cite> is valued because <cite id="e8ebacf5-6">they are linked to academic achievement, productivity and collegiality at work, positive health indicators, and the development of noncognitive</cite> capacities. In school improvement research, <cite id="e8ebacf5-4">educational equity means that each child receives what they need to develop to their full academic and social potential.</cite> Therefore, a new paradigm for elementary English teaching should not treat children as test-takers only; it should treat them as developing persons whose language learning is strengthened by emotional support, cultural recognition, and meaningful participation.

## 2. Theoretical Foundations of Holistic Empowerment

### 2.1 Whole-child development and SEL

Holistic empowerment begins with the recognition that language learning is social, emotional, and cognitive at the same time. <cite id="e8ebacf5-1">SEL helps create the conditions for student learning, while academic instruction provides a ripe opportunity for teaching and practicing social-emotional skills</cite>. This means English lessons are not separate from character, empathy, self-regulation, or collaboration; rather, they are natural sites where such capacities can be taught and practiced.

The evidence base is strong. <cite id="81483ff5-0">students in grades 1–12 who participated in universal school-based SEL programs demonstrated better academic achievement</cite>, and <cite id="81483ff5-6">participation in an SEL program significantly improved student academic achievement, school functioning, social and emotional skills, attitudes, behaviors</cite>. For elementary English teaching, this implies that classroom routines such as cooperative tasks, emotional check-ins, turn-taking, and supportive feedback are not peripheral; they are part of effective language pedagogy.

### 2.2 Culturally responsive teaching

Holistic empowerment also requires cultural responsiveness. In English classrooms, learners bring different family histories, local cultures, dialects, experiences, and identities. <cite id="69f928a9-0">Culturally responsive teaching (CRT) refers to practices designed to build on students’ cultural, historical, and linguistic backgrounds as teaching and learning occur</cite>. Research further indicates that <cite id="69f928a9-0">CRT has been found to promote student engagement and enhance learning in the classroom</cite>.

For elementary English education, this has practical consequences. Vocabulary, stories, speaking tasks, and classroom examples should connect with children’s lived worlds instead of imposing a culturally detached textbook universe. When children see their experiences reflected in the curriculum, English becomes a medium for expression rather than a symbol of distance or deficiency.

### 2.3 Multimodality and developmentally appropriate literacy

Young learners do not learn language through print alone. They learn through gesture, image, sound, movement, play, role-play, and digital interaction. As one review of early childhood literacy notes, <cite id="d9fc0422-0">the literature shows that multimodality is present in forms of play; the use of toys, devices, and technology; drama; and social interactions.</cite> It also concludes that <cite id="d9fc0422-0">Through these modality-rich avenues, literacy development can still be achieved through engaging structures for children.</cite>

This is pedagogically important because multimodal learning is not merely decorative. <cite id="d9fc0422-0">Multimodality creates opportunities to position the student as the expert in their own learning and create collaborative learning environments.</cite> In elementary English teaching, songs, picture walks, storyboards, puppets, digital recordings, mini-dramas, and visual thinking routines can all deepen comprehension and participation, especially for children whose oral confidence develops more slowly than their understanding.

### 2.4 Formative assessment for growth

A holistic paradigm replaces one-shot judgment with ongoing evidence of learning. According to a recent systematic review, <cite id="7563db54-0">Formative assessment can support the English language teaching and learning in classroom settings.</cite> The same review found that it plays a <cite id="7563db54-0">substantial role in enhancing teaching efficacy and student outcomes</cite>. This is especially important in elementary English classrooms, where learning is uneven, cumulative, and often hidden in small changes of confidence, participation, pronunciation, and strategy use.

The review also reports that <cite id="7563db54-0">Innovative methods, such as technology-assisted and peer assessments, show promise in enhancing learner outcomes.</cite> At the same time, <cite id="7563db54-0">the education system and cultural contexts present persistent challenges in implementing formative assessment in EFL classes</cite>, and <cite id="7563db54-0">the importance of ensuring professional training for educators and raising student awareness regarding the benefits of formative assessment</cite> is emphasized. Thus, holistic empowerment requires teachers to use assessment not mainly to rank students, but to diagnose needs, guide instruction, and strengthen learner agency.

## 3. A New Paradigm: The Holistic Empowerment Model

Based on the evidence above, this paper proposes a holistic empowerment model for elementary English education with six interconnected dimensions.

First, it prioritizes **language competence through meaningful communication** rather than mechanical repetition alone. English should be used for sharing ideas, feelings, experiences, and collaborative work. Second, it includes **social-emotional growth**, because <cite id="e8ebacf5-1">SEL helps create the conditions for student learning</cite> and <cite id="81483ff5-6">significantly improved student academic achievement, school functioning, social and emotional skills</cite>.

Third, the model centers **cultural and linguistic affirmation**. Since <cite id="69f928a9-0">Culturally responsive teaching (CRT) refers to practices designed to build on students’ cultural, historical, and linguistic backgrounds</cite>, elementary English teaching should treat students’ home experiences as resources, not obstacles. Fourth, it values **multimodal participation**, because <cite id="d9fc0422-0">literacy development can still be achieved through engaging structures for children</cite> and <cite id="d9fc0422-0">create collaborative learning environments</cite> through multimodal work.

Fifth, the model adopts **formative assessment for empowerment**. Instead of waiting for final tests, teachers gather evidence continuously and adjust support in real time, consistent with the finding that <cite id="7563db54-0">Formative assessment can support the English language teaching and learning in classroom settings.</cite> Sixth, it builds **family-school partnership**, especially for multilingual children, so that classroom English learning is linked to the child’s home knowledge, identity, and storytelling practices.

In this paradigm, empowerment is not only the ability to score well in English. It is the ability to participate confidently, understand and be understood, connect languages and cultures, collaborate with others, and see oneself as a capable learner.

## 4. Pedagogical Implications for Elementary English Teaching

### 4.1 Designing emotionally safe English classrooms

In practice, holistic empowerment begins with classroom climate. Teachers can open lessons with simple emotional check-ins, partner greetings, or confidence-building routines before moving into target language practice. This approach is justified because <cite id="e8ebacf5-1">SEL helps create the conditions for student learning</cite>, while <cite id="81483ff5-0">students in grades 1–12 who participated in universal school-based SEL programs demonstrated better academic achievement</cite>.

For example, a lesson on “My Day” can combine sentence patterns with self-expression: “I feel happy when…,” “I am worried about…,” or “My friend helps me when….” Such tasks build language and empathy at the same time. For younger learners, puppets, emotion cards, and cooperative games provide low-anxiety opportunities for speaking.

### 4.2 Using culturally responsive content

A holistic paradigm also changes what counts as legitimate classroom content. Since <cite id="69f928a9-0">CRT has been found to promote student engagement and enhance learning in the classroom</cite>, English materials should connect to local festivals, family routines, neighborhood spaces, and children’s own narratives. Teachers can adapt textbook topics by asking students to compare “my family breakfast,” “our market,” or “our way to school” with the examples in the book.

This shift is especially important in contexts where English may otherwise feel socially distant. When children discuss familiar people, places, and practices, they have more to say and a stronger reason to say it. Cultural responsiveness therefore supports both inclusion and oral language production.

### 4.3 Expanding multimodal English learning

Holistic empowerment requires teachers to widen the channels through which children learn and show understanding. <cite id="d9fc0422-0">the literature shows that multimodality is present in forms of play; the use of toys, devices, and technology; drama; and social interactions</cite>, and <cite id="d9fc0422-0">Multimodality creates opportunities to position the student as the expert in their own learning</cite>. In elementary English, this means that drawing, building, acting, recording, singing, and moving can be legitimate demonstrations of comprehension.

A practical unit on animals, for instance, might include a picture-book read-aloud, a chant, a group poster, a puppet dialogue, and a short tablet recording. Such variation is developmentally appropriate and can support children with different strengths. It also helps teachers see abilities that would remain invisible in a print-only lesson.

### 4.4 Reframing assessment as ongoing support

Assessment should be integrated into daily teaching rather than reserved for final judgment. <cite id="7563db54-0">Formative assessment can support the English language teaching and learning in classroom settings</cite>, and <cite id="7563db54-0">Innovative methods, such as technology-assisted and peer assessments, show promise in enhancing learner outcomes.</cite> Therefore, elementary teachers can use observation notes, exit tickets, oral rehearsal, peer response, picture labeling, mini-whiteboard answers, and audio portfolios to track progress across listening, speaking, reading, and writing.

From a practice perspective, the power of formative assessment lies in immediacy. A teacher who notices that students can recognize vocabulary but cannot use it in sentences can modify the next activity on the spot. This is more empowering than simply recording errors after instruction has ended.

## 5. Practice-Informed Discussion: What Holistic Empowerment Looks Like in Real Teaching

One strong example of practice-linked holistic teaching comes from family-based storytelling. In a multilingual early childhood classroom, families were invited to <cite id="3cfa9d46-0">audio or video record themselves narrating a short story (in Spanish) about a traveling experience they had with their children</cite>. The teacher then created QR codes linked to these recordings and displayed them with family posters; <cite id="3cfa9d46-0">The children enjoy having their families featured in the classroom virtually, and they revisit the artifacts several times a day.</cite>

Although this example is from preschool, the principle transfers directly to elementary English education. A primary English teacher can invite families to share short home-language or bilingual stories, photos, or voice notes connected to a theme such as travel, food, weather, or celebrations. The English lesson can then build from these materials into vocabulary work, retelling, comparison, sentence frames, and simple presentations. In this way, children do not enter the English classroom by leaving their family world behind; they enter it by bringing that world with them.

A second practice implication concerns participation. Teachers often observe that some children understand more than they are ready to say publicly. The same family-story example shows a child who had been <cite id="3cfa9d46-0">reluctant to speak in group settings</cite> but spoke when supported by meaningful family-based materials. This suggests that confidence in English may grow when tasks are identity-affirming and emotionally safe, not merely linguistically simplified.

A third practice implication concerns teacher professionalism. The research on formative assessment warns that <cite id="7563db54-0">the education system and cultural contexts present persistent challenges in implementing formative assessment in EFL classes</cite> and stresses <cite id="7563db54-0">the importance of ensuring professional training for educators</cite>. In real classrooms, holistic empowerment therefore depends not only on teacher goodwill but also on training in feedback, observation, task design, culturally responsive methods, and multimodal pedagogy.

## 6. Challenges and Future Directions

Despite its promise, the holistic empowerment paradigm is not easy to implement. In many systems, time pressure, test orientation, large classes, and rigid curricula can limit teachers’ freedom to integrate play, SEL, or multimodal work. This concern is consistent with the finding that <cite id="7563db54-0">the education system and cultural contexts present persistent challenges in implementing formative assessment in EFL classes</cite>.

Future research should examine how holistic empowerment operates across different elementary contexts, including urban and rural schools, multilingual classrooms, and technology-rich versus resource-limited environments. More classroom-based studies are also needed to identify which combinations of SEL, CRT, multimodality, and formative assessment most effectively support young English learners over time.

## 7. Conclusion

This paper has argued that elementary English education needs a new paradigm: holistic empowerment. The case for this shift is clear: <cite id="e8ebacf5-0">SEL programs are a low-cost, evidence-based educational intervention that improves outcomes for all students</cite>; <cite id="81483ff5-6">participation in an SEL program significantly improved student academic achievement, school functioning, social and emotional skills</cite>; <cite id="69f928a9-0">CRT has been found to promote student engagement and enhance learning in the classroom</cite>; <cite id="d9fc0422-0">literacy development can still be achieved through engaging structures for children</cite> in multimodal environments; and <cite id="7563db54-0">Formative assessment can support the English language teaching and learning in classroom settings.</cite>

Taken together, these findings suggest that the most powerful elementary English classroom is not the one that focuses on language forms alone, but the one that develops the whole child through language. A holistic empowerment paradigm makes English education more humane, equitable, and effective by integrating communication, emotion, culture, assessment, and family partnership into one coherent vision of teaching and learning.

# Report: Construction and Application of a Sports Intelligent Tutoring and Learning Guidance System Driven by Multimodal Data Fusion

## 1. Executive Summary

<cite id="5442c12b-0">Recent advances in wearable, vision-based, trajectory, physiological, and multimodal sensing technologies, together with deep learning, have enabled continuous, objective, and individualized assessment of sport performance and athlete health.</cite> <cite id="7043f1ba-0">At the same time, intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) in education generally show positive effects on learning and performance, although their advantage can be reduced when compared against strong non-intelligent alternatives.</cite> <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">Educational studies also indicate that multimodal data fusion can outperform unimodal models for tracking learner states such as distress.</cite>

<cite id="f9763854-0">In sports teaching specifically, intelligent technologies are shifting instruction away from conventional methods toward personalised education based on real-time student responses and adaptive systems.</cite> Based on this evidence, a sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system should integrate <cite id="5442c12b-0">multisource sport sensing</cite>, <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">multimodal learner-state inference</cite>, and <cite id="84cd43c3-1">adaptive functions such as goal-setting, progress tracking, self-assessment, feedback, and performance prediction</cite> into one closed-loop platform.

## 2. Background and Significance

<cite id="7043f1ba-0">The use of AI in education has grown rapidly, particularly through ITSs, and the reviewed K-12 evidence suggests generally positive impacts on learning and performance.</cite> <cite id="b6326909-0">Recent ITS literature also highlights adaptive feedback mechanisms as a way to enhance comprehension and accelerate learning.</cite> These findings matter for sports because motor-skill learning depends not only on content delivery, but also on <cite id="f9763854-0">real-time responses, personalization, and adaptive systems in measurable skill domains such as track and field.</cite>

<cite id="84cd43c3-5">The evolution from unimodal to multimodal learning analytics represents a significant methodological shift in educational research.</cite> <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">One practical reason is that multimodal fusion has been shown to improve the tracking of learner distress compared with unimodal classifiers.</cite> In sports instruction, where performance quality, fatigue, technique, and engagement are all partially observable, that shift strongly supports a multimodal design.

## 3. Conceptual Definition of the Proposed System

A **sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system driven by multimodal data fusion** can be defined as an AI-enabled platform that collects heterogeneous sport and learning data, fuses them to model both skill execution and learner state, and then delivers adaptive guidance for training, teaching, and self-regulation. This definition is grounded in evidence that <cite id="5442c12b-0">heterogeneous sport data streams can be transformed into performance- and health-related decision support</cite> and that <cite id="84cd43c3-1">adaptive learning tools should include goal-setting, progress tracking, self-assessment, feedback mechanisms, and performance prediction.</cite>

In practical terms, the system sits at the intersection of sports analytics and tutoring. It should treat the learner not just as an athlete to be monitored, but as a student who needs <cite id="7043f1ba-0">learning support that improves performance</cite> and <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">state-aware interventions informed by multimodal evidence.</cite>

## 4. Theoretical and Technical Foundations

### 4.1 Multimodal Sports Intelligence

<cite id="5442c12b-0">The current sports-intelligence literature covers wearable, vision-based, trajectory, physiological, and multimodal sensing streams across both performance analysis and athlete health monitoring.</cite> <cite id="5442c12b-0">Reviewed applications include athlete and ball perception, multi-object tracking, pose estimation, action recognition, trajectory and tactical analysis, training-load and fatigue monitoring, injury-risk prediction, rehabilitation monitoring, and return-to-play support.</cite>

This is highly relevant for a tutoring system because sports learning is embodied: technique, workload, and readiness are all reflected in observable signals. A robust tutoring architecture should therefore use <cite id="5442c12b-0">visual, temporal, spatial, physiological, and multisource data</cite> rather than relying on only one modality.

### 4.2 Intelligent Tutoring and Adaptive Guidance

<cite id="7043f1ba-0">The systematic review of ITSs found generally positive effects on learning and performance, though more diverse and longer studies are still needed.</cite> <cite id="84cd43c3-1">Recommended adaptive features in learning analytics dashboards include goal-setting, progress tracking, self-assessment, feedback mechanisms, and performance prediction.</cite> These functions map naturally onto sports pedagogy: technique targets, workload goals, skill reflection, corrective feedback, and estimated readiness or achievement.

<cite id="f9763854-0">Track and field teaching has been identified as especially suitable for intelligent technologies because of its measurable objectives and quantifiable motor skills.</cite> This makes sports an excellent domain for ITS deployment, since many training outcomes can be instrumented and fed back in near real time.

### 4.3 Multimodal Learning Analytics for Learner-State Modeling

<cite id="2d72d0e4-0">In educational gameplay, multimodal data fusion using facial-expression recordings and gameplay logs improved distress-state tracking compared with unimodal classifiers.</cite> <cite id="84cd43c3-5">More broadly, multimodal learning analytics has become a major methodological direction in educational research.</cite> For sports tutoring, the implication is that learner support should not depend only on performance metrics; it should also infer states such as frustration, overload, disengagement, or confidence from multiple channels.

## 5. Proposed System Architecture

### 5.1 Layer 1: Multimodal Data Acquisition

The system should acquire at least four categories of input:

1. **Motion and biomechanics data** from IMUs, accelerometers, gyroscopes, or smart wearables, because <cite id="5442c12b-0">wearable sensing is now central to continuous and individualized sport assessment.</cite>  
2. **Video and pose data** from cameras or mobile phones, because <cite id="5442c12b-0">pose estimation, action recognition, and multi-object tracking are core reviewed applications in sport intelligence.</cite>  
3. **Physiological data** such as heart rate or fatigue-related indicators, because <cite id="5442c12b-0">training-load and fatigue monitoring, athlete health monitoring, and injury-risk prediction are established application areas.</cite>  
4. **Learning interaction data** such as task completion, error logs, response latency, self-reports, and practice history, because <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">gameplay logs can contribute meaningfully to multimodal learner-state prediction</cite> and <cite id="84cd43c3-1">progress tracking and self-assessment are recommended adaptive-learning features.</cite>

### 5.2 Layer 2: Preprocessing and Feature Engineering

The preprocessing layer should synchronize streams across time, clean noise, normalize sensor scales, extract kinematic or physiological features, and align these with instructional events. This is justified because <cite id="5442c12b-0">sport intelligence relies on heterogeneous data streams</cite> and because <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">multimodal educational data require data wrangling across multiple sources before supervised models can be built.</cite>

### 5.3 Layer 3: Multimodal Data Fusion and Modeling

Fusion can be implemented at early, intermediate, or late stages, depending on device constraints and model goals. The need for fusion is directly supported by evidence that <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">multimodal fusion improved learner-state classification over unimodal approaches</cite> and that <cite id="5442c12b-0">reliable multimodal data fusion strategies are a key research priority for sports intelligence.</cite>

The modeling layer should support at least three inference tasks:

- **Skill diagnosis**, using <cite id="5442c12b-0">pose estimation, action recognition, and trajectory analysis</cite>.  
- **Load and safety diagnosis**, using <cite id="5442c12b-0">training-load and fatigue monitoring, injury-risk prediction, and rehabilitation monitoring</cite>.  
- **Learner-state diagnosis**, using <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">multimodal prediction of states such as distress</cite> plus reflective learning features such as <cite id="84cd43c3-1">self-assessment and progress tracking.</cite>

### 5.4 Layer 4: Student/Athlete Model

A high-value sports ITS should maintain a dynamic learner profile containing technique level, physical readiness, learning pace, motivational state, and recent error patterns. This recommendation follows from evidence that <cite id="f9763854-0">sports teaching is moving toward personalized education based on real-time student responses</cite> and that <cite id="84cd43c3-1">adaptive systems should use performance prediction and feedback mechanisms.</cite>

### 5.5 Layer 5: Tutoring and Guidance Engine

The tutoring engine should translate model outputs into instructional actions, such as corrective cues, drill recommendations, rest prompts, challenge adjustment, and reflective questions. This is grounded in the educational literature showing that <cite id="b6326909-0">adaptive feedback mechanisms can enhance comprehension and accelerate learning</cite> and in sports-teaching evidence that <cite id="f9763854-0">intelligent optimization supports personalization through adaptive systems.</cite>

### 5.6 Layer 6: Interface and Delivery

The final layer should provide dashboards and feedback through coach terminals, athlete mobile apps, classroom screens, or wearable prompts. This aligns with <cite id="84cd43c3-1">recommended adaptive dashboard features such as goal-setting, progress tracking, self-assessment, feedback, and performance prediction.</cite>

## 6. Core Functional Modules

### 6.1 Technical Action Analysis

A core module should evaluate movement quality, posture, rhythm, and execution consistency. This is justified because <cite id="5442c12b-0">pose estimation and action recognition are key applications of deep learning in sensor-based sport performance monitoring.</cite>

### 6.2 Training Load and Health Monitoring

A second module should estimate load accumulation, fatigue risk, and readiness to continue training. The need is clear because <cite id="5442c12b-0">training-load and fatigue monitoring, injury-risk prediction, rehabilitation monitoring, and return-to-play support are major reviewed functions of modern sports intelligence.</cite>

### 6.3 Learning Process Monitoring

The system should also monitor whether the learner is engaged, confused, distressed, or progressing normally. This function is supported by <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">evidence that multimodal fusion can improve tracking of student distress during educational gameplay</cite> and by <cite id="84cd43c3-5">the broader rise of multimodal learning analytics.</cite>

### 6.4 Personalized Guidance and Feedback

The system should generate personalized prescriptions, such as “slow down arm recovery,” “repeat drill with lower intensity,” or “switch to scaffolding mode.” This design follows from <cite id="b6326909-0">evidence on the learning value of adaptive feedback</cite> and from <cite id="f9763854-0">sports-teaching research emphasizing personalized education driven by real-time responses.</cite>

### 6.5 Evaluation and Progress Forecasting

A final module should estimate future attainment, identify plateaus, and recommend next steps. This is directly aligned with <cite id="84cd43c3-1">performance prediction, progress tracking, and goal-setting as recommended adaptive features.</cite>

## 7. Major Application Scenarios

### 7.1 School Physical Education

In school PE, the system can help teachers manage large groups by automating technique assessment, attendance of effort, and differentiated guidance. This use case is plausible because <cite id="7043f1ba-0">ITSs have shown generally positive effects on learning and performance</cite> and because <cite id="f9763854-0">sports teaching with intelligent technologies supports personalized education in measurable motor-skill settings.</cite>

### 7.2 Track and Field Instruction

Track and field is a particularly strong initial deployment domain because <cite id="f9763854-0">it has measurable objectives and quantifiable motor skills</cite> and because the cited study frames intelligent optimization around <cite id="f9763854-0">real-time student responses and adaptive systems.</cite>

### 7.3 Competitive Training Support

For teams or elite development programs, the platform can combine coaching analytics with individualized tutoring. This follows from the sports review showing that <cite id="5442c12b-0">multimodal sports intelligence already supports tactical analysis, training-load monitoring, injury-risk prediction, and performance assessment.</cite>

### 7.4 Rehabilitation and Return to Play

The system can also guide recovering athletes by adjusting exercise difficulty, monitoring compliance, and flagging risky patterns. This application is grounded in <cite id="5442c12b-0">reviewed uses of deep learning for rehabilitation monitoring and return-to-play support.</cite>

### 7.5 Home and Remote Learning

A lighter version can deliver self-guided practice through a phone camera and wearable devices. This is reasonable because <cite id="5442c12b-0">vision-based and wearable sensing are both established in sport assessment</cite> and because <cite id="84cd43c3-1">feedback, self-assessment, and goal-setting are central adaptive-learning functions that can be surfaced remotely.</cite>

## 8. Construction Path and Implementation Roadmap

### 8.1 Stage 1: Requirement Analysis

The first step is to define sport-specific instructional objectives, observable indicators, and intervention rules. This is especially important because <cite id="f9763854-0">different sports tasks are measurable in distinct ways</cite> and because <cite id="5442c12b-0">modality-task-model relationships must be clarified for translational use.</cite>

### 8.2 Stage 2: Data Infrastructure and Labeling

The project should then build a multimodal dataset that aligns movement, physiology, instruction events, and outcomes. This is necessary because <cite id="5442c12b-0">data heterogeneity and annotation scarcity are key challenges</cite> and because <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">successful multimodal educational modeling depended on structured data collection and wrangling across sources.</cite>

### 8.3 Stage 3: Fusion-Model Development

Next, the project should compare early-, intermediate-, and late-fusion strategies for skill diagnosis and learner-state inference. The rationale is that <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">confidence-based multimodal fusion improved prediction</cite> and that <cite id="5442c12b-0">sports-intelligence research calls for reliable multimodal fusion strategies.</cite>

### 8.4 Stage 4: Tutoring Strategy Design

After model development, researchers should encode pedagogical policies for when and how to intervene. Those policies should include <cite id="84cd43c3-1">goal-setting, progress tracking, self-assessment, feedback mechanisms, and performance prediction</cite> and should be sensitive to <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">learner distress or other state changes.</cite>

### 8.5 Stage 5: Pilot Deployment

A phased pilot in one sport, one age band, and one institutional setting is preferable to immediate large-scale rollout. This caution is supported by <cite id="7043f1ba-0">the review’s call for longer and more diverse evaluations</cite> and by <cite id="5442c12b-0">ongoing concerns about cross-sport and cross-device generalization.</cite>

## 9. Evaluation Framework

A rigorous evaluation should cover three dimensions:

**Learning effectiveness.** The system should test whether users improve technique, understanding, and retention, because <cite id="7043f1ba-0">ITS research ultimately evaluates effects on learning and performance.</cite>

**Inference accuracy.** It should measure whether multimodal fusion improves prediction over single modalities, because <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">that advantage was observed in learner-distress tracking.</cite>

**Operational value.** It should assess latency, usability, and coach trust, especially because <cite id="5442c12b-0">real-time deployment constraints and model interpretability are recognized challenges.</cite>

## 10. Challenges and Risks

<cite id="5442c12b-0">Current challenges in sensor-based sports intelligence include data heterogeneity, annotation scarcity, limited cross-sport and cross-device generalization, real-time deployment constraints, model interpretability, privacy protection, and ethical governance.</cite> These are not peripheral issues; they directly affect whether a tutoring system can generalize, be trusted, and be adopted in real teaching environments.

Ethical issues are equally important on the educational side. <cite id="7043f1ba-0">The ITS review explicitly notes that the ethical implications of using AI for teaching should be investigated.</cite> Therefore, any deployed system should include informed consent, role-based data access, model-audit procedures, and minimally invasive sensing.

## 11. Practical Design Recommendations

Based on the retrieved evidence, the following design choices are the most defensible:

- Build the first version around <cite id="f9763854-0">sports with measurable objectives and quantifiable motor skills</cite>, such as track and field.  
- Combine <cite id="5442c12b-0">wearable, vision-based, and physiological sensing</cite> with <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">learning interaction logs</cite>.  
- Prioritize fusion models that can support both <cite id="5442c12b-0">skill/performance analysis</cite> and <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">learner-state detection.</cite>  
- Implement adaptive guidance around <cite id="84cd43c3-1">goal-setting, progress tracking, self-assessment, feedback, and performance prediction.</cite>  
- Treat interpretability and privacy as first-class requirements because <cite id="5442c12b-0">they are already recognized bottlenecks for real-world deployment.</cite>

## 12. Conclusion

<cite id="5442c12b-0">The convergence of deep learning with wearable, vision, trajectory, physiological, and multimodal sensing has made individualized sports assessment technically feasible.</cite> <cite id="7043f1ba-0">In parallel, ITS research provides evidence that AI-guided tutoring can improve learning and performance, even if stronger long-term evaluation is still needed.</cite> <cite id="2d72d0e4-0">Multimodal fusion further strengthens the case by improving learner-state tracking over unimodal approaches.</cite>

Taken together, these findings support the construction of a sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system that does more than monitor athletes: it diagnoses skill, interprets learner state, and delivers adaptive pedagogical support. The most promising path is a multimodal, personalized, and ethically governed platform that joins <cite id="5442c12b-0">sports decision support</cite> with <cite id="84cd43c3-1">adaptive learning functions</cite> in a single closed loop.

## References Used in This Report

# Report: A Data-Fusion-Driven Tutoring and Learning Guidance System

## Executive Summary

A strong case exists for building a tutoring and learning-guidance system around data fusion rather than a single data stream. <cite id="d090d766-0">Multimodal learning analytics (MMLA) can help provide an accurate understanding of learning processes</cite>, and its evidence base shows that <cite id="d090d766-0">the data in MMLA are classified into digital data, physical data, physiological data, psychometric data, and environment data</cite> while <cite id="d090d766-0">the learning indicators are behavior, cognition, emotion, collaboration, and engagement</cite>. For tutoring specifically, the broader ITS literature suggests that <cite id="ddb9063a-0">the effects of ITSs on learning and performance in K-12 education are generally positive</cite>, although <cite id="ddb9063a-0">their effects are mitigated when compared to non-intelligent tutoring systems</cite> and <cite id="ddb9063a-0">additional research with longer interventions and increased sample sizes with greater diversity is warranted</cite>.

The practical implication is that a next-generation tutoring platform should not merely recommend content from quiz scores alone. It should fuse multiple signals into a dynamic learner model, then use that model to drive personalized tutoring, learning guidance, and teacher-facing support. That direction is promising because <cite id="63450cfc-4">fusion of multimodal data brings significantly better prediction of learning outcomes and helps us to interpret complex learning processes</cite>, and task-level studies show that <cite id="63450cfc-0">the classifier with multimodal data fusion improves the performance of tracking distress states during educational activities</cite>. But any such system must be governed carefully, because <cite id="7e6e2a26-0">educational systems must govern their use of AI systems</cite> and leading ethics work highlights <cite id="1839651b-4">transparency, privacy, accountability, fairness</cite> as core principles.

## 1) What “data fusion” means in a tutoring context

In this domain, data fusion means combining heterogeneous learner data so the system can infer states that no single signal captures well on its own. The most useful current framing comes from multimodal learning analytics, where <cite id="d090d766-0">the relationships between multimodal data and learning indicators are one-to-one, one-to-any, and many-to-one</cite> and <cite id="d090d766-0">the complex relationships between multimodal data and learning indicators are the key for data fusion</cite>. In other words, a tutoring system should expect that one observed signal may reflect multiple latent learning states, and that one learning state may require several data sources to estimate reliably.

The same review also clarifies the main technical patterns. <cite id="d090d766-0">The main data fusion methods in MMLA are many-to-one, many-to-many and multiple validations among multimodal data</cite>. For a tutoring platform, that translates into combining activity logs, assessments, timing data, self-reports, and possibly classroom or sensor data into a learner model that estimates mastery, engagement, confusion, help-seeking, and risk.

## 2) Why data fusion is relevant to tutoring and learning guidance

A traditional ITS often focuses on problem-solving traces and correctness data, but a data-fusion-driven system aims to guide both learning and learning conditions. This matters because <cite id="63450cfc-4">fusion of multimodal data brings significantly better prediction of learning outcomes</cite> and also <cite id="63450cfc-4">helps us to interpret complex learning processes</cite>. That second benefit is important: learning guidance is not just about selecting the next exercise, but also about identifying why a learner is struggling, disengaged, overconfident, or distressed.

The evidence is especially compelling when the target is hard to observe directly. For example, <cite id="63450cfc-0">multimodal data fusion improves the performance of tracking distress states during educational activities</cite>. In a tutoring setting, better detection of distress or disengagement can support timely interventions such as switching difficulty, adding hints, prompting a break, or escalating to a teacher or counselor when appropriate.

## 3) Proposed system concept

### 3.1 Core objective

The proposed system should be designed to do three things simultaneously:

1. diagnose learner state,
2. deliver personalized tutoring,
3. generate actionable learning guidance for students and teachers.

This orientation is justified because ITS research centers on <cite id="5a362a43-0">adaptive learning, student modeling</cite>, while multimodal analytics shows that effective diagnosis requires multiple forms of evidence rather than a single score stream. A data-fusion-driven architecture therefore extends classic ITS design by making the learner model broader, more contextual, and more responsive.

### 3.2 Data inputs

A practical input layer should prioritize the sources most directly supported by current evidence. At minimum, the system should ingest academic and behavioral data such as problem attempts, correctness, hints requested, time-on-task, revision history, and assessment results. This aligns with the review evidence that <cite id="d090d766-0">the data in MMLA are classified into digital data, physical data, physiological data, psychometric data, and environment data</cite>.

In higher-maturity deployments, the system can add optional streams such as self-reported confidence, attention proxies, collaboration traces, or classroom context. The goal is not to collect all possible data, but to capture the signals most predictive of learning and most defensible ethically.

### 3.3 Fusion and learner modeling layer

The system’s analytic core should transform raw multimodal streams into a continually updated learner profile. Because <cite id="d090d766-0">the learning indicators are behavior, cognition, emotion, collaboration, and engagement</cite>, the learner model should represent more than mastery alone. It should estimate at least:

- current knowledge/mastery,
- engagement level,
- confusion/distress risk,
- help-seeking style,
- persistence/self-regulation,
- collaboration quality where group work exists.

Technically, the platform can use staged fusion rather than a monolithic model. Early-stage fusion can align timestamps and normalize events; mid-stage fusion can create features by modality; late-stage fusion can combine submodel outputs into final predictions. This is a reasonable design implication of the finding that <cite id="d090d766-0">the main data fusion methods in MMLA are many-to-one, many-to-many and multiple validations among multimodal data</cite>.

### 3.4 Tutoring engine

The tutoring engine should map learner-state estimates to instructional actions. Examples include:

- selecting the next task,
- adjusting difficulty,
- choosing explanation depth,
- timing hints,
- recommending review,
- suggesting peer or teacher support.

This is where the system becomes more than analytics. Because the ITS evidence suggests <cite id="ddb9063a-0">the effects of ITSs on learning and performance in K-12 education are generally positive</cite>, a well-designed tutoring engine is likely to add value. But the same review warns against overclaiming, since <cite id="ddb9063a-0">their effects are mitigated when compared to non-intelligent tutoring systems</cite>. So the system should be framed as augmenting instruction, not replacing sound pedagogy.

### 3.5 Learning-guidance layer

A distinctive feature of this proposed system is a separate guidance layer for students and teachers. For students, guidance should explain what to do next: revise concept X, attempt two scaffolded problems, ask for help on step Y, or slow down because accuracy is dropping. For teachers, guidance should prioritize who needs intervention, what pattern is emerging, and whether the issue looks cognitive, emotional, or behavioral.

This design follows directly from the evidence that multimodal fusion improves both prediction and interpretability. <cite id="63450cfc-4">Fusion of multimodal data brings significantly better prediction of learning outcomes</cite> and <cite id="63450cfc-4">helps us to interpret complex learning processes</cite>, which is exactly what teacher-facing guidance requires.

## 4) Expected benefits

### 4.1 Better diagnosis than single-source systems

The main benefit is a more complete view of the learner. A single quiz score can indicate poor performance, but not whether the cause is low mastery, low engagement, confusion, anxiety, or poor self-regulation. Multimodal analytics is promising here because <cite id="d090d766-0">multimodal learning analytics can help provide an accurate understanding of learning processes</cite>.

### 4.2 Stronger prediction and earlier intervention

A fused system should detect risk earlier than score-only dashboards. The evidence base supports that expectation: <cite id="63450cfc-4">fusion of multimodal data brings significantly better prediction of learning outcomes</cite>. It also supports sensitive state detection, as <cite id="63450cfc-0">multimodal data fusion improves the performance of tracking distress states</cite>. In practice, that means earlier support for struggling learners and more timely escalation when a student is not merely wrong, but overwhelmed.

### 4.3 More personalized tutoring and guidance

Because learner state is modeled more richly, intervention can be more personalized. A student with low mastery and high engagement may need more worked examples; a student with moderate mastery but rising distress may need encouragement, a simpler step, or teacher contact. This personalization logic is consistent with ITS work emphasizing <cite id="5a362a43-0">adaptive learning, student modeling</cite>.

## 5) Risks, limitations, and governance

### 5.1 Evidence is promising, not definitive

The most important limitation is that the educational effect size of ITS is not uniformly transformative. The best recent synthesis found that <cite id="ddb9063a-0">the real educational value remains unclear</cite> and that <cite id="ddb9063a-0">the effects of ITSs on learning and performance in K-12 education are generally positive but are found to be mitigated when compared to non-intelligent tutoring systems</cite>. Therefore, a data-fusion-driven tutoring system should be evaluated as a school improvement intervention, not assumed effective by design.

### 5.2 Privacy and surveillance risk

Data fusion increases capability, but it also increases sensitivity. Ethics research in K-12 AI warns that <cite id="1839651b-9">one of the biggest ethical issues surrounding the use of AI in K-12 education relates to the privacy concerns of students and teachers</cite>. This matters especially if the system uses physiological, video, audio, or affective signals, because these can be much more intrusive than clickstream or assessment data.

### 5.3 Bias, opacity, and accountability

A fusion model can amplify hidden bias if certain students are overrepresented in training data or if proxies reflect disability, language background, or socioeconomic conditions. That is why educational AI ethics frameworks emphasize <cite id="1839651b-4">transparency, privacy, accountability, fairness</cite>. If a system recommends interventions or flags student distress, schools must know how decisions are made, who can challenge them, and how model performance differs across groups.

### 5.4 Responsible deployment is a governance problem, not just a technical one

The public-sector AI guidance is explicit that <cite id="7e6e2a26-0">educational systems must govern their use of AI systems</cite>. A school or university therefore needs policies for consent, data minimization, retention, human review, procurement, security, and incident response—not just a good model.

## 6) Recommended design principles

Based on the evidence, a credible system should follow these principles.

First, fuse only data that clearly improve educational decisions. This follows from the fact that multimodal data are valuable when they improve diagnosis or prediction, not merely because they are available. The review literature supports fusion where <cite id="63450cfc-4">it brings significantly better prediction of learning outcomes</cite> and <cite id="63450cfc-4">helps us to interpret complex learning processes</cite>.

Second, keep the learner model educationally meaningful. Since <cite id="d090d766-0">the learning indicators are behavior, cognition, emotion, collaboration, and engagement</cite>, the model should report actionable constructs teachers recognize, rather than opaque raw scores.

Third, build human-in-the-loop workflows. This is the safest implication of the combined evidence: ITS can help, but <cite id="ddb9063a-0">additional research with longer interventions and increased sample sizes with greater diversity is warranted</cite>, while ethical risks remain substantial. Teacher review should therefore be built into high-stakes interventions or student-risk flags.

Fourth, prioritize responsible AI controls from the outset. The governance baseline should reflect <cite id="1839651b-4">transparency, privacy, accountability, fairness</cite> and the broader warning that <cite id="7e6e2a26-0">educational systems must govern their use of AI systems</cite>.

## 7) Suggested implementation roadmap

A prudent rollout would begin with low-risk, high-value data: LMS logs, assessments, assignment history, and self-reported confidence. That phase would test whether fusion improves prediction and tutoring decisions over a score-only baseline, consistent with the evidence that <cite id="63450cfc-4">fusion of multimodal data brings significantly better prediction of learning outcomes</cite>.

A second phase could add richer guidance features, including teacher dashboards and student next-step recommendations. Only after demonstrating benefit and establishing privacy protections should the institution consider more sensitive modalities. This is especially important given that <cite id="1839651b-9">privacy concerns of students and teachers</cite> are among the biggest ethical issues in school AI.

Evaluation should include not just accuracy, but educational impact: learning gains, persistence, engagement, subgroup fairness, false-alert rates, and teacher trust. That emphasis is justified because the ITS review found both promise and remaining uncertainty: <cite id="ddb9063a-0">the effects of ITSs on learning and performance are generally positive</cite>, yet <cite id="ddb9063a-0">their real educational value remains unclear</cite> without stronger evidence.

## Conclusion

A tutoring and learning-guidance system driven by data fusion is a credible and forward-looking educational architecture. The research base supports the idea that <cite id="d090d766-0">multimodal learning analytics can help provide an accurate understanding of learning processes</cite>, that <cite id="63450cfc-4">fusion of multimodal data brings significantly better prediction of learning outcomes</cite>, and that ITS themselves usually have <cite id="ddb9063a-0">generally positive</cite> effects. The most defensible conclusion is therefore not that data fusion guarantees better tutoring, but that it creates a stronger foundation for diagnosis, personalization, and guidance—provided the system is implemented with rigorous evaluation and strong safeguards for <cite id="1839651b-4">transparency, privacy, accountability, fairness</cite>.

# Report on the Construction and Application of a Sports Intelligent Tutoring and Learning Guidance System Driven by Multimodal Data Fusion

## 1. Executive Summary

A sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system driven by multimodal data fusion should combine learner-performance sensing, AI-based analysis, and adaptive feedback into a closed instructional loop. In education research, <cite id="e5e93d17-0">multimodal learning analytics (MMLA) can provide an accurate understanding of learning processes</cite>, and its data sources can include <cite id="e5e93d17-0">digital, physical, physiological, psychometric, and environment data</cite>. In physical education, recent evidence shows that digital-intelligent technologies now form <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">a closed-loop system that includes intelligent instructional design, real-time process visualization, and data-driven evaluation and feedback</cite>. This makes multimodal fusion a strong foundation for sports tutoring systems, where skill learning depends on movement quality, workload, cognition, and motivation rather than on text-based performance alone.

The proposed system should therefore fuse video, wearable, physiological, and interaction data to generate personalized diagnosis and coaching. This design is well aligned with both intelligent tutoring and sports biomechanics research: ITSs are intended to <cite id="4ad245a3-7">provide immediate and customized instruction or feedback to learners</cite>, while AI in sports biomechanics is being used for <cite id="f920f458-0">enhancing performance and preventing injuries</cite>. A practical implementation goal is not merely automation, but a safe and explainable assistant for teachers, coaches, and learners.

## 2. Why Multimodal Fusion Is Necessary in Sports Tutoring

Sports learning is intrinsically multimodal. A learner’s progress cannot be inferred reliably from a single source because technical execution, physiological load, engagement, and tactical understanding may diverge during practice. MMLA research specifically notes that the key challenge is the <cite id="e5e93d17-0">complex relationships between multimodal data and learning indicators</cite>, and that the main fusion patterns include <cite id="e5e93d17-0">many-to-one, many-to-many and multiple validations among multimodal data</cite>. That insight is especially relevant in sport, where multiple data streams must often be fused to infer one coaching judgment such as “movement quality,” “fatigue risk,” or “mastery of a drill.”

The physical-education literature also supports this direction. A recent systematic review found that digital-intelligent technologies in PE have enabled <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">more intelligent, personalized, and data-informed instructional practices</cite>, with key innovations including <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">adaptive learning platforms, virtual simulation tools, multimodal assessment systems, and health behavior monitoring</cite>. Together, these findings suggest that multimodal fusion is not a peripheral feature but the core technical mechanism needed to turn fragmented sports data into actionable teaching decisions.

## 3. Conceptual Objectives of the System

The system should pursue three coordinated objectives. First, it should support skill acquisition by detecting technique quality and offering timely guidance. This is consistent with ITS research showing that such systems enable <cite id="4ad245a3-1">personalized instruction and real-time adaptability</cite> and can use <cite id="4ad245a3-0">adaptive feedback mechanisms</cite> to enhance learning. Second, it should support physical safety by integrating movement and workload analytics for injury prevention. Sports biomechanics evidence shows AI is already used for <cite id="f920f458-0">injury prediction</cite> and that <cite id="f920f458-0">integrated AI systems resulted in a 23% reduction in reinjury rates</cite>. Third, it should support teaching efficiency by helping coaches and PE instructors scale individualized supervision across many learners.

In practice, this means the system should not only score performance but also explain what to improve, when to reduce load, and how instruction should adapt to the learner’s current state. That combination of diagnosis, recommendation, and progression control is what turns analytics into tutoring.

## 4. System Construction: Recommended Architecture

### 4.1 Layer 1: Multimodal Data Acquisition

The sensing layer should collect complementary modalities that reflect both learning and physical execution. MMLA research classifies relevant data into <cite id="e5e93d17-0">digital data, physical data, physiological data, psychometric data, and environment data</cite>. For a sports tutoring system, these categories can be translated as follows:

- **Digital data:** drill completion, app interactions, quiz/tactics answers, training history  
- **Physical data:** pose, kinematics, trajectory, repetition counts, velocities  
- **Physiological data:** heart rate, HRV, fatigue proxies, energy expenditure  
- **Psychometric data:** self-efficacy, perceived exertion, motivation, confidence  
- **Environment data:** venue, weather, equipment, surface, class context

The sports and PE literature gives direct support for such sensing. In PE, <cite id="12fff2cb-0">wearable devices were used to collect students' movement data</cite>. In sports biomechanics, AI systems increasingly use <cite id="f920f458-0">wearable technology, motion analysis, and injury prevention</cite> approaches, while computer vision has achieved <cite id="f920f458-0">accuracy within 15 mm compared to marker-based systems</cite>. This indicates that a practical sensing stack can combine camera-based pose estimation with inertial or physiological wearables, depending on cost and context.

### 4.2 Layer 2: Data Management and Synchronization

A multimodal system must align heterogeneous streams in time and context. Because MMLA emphasizes the importance of relationships between data types and indicators, <cite id="e5e93d17-0">the complex relationships between multimodal data and learning indicators are the key for data fusion</cite>. System construction should therefore include timestamp alignment, session segmentation, learner identifiers, missing-data handling, and quality scoring for each sensor stream.

This layer should also support privacy-preserving storage policies because bodily and behavioral data are particularly sensitive in sports education. Learning analytics research identifies <cite id="8a4cfe59-4">student privacy</cite> as <cite id="8a4cfe59-4">one of the most pressing concerns</cite> in collecting and using educational data, and PE reviews likewise report <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">data privacy</cite> among major implementation challenges.

### 4.3 Layer 3: Multimodal Fusion and AI Modeling

The intelligence core should use multimodal fusion methods to transform sensor data into interpretable indicators. MMLA reviews identify the major fusion categories as <cite id="e5e93d17-0">many-to-one, many-to-many and multiple validations among multimodal data</cite>. For sports tutoring, representative modeling tasks include:

- technique classification from video + IMU
- fatigue/risk estimation from workload + physiological signals + movement degradation
- engagement inference from participation logs + facial/voice or self-report signals
- learning progression estimation from repeated drill performance across sessions

Sports biomechanics research supports this AI-centered approach. The field has seen <cite id="f920f458-0">a shift from traditional statistical models to advanced machine learning methods</cite>. Moreover, <cite id="f920f458-0">convolutional neural networks reached 94% agreement with international experts in technique assessment</cite>, suggesting that expert-level movement evaluation is increasingly feasible for selected tasks. However, model choice should balance performance with explainability, since deployment still faces <cite id="f920f458-0">challenges remain, including standardizing data, improving model interpretability, validating models in real-world settings, and integrating them into coaching routines</cite>.

### 4.4 Layer 4: Student Model and Domain Model

A true tutoring system needs an internal learner model, not just analytics dashboards. ITS literature characterizes these systems as tools that <cite id="4ad245a3-7">provide immediate and customized instruction or feedback to learners</cite> and enable <cite id="4ad245a3-1">real-time adaptability</cite>. In sports, the learner model should represent at least four dimensions:

1. **Skill mastery:** correctness and consistency of movement patterns  
2. **Physical state:** workload tolerance, fatigue, recovery, injury risk  
3. **Cognitive understanding:** rules, tactics, training concepts  
4. **Affective/motivational state:** engagement, confidence, frustration, adherence

The domain model should encode expert knowledge about movement phases, common errors, drill progressions, safety thresholds, and sport-specific training principles. This is where the system translates raw predictions into pedagogically meaningful guidance.

### 4.5 Layer 5: Tutoring, Feedback, and Guidance Engine

The guidance engine should convert model outputs into personalized interventions. ITS evidence indicates that <cite id="4ad245a3-0">adaptive feedback mechanisms can enhance comprehension and accelerate learning</cite>, and that systems are designed for <cite id="4ad245a3-1">real-time personalized and adaptive learning</cite>. In sports, this can be implemented through:

- **Immediate corrective feedback:** “Your knee valgus increases during landing; widen stance and soften hip flexion.”
- **Session-level guidance:** “Reduce volume due to rising fatigue indicators.”
- **Progressive drill recommendation:** “Advance from assisted to unassisted movement.”
- **Teacher/coach alerts:** “High-risk pattern repeated across 5 trials.”
- **Reflective feedback:** trend charts on consistency, adherence, and improvement

The PE literature supports this design, showing that digital-intelligent technologies enable <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">real-time process visualization</cite> and <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">data-driven evaluation and feedback</cite>. Sports biomechanics research also reports that <cite id="f920f458-0">learning management systems enhanced knowledge transfer, raising coaches’ understanding by 45% and athlete adherence by 3.4 times</cite>, which implies that the system should serve both learners and instructors rather than replacing either.

## 5. Core Functional Modules

### 5.1 Technical Skill Diagnosis Module

This module uses video, pose, IMU, and repetition history to assess technique quality and error patterns. Its value is strongly supported by evidence that in sports biomechanics, <cite id="f920f458-0">convolutional neural networks reached 94% agreement with international experts in technique assessment</cite>. For sports like sprinting, jumping, racket sports, or resistance training, this module can provide frame-level or phase-level feedback.

### 5.2 Load Monitoring and Injury Prevention Module

This module fuses workload, biomechanics, and physiology to estimate risk and optimize training dosage. The rationale is clear: the sports biomechanics review reports that <cite id="f920f458-0">random forest models predicted hamstring injuries with 85% accuracy</cite> and that integrated AI deployment produced <cite id="f920f458-0">a 23% reduction in reinjury rates</cite>. In educational settings, this module is especially important because novice learners often lack self-regulation about fatigue and overuse.

### 5.3 Personalized Learning Path Module

This module selects drills, difficulty, pacing, and review tasks for each learner. ITS research supports this by describing systems that enable <cite id="4ad245a3-1">personalized instruction and real-time adaptability</cite> and <cite id="4ad245a3-7">immediate and customized instruction or feedback</cite>. In PE settings, the broader review also found the use of <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">adaptive learning platforms</cite>.

### 5.4 Teacher/Coach Decision Support Module

This module summarizes class and individual data to help teachers intervene efficiently. The goal is not simply automation but decision support. That orientation is consistent with the finding that digital-intelligent technologies in PE support <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">data-driven evaluation and feedback</cite> and with evidence from sports biomechanics that LMS-supported AI tools improved <cite id="f920f458-0">coaches’ understanding</cite> and learner adherence.

### 5.5 Learning Reflection and Motivation Module

Because sports learning depends on persistence and confidence, the system should visualize improvement trajectories and provide self-regulation prompts. MMLA research explicitly tracks learning indicators such as <cite id="e5e93d17-0">behavior, cognition, emotion, collaboration, and engagement</cite>. That means a good sports tutoring system should monitor not only biomechanics but also engagement and emotional response to training.

## 6. Application Scenarios

### 6.1 School Physical Education

The strongest immediate application is school PE, where one teacher supervises many students with limited time. The PE systematic review concludes that digital-intelligent technologies have been adopted <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">across all stages of PE</cite> and have reshaped the field through <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">personalized, and data-informed instructional practices</cite>. In this setting, the system can support movement screening, differentiated instruction, health monitoring, and formative assessment.

### 6.2 University Sports Instruction and Skill Courses

In higher education, the system can support technique-intensive courses such as athletics, gymnastics, swimming, tennis, and strength training. MMLA’s ability to integrate diverse indicators is useful here because performance evaluation often mixes technical execution, attendance, knowledge, and progression. The system can offer semi-automated scoring while retaining teacher oversight.

### 6.3 Competitive Coaching and Athlete Development

At the competitive level, the same architecture can be extended with higher-resolution sensing and more advanced biomechanical models. This is supported by sports biomechanics evidence showing AI’s role in <cite id="f920f458-0">enhancing performance and preventing injuries</cite>. Compared with school PE, the emphasis shifts toward precision technique assessment, individualized load management, and return-to-play support.

### 6.4 Rehabilitation and Return-to-Sport Learning

A sports tutoring system can also guide learners recovering from injury, where the distinction between “training” and “learning” is blurred. The value proposition is strong because <cite id="f920f458-0">integrated AI systems resulted in a 23% reduction in reinjury rates</cite>. Here, tutoring focuses on safe movement reacquisition, graded progression, and adherence.

## 7. Implementation Roadmap

### 7.1 Phase 1: Define Pedagogical Targets

Start with a narrow instructional scope such as sprint starts, squat technique, badminton overhead stroke, or jump landing. The chosen unit should have clear skill rubrics, common error taxonomies, and measurable outcomes. This approach improves feasibility and addresses the sports-biomechanics concern that models still need <cite id="f920f458-0">validating in real-world settings</cite>.

### 7.2 Phase 2: Build the Multimodal Dataset

Collect synchronized data from a pilot cohort using selected modalities such as mobile video, IMU, heart rate, and learner self-report. Because MMLA highlights <cite id="e5e93d17-0">the key stages in data fusion</cite>, dataset design should explicitly connect sensor streams to target indicators like technique quality, fatigue, or engagement.

### 7.3 Phase 3: Train and Validate Models

Use expert-labeled movement data for supervised tasks and repeated-session data for progression modeling. A key principle is triangulation: since MMLA supports <cite id="e5e93d17-0">multiple validations among multimodal data</cite>, the system should confirm important decisions across more than one signal where possible.

### 7.4 Phase 4: Design Feedback Interfaces

Feedback should differ by user role. Learners need simple, actionable prompts; teachers need interpretable evidence and confidence indicators; coaches may need trend dashboards and risk alerts. The PE review supports such design with its emphasis on <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">real-time process visualization</cite> and <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">data-driven evaluation and feedback</cite>.

### 7.5 Phase 5: Deploy as Human-in-the-Loop Tutoring

Initial deployment should keep coaches and teachers in the loop. This is advisable because implementation barriers include <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">algorithmic accuracy, data privacy, and unequal access to digital resources</cite>, while sports biomechanics research warns that integration into coaching routines remains challenging. Human oversight reduces the risk of overtrust and makes the feedback educationally accountable.

## 8. Evaluation Framework

A robust evaluation should cover instructional, technical, and organizational performance.

**Instructional outcomes** should include skill improvement, error reduction, transfer, retention, motivation, and adherence. There is reason for optimism because ITS evidence indicates learning benefits are generally positive, with systems using <cite id="4ad245a3-0">adaptive feedback mechanisms</cite> and <cite id="4ad245a3-1">real-time personalized and adaptive learning</cite>.

**Technical outcomes** should include sensing reliability, fusion accuracy, latency, robustness to missing data, and model calibration. This matters because the sports biomechanics literature still points to challenges in <cite id="f920f458-0">standardizing data</cite> and <cite id="f920f458-0">improving model interpretability</cite>.

**Operational outcomes** should include teacher workload, usability, acceptance, and equity of access. This aligns with the PE review’s identification of <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">unequal access to digital resources</cite> as a practical barrier.

## 9. Risks, Ethics, and Governance

A sports tutoring system built on multimodal fusion raises substantial ethical issues because it collects bodily, behavioral, and sometimes health-related data. Learning analytics literature identifies <cite id="8a4cfe59-4">student privacy</cite> as <cite id="8a4cfe59-4">one of the most pressing concerns</cite>, and MMLA-specific work also points to the tension between analytics and privacy. In PE, implementation challenges explicitly include <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">data privacy</cite>.

Beyond privacy, fairness and interpretability are crucial. If models are trained on narrow populations or specific camera conditions, they may generalize poorly across age groups, genders, body types, or sports levels. This risk is consistent with the broader finding that deployment still requires better <cite id="f920f458-0">validating models in real-world settings</cite>. Governance should therefore include consent protocols, data minimization, retention limits, explainable feedback, human appeal mechanisms, and periodic bias audits.

## 10. Key Design Recommendations

A high-quality sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system should:

1. Use multimodal sensing by default, because <cite id="e5e93d17-0">multimodal data fusion can be characterized by the multimodality of data, multi-dimension of indicators, and diversity of methods</cite>.  
2. Implement a closed teaching loop, reflecting PE evidence that effective digital-intelligent systems combine <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">intelligent instructional design, real-time process visualization, and data-driven evaluation and feedback</cite>.  
3. Prioritize adaptive feedback and personalization, consistent with ITS research on <cite id="4ad245a3-7">immediate and customized instruction</cite> and <cite id="4ad245a3-1">real-time adaptability</cite>.  
4. Include injury-prevention analytics alongside skill tutoring, since AI in sports biomechanics supports both <cite id="f920f458-0">enhancing performance and preventing injuries</cite>.  
5. Retain human oversight because implementation still faces <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">algorithmic accuracy</cite>, privacy, and equity constraints, and because sports models need stronger real-world validation.

## 11. Conclusion

The construction of a sports intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system should be understood as the integration of MMLA, intelligent tutoring, and sports biomechanics into one coherent educational platform. The research base shows that MMLA offers <cite id="e5e93d17-0">an accurate understanding of learning processes</cite>, ITSs provide <cite id="4ad245a3-7">immediate and customized instruction or feedback</cite>, and AI in sports can support <cite id="f920f458-0">enhancing performance and preventing injuries</cite>. Physical-education evidence further suggests that the most effective implementations operate as a <cite id="1b47d1ac-0">closed-loop system</cite> linking design, monitoring, and feedback.

Overall, the most promising path is a human-centered, multimodal, adaptive system that supports teachers and coaches rather than replacing them. If built with careful fusion design, strong pedagogy, privacy safeguards, and real-world validation, such a system can make sports instruction more personalized, data-informed, and safer for learners.
