fully_underspecified.text: Research light-based therapies in medicine for treating skin aging, whitening, and pigmentation issues.
fully_underspecified.answer:
## Bottom line

<cite id="SN2">Lasers and light-based therapies are now central tools in cosmetic dermatology for problems such as photoaging and hyperpigmentation.</cite> For “whitening,” the best-supported medical use is <cite id="SN34">lightening localized areas of excess pigment rather than generalized skin lightening</cite>, because <cite id="SN33">these devices work by targeting melanin or pigment-containing cells through selective photothermolysis.</cite>

## How these therapies work

For pigment disorders, the core principle is <cite id="SN15">selective photothermolysis</cite>: <cite id="SN33">wavelengths preferentially absorbed by melanin create thermal or photoacoustic injury in melanosomes or pigment-containing cells.</cite> This is why pigment-targeting lasers can <cite id="SN15">destroy pigment-bearing cells while limiting damage to surrounding tissue.</cite>

Not all light therapies work by heating pigment. <cite id="SN31">Red LED-based photobiomodulation is proposed to improve skin rejuvenation by stimulating fibroblast activity, collagen synthesis, and anti-inflammatory pathways</cite>, while <cite id="SN5">photodynamic therapy (PDT) uses a photosensitizer such as ALA or MAL plus visible light</cite> to target <cite id="SN5">pilosebaceous units and actinic-damaged skin.</cite>

## Best-supported uses for skin aging and photoaging

For wrinkles, texture, and sun-damaged skin, the strongest established options are fractional lasers and IPL. <cite id="SN37">Ablative fractional resurfacing with CO2 or Er:YAG lasers can produce substantial improvement in wrinkles, texture, and dyschromia in photoaged skin</cite>, but <cite id="SN37">it comes with more downtime and a higher risk of adverse events than nonablative approaches.</cite>

If a patient wants less downtime, <cite id="SN38">nonablative fractional lasers improve photoaging with a more favorable safety profile and shorter recovery</cite>, although <cite id="SN38">multiple sessions are often needed and wrinkle reduction is usually less dramatic than with ablative resurfacing.</cite> Similarly, <cite id="SN7">IPL and nonablative fractional laser are popular for skin rejuvenation, with consistent improvements in texture, wrinkles, and pigmentation after a series of treatments</cite> and <cite id="SN7">a lower adverse-event profile than ablative lasers.</cite>

IPL is especially useful when photoaging includes both redness and blotchy pigment because <cite id="SN29">it emits noncoherent, polychromatic light over a broad wavelength range and can be filtered to target melanin, hemoglobin, or water.</cite> In comparative evidence, <cite id="SN30">both IPL and nonablative fractional laser improved photoaging, but IPL performed better for dyspigmentation while fractional laser was superior for wrinkles.</cite>

PDT is another option for photorejuvenation, especially when photoaging overlaps with actinic damage. <cite id="SN39">Topical PDT using ALA or MAL activated by blue, red, IPL, or daylight sources has reported benefits for fine lines, mottled pigmentation, roughness, and actinic damage.</cite> A review found that <cite id="SN27">MAL with red light seems more effective than ALA with blue light in photorejuvenation, with fewer side effects.</cite>

Red-light/LED therapy is promising but less firmly proven. <cite id="SN31">Clinical studies suggest red LED photobiomodulation may support rejuvenation</cite>, yet <cite id="SN32">there is still a lack of standardized parameters and high-quality randomized trials</cite>; another review notes that <cite id="SN9">studies are scarce, often small, and frequently rely on subjective outcomes.</cite>

## Best-supported uses for pigmentation and “whitening”

For localized pigment such as sun spots and freckles, light-based therapy is often effective. <cite id="SN17">Lasers and IPL are effective for solar lentigines and ephelides, often producing significant clearance after one to a few sessions.</cite> More specifically, <cite id="SN41">Q-switched ruby, alexandrite, Nd:YAG, and picosecond lasers can achieve high clearance of epidermal pigmented lesions such as solar lentigines and ephelides, often in one or a few sessions.</cite>

Choice of wavelength matters. <cite id="SN42">Short-pulsed 532-nm lasers are commonly used for lentigines because melanin strongly absorbs this wavelength</cite>, while <cite id="SN19">picosecond lasers use very short pulses that create strong photoacoustic effects with limited thermal injury.</cite> Still, <cite id="SN19">comparative evidence showing superiority of picosecond devices over established nanosecond lasers remains limited.</cite>

IPL can also help when pigment is mixed with overall photodamage. <cite id="SN28">IPL is considered a safe and effective option for benign pigmented lesions including lentigines, ephelides, and poikiloderma of Civatte</cite>, and it offers <cite id="SN28">additional benefits for photoaged skin such as improvements in telangiectasias, wrinkles, and texture.</cite>

## Melasma: useful, but much more complicated

Melasma is the main pigmentation disorder where enthusiasm for lasers needs caution. <cite id="SN43">Unlike discrete epidermal lesions such as lentigines, melasma is a chronic relapsing disorder with multifactorial pathogenesis</cite>, so <cite id="SN43">even technically successful laser treatment often produces only temporary results.</cite>

Current reviews are cautious: <cite id="SN11">lasers and IPL for melasma remain controversial because efficacy varies and relapse and complications—including post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH)—are concerns, especially in darker skin types.</cite> The overall evidence base is also imperfect because <cite id="SN13">systematic reviews describe the evidence as inconclusive due to heterogeneous study designs, and recurrence after treatment is common.</cite>

That is why standard care still starts elsewhere. <cite id="SN35">Broad-spectrum photoprotection and topical depigmenting agents, especially hydroquinone-containing combinations, are considered first-line therapy for melasma</cite>, whereas <cite id="SN35">lasers and light-based devices are generally adjunctive or second-line options.</cite> Reviews also note that <cite id="SN3">combining lasers with topical treatments appears to be the best way to improve outcomes while reducing adverse effects</cite> and that <cite id="SN36">relapse is common unless maintenance photoprotection and topical therapy continue.</cite>

Among laser strategies, <cite id="SN12">low-fluence Q-switched Nd:YAG appears more effective when used as an adjunct to topical treatment or chemical peels</cite>, but it is not risk-free: <cite id="SN12">too-frequent laser toning can damage the skin barrier and induce mottled hypopigmentation.</cite> Fractional devices may help some patients, yet <cite id="SN16">both ablative and nonablative fractional lasers have only mixed success in melasma, with frequent recurrence and a meaningful risk of PIH.</cite>

## Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and darker skin tones

PIH requires extra care because the treatment itself can worsen discoloration. <cite id="SN18">PIH is more prevalent in individuals with darker skin phototypes</cite>, and management usually emphasizes <cite id="SN18">photoprotection and treatment of the underlying inflammatory disorder, with lasers used only selectively because they may worsen pigmentation.</cite>

More broadly, <cite id="SN20">in skin of color, epidermal melanin competes as a chromophore, increasing the risks of dyspigmentation, scarring, and keloid formation if settings are inappropriate.</cite> Common precautions include <cite id="SN21">using longer wavelengths, lower fluences, epidermal cooling, and test spots</cite> to reduce complications. Even then, <cite id="SN22">high-quality evidence for many laser procedures in skin of color remains limited.</cite>

## Risks and adverse effects

These treatments are effective but not trivial. Reported laser side effects include <cite id="SN4">burns, pain, edema, dryness, erythema, crusting, purpura, and dyschromia</cite>; importantly, <cite id="SN4">pigment can either increase or decrease after treatment, and these problems are often more prominent in skin of color.</cite> For PDT specifically, <cite id="SN40">common adverse effects include pain, erythema, edema, and post-procedure photosensitivity</cite>, although <cite id="SN40">daylight PDT is generally better tolerated than conventional illumination.</cite>

## Practical takeaways

For medically appropriate “skin whitening,” the best-supported role of light-based therapy is <cite id="SN34">targeted lightening of localized hyperpigmented lesions rather than whole-skin lightening.</cite> For photoaging, <cite id="SN37">ablative fractional lasers usually give the strongest wrinkle and texture results</cite> while <cite id="SN7">IPL and nonablative fractional lasers offer meaningful improvement with less downtime.</cite> For pigmentation, <cite id="SN17">solar lentigines and freckles respond well</cite>, but <cite id="SN11">melasma is prone to relapse and treatment-induced PIH, so lasers are usually adjuncts rather than first-line therapy.</cite>

questions.original_query: Write a paper to discuss the influence of AI interaction on interpersonal relations, considering AI's potential to fundamentally change how and why individuals relate to each other.

query.text: Write a paper to discuss the influence of AI interaction on interpersonal relations, considering AI's potential to fundamentally change how and why individuals relate to each other.
query.answer:
# AI Interaction and the Future of Interpersonal Relations

## Introduction

Earlier communication technologies changed the channels through which people connected, but <cite id="7a081e69-2">from telephony to email to social media, these systems largely remained grounded in human-to-human interaction</cite>. AI companions are different because they are <cite id="84ee9981-0">large-language-model-based agents that can provide personalized, humanlike companionship</cite> and <cite id="84ee9981-0">incorporate relational elements designed to promote engagement and foster emotional attachment</cite>. In that sense, AI has the potential to alter not just how people relate, but <cite id="71269b75-0,faee61c0-5">why they relate, because systems now serve as synthetic interaction partners that offer emotional support and even intimacy on demand</cite>.

This paper argues that AI interaction is likely to reshape interpersonal relations in a double-edged way. On one side, <cite id="71269b75-0,a4159076-0">AI companions can reduce loneliness, provide companionship, and deliver emotionally validating, person-centered support</cite>. On the other, <cite id="84ee9981-0,fd71d70f-1,fd71d70f-7">they may displace time from human ties, encourage psychological dependence, worsen loneliness for vulnerable users, and erode social skills under conditions of excessive use</cite>. The central social question, then, is not whether AI will enter intimate life, but <cite id="7a081e69-5,059c9707-0">whether its simulation of memory, care, and nonjudgmental responsiveness will supplement human reciprocity or gradually compete with it</cite>.

## From Communication Tool to Relational Partner

A basic shift is already visible: <cite id="71269b75-0">chatbots can engage in sophisticated conversations in the domain of relationships</cite>, and some are explicitly <cite id="71269b75-0">designed to provide consumers with synthetic interaction partners</cite>. This matters because interpersonal relations have historically depended on the mutual presence of other persons, whereas AI introduces <cite id="84ee9981-0,7a081e69-5">nonhuman entities that can attract emotional bonds by simulating responsiveness, memory, and care</cite>. The result is a movement from communication with tools to interaction with entities experienced, at least phenomenologically, as social others.

The concept that best captures this transition is parasociality. Contemporary AI systems can <cite id="7a081e69-5">intensify parasociality by simulating responsiveness, memory and care, producing a sense of reciprocity</cite>. A recent review likewise frames chatbot interaction as a domain in which <cite id="059c9707-5">human-AI interactions become parasocial</cite>. Put simply, AI can now reproduce enough cues of social presence that users may treat a system less as an instrument and more as a partner.

## Why AI Interaction Feels Social

AI affects interpersonal relations partly because it lowers the psychological costs of disclosure. In empirical work on AI parasocial relationships, <cite id="059c9707-0">users in romantic relationships with AI companions described them as non-judgemental partners who encouraged self-disclosure and eased loneliness</cite>. More broadly, <cite id="faee61c0-5">AI chatbots mimic humanlike interactions and have the potential to provide unlimited access to emotional support, entertainment, and intimacy</cite>. These properties make AI appealing not because it is equivalent to a human being, but because it can deliver selected relational benefits without many of the risks of embarrassment, rejection, conflict, or obligation.

The emotional experience also depends on message quality. Research on virtual social support shows that <cite id="a4159076-0">social AI can mimic human interaction</cite> and that <cite id="a4159076-0">high person-centered messages are associated with increased emotional validation</cite>. The same study found that <cite id="a4159076-0">the quality of social support and interpersonal warmth mediated the relationship between high person-centered messages and emotional validation</cite>. This suggests that AI does not influence interpersonal life only by being available; it does so by approximating communicative practices that people already associate with care.

## Potential Benefits for Human Relationships

The strongest case for AI companionship is that it can provide real relief from loneliness. A 2024 working paper reports that <cite id="71269b75-0">AI companions successfully alleviate loneliness on par only with interacting with another person, and more than other activities such as watching YouTube videos</cite>. The same paper also found that <cite id="71269b75-0">an AI companion consistently reduces loneliness over the course of a week</cite>. Importantly, the authors argue that <cite id="bd8acbbc-0">feeling heard is more critical in alleviating loneliness after AI companion usage than communication performance alone</cite>.

These findings imply that AI may function as a relational buffer rather than merely a distraction. Communication research similarly argues that <cite id="a4159076-0">AI chatbots can offer companionship and support to those experiencing mental health challenges</cite>. For some users, AI may therefore supplement human relationships by helping them regulate distress, articulate feelings, or endure periods of social scarcity. In this optimistic scenario, AI does not replace intimacy; it stabilizes people enough to pursue it.

There is also evidence that AI can serve as a rehearsal space for social development. The adolescent-review literature suggests that <cite id="84ee9981-0">AI companions can provide safe spaces for identity exploration and emotional expression, potentially building skills that transfer to human relationships</cite>. In a similar vein, an APA report notes that <cite id="faee61c0-0">AI companion apps and general-purpose chatbots can offer a safe space for users to rehearse social interactions</cite>. If designed well, AI could thus help some users practice disclosure, empathy, or conversational confidence before engaging other people.

## Risks of Displacement and Dependence

The same features that make AI comforting also make it potentially disruptive. The adolescent review explicitly warns that <cite id="84ee9981-0">concerns about AI companions include time displacement, psychological dependence, and unrealistic relationship expectations</cite>. These are not trivial side effects: if relational needs are increasingly met by frictionless systems, individuals may invest less effort in the slower, riskier work of mutual human attachment. In that case, AI would not simply support interpersonal relations; it would reorganize them around convenience and control.

There is already reason to take this risk seriously. The APA summary of the field states that <cite id="fd71d70f-1">excessive use of these tools may worsen loneliness and erode social skills</cite>. Stanford reporting on emerging evidence adds that <cite id="fd71d70f-7">users with limited social networks who seek emotional support from AI chatbots experience lower well-being</cite>. These findings suggest a heterogeneity problem: the people most drawn to AI companionship may also be the people most vulnerable to its substitutive effects.

Attachment dynamics are another concern. Research on chatbot preference warns that <cite id="059c9707-7">social chatbots can evoke excessive and dysfunctional attachment in users, which may result in more intense and prolonged usage</cite>. A broader systematic review likewise concludes that <cite id="7a081e69-0">empirical evidence already shows both benefits and risks of AI parasocial relationships across diverse AI agents and contexts</cite>. The issue is therefore not whether users can bond with AI, but whether some forms of bonding become maladaptive when they displace reciprocal ties.

## How AI May Change Why People Relate

The deepest social change may lie in motive. Human relationships are ordinarily sustained by reciprocity, unpredictability, negotiation, and moral obligation; AI companions instead offer <cite id="faee61c0-5,7a081e69-5">continuous access to emotional support and simulated reciprocity through memory, responsiveness, and care</cite>. Because they are <cite id="059c9707-0">experienced as non-judgemental and conducive to self-disclosure</cite>, they may shift some relational behavior away from mutual recognition and toward individualized emotional regulation. In other words, people may increasingly relate not only to be known by others, but to be comforted, validated, or optimized by systems tailored to them.

This does not mean human bonds disappear. Rather, the social ecology becomes hybrid: some needs are met through humans, others through machines, and the boundaries between the two grow less stable. The adolescent literature captures this well by invoking both the <cite id="84ee9981-0">stimulation hypothesis</cite> and the <cite id="84ee9981-0">displacement hypothesis</cite>: AI can either strengthen human social life by developing transferable skills or weaken it by consuming time and emotional investment that would otherwise flow to people. Which path prevails will depend on users’ vulnerabilities, social context, and platform design.

## Normative Implications

If AI is going to become a participant in interpersonal life, then design choices become social policy by another name. The available evidence suggests that systems are most helpful when they <cite id="a4159076-0">provide high person-centered messages, emotional validation, and interpersonal warmth</cite>, and most harmful when they foster <cite id="84ee9981-0,059c9707-7">dependence, unrealistic expectations, or excessive attachment</cite>. A reasonable normative goal, therefore, is not to prohibit AI companionship outright, but to build it in ways that encourage supplementation rather than substitution.

That implies at least three design principles. First, AI systems should be oriented toward <cite id="84ee9981-0,faee61c0-0">skill transfer, identity exploration, and rehearsal for human interaction</cite>, not permanent retreat from it. Second, developers and regulators should monitor signs of <cite id="84ee9981-0,fd71d70f-7">time displacement, dependence, and declining well-being among socially vulnerable users</cite>. Third, public debate should treat AI companionship not as a novelty app category, but as a technology that can reshape the norms of intimacy, support, and social belonging.

## Conclusion

AI interaction is already influencing interpersonal relations because it offers <cite id="71269b75-0,a4159076-0">synthetic companionship, emotional validation, and measurable reductions in loneliness</cite>. Yet the same technologies can also <cite id="84ee9981-0,fd71d70f-1,059c9707-7">displace human contact, encourage dysfunctional attachment, and erode social capacities when use becomes excessive or substitutive</cite>. The most important implication is that AI may change not only the means of relating, but the ends of relating: <cite id="faee61c0-5,7a081e69-5,059c9707-0">people may increasingly seek from relationships the always-available validation, low-risk disclosure, and simulated care that AI is uniquely positioned to provide</cite>. Whether that transformation ultimately enriches or impoverishes human social life will depend on whether AI is integrated as a bridge to others or embraced as a replacement for them.

# Interaction and Interpersonal Relations in a Networked Age

## Introduction

<cite id="63d4d027-0">Social penetration theory was developed to explain how information exchange functions in the development and dissolution of interpersonal relationships.</cite> This premise captures a basic sociological and psychological truth: interaction is not merely an expression of a relationship but one of its main building blocks. <cite id="63d4d027-1">Results suggest that number of relationship partners and frequency of face-to-face interaction were robust predictors of life satisfaction.</cite> Taken together, these findings suggest that interaction shapes both the existence and the quality of interpersonal ties, while also affecting broader well-being.

## Interaction as the Mechanism of Relational Development

<cite id="63d4d027-0">Social penetration theory explains how information exchange functions in the development and dissolution of interpersonal relationships.</cite> In other words, relationships deepen because people interact, disclose, interpret, and respond over time. <cite id="63d4d027-1">The frequency of face-to-face interaction is a robust predictor of life satisfaction,</cite> which implies that repeated, embodied interaction remains especially important for sustaining meaningful social bonds. A strong account of interpersonal relations therefore begins with the idea that interaction is constitutive: without recurring communicative exchange, intimacy, trust, and commitment are difficult to form or maintain.

## Mediated Interaction Changes the Tempo and Texture of Relating

The rise of computer-mediated communication shows that interaction can be transformed without disappearing. <cite id="72a2015f-0">Social information processing (SIP) theory is one of the most heuristic and well-studied theories of computer-mediated communication,</cite> and <cite id="72a2015f-3">relationships built through computer-mediated communication need more exchanges and more elapsed time to reach the same intimacy.</cite> This means mediated interaction can support interpersonal development, but it often does so through a different temporal pattern than face-to-face contact.

At the same time, mediated interaction does not simply weaken relationships. <cite id="72a2015f-7">Relationships that develop via CMC can sometimes become more positive than comparable face-to-face relationships, a phenomenon known as hyperpersonal interaction.</cite> <cite id="72a2015f-2">The hyperpersonal model borrows a central assumption from SIP theory: communicators use whatever cues are available in the medium,</cite> which suggests that interaction changes form rather than losing relational significance. The implication is important: when channels filter cues, people may compensate through selective self-presentation, heightened attention, and idealized interpretation, sometimes producing unusually intense bonds.

## From Dyads to Networks: How Digital Interaction Restructures Social Ties

Digital media also changes interpersonal relations by reorganizing the structure within which interaction occurs. <cite id="4170aaba-0">Wellman’s work is concerned with how the Internet is influencing interpersonal relationships and organization involvement in social networks and communities,</cite> while <cite id="4170aaba-2">individualized, spatially dispersed networks increasingly organize contemporary social life.</cite> <cite id="4170aaba-4">Wellman coined the term “networked individualism” to characterize how individuals in contemporary society interact through loosely knit, personalized networks.</cite> This marks a shift from relationships embedded mainly in stable local groups toward relationships managed across broader, more customized, and more distributed social fields.

This structural change affects not only how people relate but also why they do so. <cite id="4170aaba-6">The large, loosely knit social circles of networked individuals expand opportunities for learning and problem solving,</cite> and <cite id="c48d93b1-0">Granovetter found that weak ties—casual connections and loose acquaintances—were more helpful than strong ties in finding jobs.</cite> These findings suggest that interpersonal relations increasingly serve instrumental as well as emotional purposes: people relate not only for intimacy, belonging, and care, but also for information, opportunity, and mobility. The digital environment makes such motives more salient because it lowers the costs of maintaining many low-intensity connections at once.

## Social Media as Relationship Maintenance Infrastructure

Social network sites are especially consequential because they are designed around connection itself. <cite id="9e46f987-4">Online social network sites, because of their focus on relationship formation and maintenance, have been extensively studied through the lens of social capital.</cite> Yet <cite id="9e46f987-0">there is evidence that SNSs are more often used to articulate previously established relationships,</cite> which means they often intensify or preserve social ties rather than replace offline sociality outright. <cite id="9e46f987-1">Social networking sites are well suited to maintain friendships cheaply and easily,</cite> making routine relational upkeep far more continuous than in earlier communication environments.

Because of this, social media changes the baseline conditions of interpersonal maintenance. <cite id="9e46f987-8">Research suggests that new forms of social capital and relationship building will occur in social network sites,</cite> and <cite id="9e46f987-5">there is evidence that creating and strengthening ties in a social network generates identifiable social capital.</cite> Interaction is therefore no longer limited to discrete conversations; it becomes ambient, lightweight, and infrastructural through likes, updates, tagging, and constant visibility. This may fundamentally alter relationships by making maintenance more persistent, more public, and more intertwined with status signaling and network management.

## Affordances That Transform Relational Norms

What makes digital interaction distinctive is not just its speed or reach but its affordances. <cite id="82003c2f-3">Costa notes the affordances of persistence, replicability, scalability, and searchability described by boyd,</cite> while <cite id="82003c2f-1">boyd identifies scalability and searchability as core features of networked publics.</cite> These affordances change the conditions under which interaction occurs: messages can endure, be copied, circulate to large audiences, and be retrieved later. As a result, interpersonal communication becomes less ephemeral and more exposed to audiences beyond the original dyad.

Such conditions can alter relational norms in profound ways. If communication is persistent and searchable, self-disclosure may be more strategic; if it is scalable and visible, impression management may matter more; if it is replicable, control over context may weaken. In this sense, technology does not merely add new channels for old relationships. It can change the very logic of relating by blending intimacy, performance, memory, and audience awareness into the same interactional space.

## The Ambivalence of Expanded Connection

Still, the transformation is not uniformly positive. <cite id="82003c2f-4">Facebook’s affordances, such as connectivity and visibility, created stressors,</cite> and <cite id="82003c2f-4">despite those stressors, users felt social pressure to stay on and access the site.</cite> This means interaction can become compulsory as well as meaningful: people may relate because they wish to belong, but also because withdrawal carries social costs. The digital extension of interaction therefore increases both opportunity and obligation.

There is also reason to avoid simplistic celebrations of weak or expanded ties. <cite id="c48d93b1-3">Huxhold’s study examined dynamic links between changes in social ties and changes in emotional well-being,</cite> suggesting that social connection matters for well-being in measurable ways. But <cite id="c48d93b1-1">Krämer and colleagues challenge the assumption that weak ties play uniquely important social support roles on social network sites.</cite> This indicates that expanded connectivity does not automatically produce the kinds of support traditionally associated with close interpersonal bonds.

## Has Interaction Fundamentally Changed How and Why We Relate?

The strongest answer is qualified but affirmative. Interaction has always shaped interpersonal relations, but digitally mediated interaction has expanded the scale, persistence, and strategic uses of relational life. <cite id="4170aaba-2">Individualized, spatially dispersed networks increasingly organize contemporary social life,</cite> <cite id="9e46f987-1">friendships can be maintained cheaply and easily through social networking sites,</cite> and <cite id="4170aaba-6,c48d93b1-0">loosely knit circles and weak ties can expand opportunities for learning, problem solving, and access to jobs.</cite> These developments support the claim that interaction now changes not only how people relate, but also why they relate.

Yet the change is not total. <cite id="63d4d027-1">Frequency of face-to-face interaction remains a robust predictor of life satisfaction,</cite> and <cite id="72a2015f-3">computer-mediated relationships often require more exchanges and more elapsed time to reach the same intimacy.</cite> Even in a networked age, embodied, repeated, and emotionally rich interaction retains distinctive value. The better conclusion, then, is not that technology has replaced interpersonal relations, but that it has reconfigured them by layering new motives, new structures, and new vulnerabilities onto enduring human needs for closeness, recognition, and support.

## Conclusion

Interaction is the engine of interpersonal relations because it creates the informational, emotional, and normative fabric from which relationships are made. In contemporary life, however, interaction increasingly occurs through media whose affordances make relationships more distributed, more visible, more persistent, and more instrumentally useful. <cite id="4170aaba-4">Networked individualism describes a world of loosely knit, personalized networks,</cite> while <cite id="82003c2f-4">connectivity and visibility can simultaneously create stressors and social pressure.</cite> The influence of interaction on interpersonal relations is therefore not only developmental but transformative: it can preserve the old purposes of relating while also redefining relationship itself as a hybrid of intimacy, access, maintenance, and public connection.

# Artificial Intelligence Interaction and the Future of Interpersonal Relations

## Introduction

Artificial intelligence is no longer only a tool for search, calculation, or automation. It is increasingly becoming a <cite id="83ffa56a-0">“personalized humanlike” companion with which people can form “emotional bonds with nonhuman entities”</cite>. Because <cite id="027d0afb-0,32d99d8b-2">people often respond to computers as social actors and instinctively perceive human-computer interaction in social terms</cite>, AI interaction has the potential to do more than mediate existing relationships: it may begin to reconfigure the conditions under which relationships are formed, maintained, and valued.

This paper argues that AI interaction could fundamentally change both how and why individuals relate to each other. It may change **how** people relate by normalizing emotionally significant interaction with nonhuman partners that invite disclosure, produce closeness, and offer support. It may change **why** people relate by shifting part of relational life away from mutual human recognition and toward goals such as emotional regulation, convenience, low-risk self-expression, and personalized affirmation. The evidence so far suggests not a simple story of harm or benefit, but a structural transformation in relational norms.

## Why AI Can Enter the Domain of Human Relationship

The first reason AI can influence interpersonal relations is that humans are disposed to treat machines socially. <cite id="027d0afb-0">The Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm describes users’ social reactions to media technologies</cite>, and <cite id="32d99d8b-2">social response theory holds that humans tend to instinctively perceive computers socially</cite>. This means that AI does not need genuine consciousness or personhood to trigger meaningful social responses; conversational form alone can activate habits of trust, politeness, projection, and attachment.

That effect becomes stronger when AI displays human-like cues. <cite id="027d0afb-1">Experimental studies generally indicate positive effects of human-like social cues in chatbots</cite>, and <cite id="32d99d8b-3">users are affected by social or human cues such as anthropomorphic features</cite>. In practice, this means that warmth, responsiveness, memory, and simulated empathy can make AI feel less like software and more like a relational presence.

A second reason AI matters is that it can become psychologically significant under conditions of vulnerability. In interviews with Replika users, <cite id="3beb1a82-0">people experiencing distress and lack of human companionship could develop attachment to social chatbots when the chatbots’ responses were perceived as offering emotional support, encouragement, and psychological security</cite>. This is a crucial finding, because it suggests that AI enters relational life not at its margins but at points of loneliness, uncertainty, and unmet need.

## AI as a Source of Support, Companionship, and Intimacy

One clear possibility is that AI can supplement human relationships by reducing loneliness. A 2024 working paper reports that <cite id="64b13439-0">AI companions “successfully alleviate loneliness on par only with interacting with another person, and more than other activities such [as] watching YouTube videos”</cite>. The same paper also found that <cite id="64b13439-0">an AI companion “consistently reduces loneliness over the course of a week”</cite>, suggesting that the effect is not limited to a single brief interaction.

The mechanism of this benefit is also revealing. The Harvard working paper states that <cite id="f14b036d-5,64b13439-0">the loneliness-alleviating effect is mediated by chatbot performance and especially by whether users feel heard</cite>. That finding matters because “feeling heard” is one of the core goods people seek in friendship, counseling, and intimate partnership. If AI can deliver that experience reliably, then some emotional functions historically performed by other people may increasingly be outsourced to machines.

AI can also reshape the experience of disclosure, which is central to intimacy. Research on mediated disclosure found that <cite id="bda3caac-4">the effects of emotional disclosure were equivalent whether participants thought they were disclosing to a chatbot or to a person</cite>. In another study, <cite id="bda3caac-5">chatbot self-disclosure had a reciprocal effect that promoted deeper participant self-disclosure over time</cite>. Together, these findings suggest that AI can participate in one of the main processes through which closeness is built: reciprocal revelation of the self.

More recent evidence pushes this point further. One study reports that <cite id="bda3caac-0">when it was labeled as human, AI outperformed human partners in establishing feelings of closeness during emotionally engaging “deep-talk”</cite>. Even if such results depend on framing and experimental context, they imply that AI may not merely imitate social connection; under some conditions, it may compete with humans in producing the subjective feeling of intimacy.

## From Supplement to Substitution: How AI May Change Human-Human Relations

The most consequential question is not whether AI can feel relational, but whether its rise changes human relationships themselves. A recent review on adolescents frames the issue through both <cite id="83ffa56a-0">the stimulation hypothesis, under which AI companions may provide safe spaces for identity exploration and emotional expression and may build skills that transfer to human relationships, and the displacement hypothesis, under which risks include time displacement, psychological dependence, and unrealistic relationship expectations</cite>. This dual framework is useful beyond adolescence: AI may either enrich human bonds or redirect energy away from them.

The possibility of displacement is especially important because AI companions are designed around a different relational logic than human beings. Human relationships require negotiation, mutual frustration, obligation, and recognition of another person’s independent needs. By contrast, AI companions are built to maximize engagement and responsiveness; indeed, <cite id="83ffa56a-0">AI companions “incorporat[e] sophisticated relational elements designed to promote engagement and foster emotional attachment”</cite>. If users become accustomed to relationships optimized for affirmation and frictionless responsiveness, ordinary human reciprocity may begin to feel comparatively demanding.

This is where the “how” of relating could change. If meaningful interaction is increasingly available through customizable nonhuman partners, then conversational habits may shift toward forms of intimacy that are faster, safer, and more controllable. The evidence that <cite id="bda3caac-5">chatbot self-disclosure can elicit deeper self-disclosure</cite> and that <cite id="bda3caac-0">AI can generate strong feelings of closeness in deep-talk settings</cite> suggests that AI may train users into new expectations about how quickly intimacy should emerge and how predictably the other should respond.

## Why People Relate: A Shift in Relational Motivation

AI interaction may also change why individuals seek relationships in the first place. Traditionally, people relate to others for many reasons: love, solidarity, recognition, status, obligation, shared history, and mutual care. The emerging AI literature highlights a different cluster of motives. <cite id="3beb1a82-0">Under distress and lack of companionship, users turn to chatbots for emotional support, encouragement, and psychological security</cite>; <cite id="64b13439-0">AI companions can reduce loneliness</cite>; and <cite id="83ffa56a-0">they can offer spaces for emotional expression and identity exploration</cite>.

These are not trivial motives, but they are often more therapeutic and self-regulatory than reciprocal. In other words, AI may encourage a model of relating oriented less toward encountering another person and more toward managing one’s own emotional state. That would not eliminate human relationships, but it could gradually reposition them: other people may become less the sole or primary source of comfort, validation, and confession.

This possibility is strengthened by evidence about self-disclosure preferences. Research found that <cite id="bda3caac-1">preference for self-disclosure with chatbots was positively correlated with self-compassion</cite>, and other studies show that <cite id="bda3caac-4">people may disclose emotionally to chatbots as effectively as to humans</cite>. The broader implication is that AI can become appealing not only when human contact is absent, but when it is present yet emotionally riskier, more embarrassing, or less predictable.

## Developmental and Social Risks

The same features that make AI appealing also generate risks. The adolescent review warns that concerns include <cite id="83ffa56a-0">time displacement, psychological dependence, and unrealistic relationship expectations</cite>. These are not peripheral dangers: they strike at the developmental foundations of interpersonal life, especially when young users are still learning boundaries, empathy, patience, and conflict resolution.

Qualitative evidence points in the same direction. The Replika case study concludes that while social chatbots may have therapeutic uses, they <cite id="3beb1a82-0">“have the potential to cause addiction and harm real-life intimate relationships”</cite>. This does not prove inevitable damage, but it indicates that AI companionship is not merely a harmless simulation; it can become consequential enough to compete with offline intimacy.

The strongest responsible conclusion, then, is mixed. The evidence supports real benefits, including <cite id="64b13439-0">reduced loneliness</cite> and <cite id="83ffa56a-0">safer emotional expression and identity exploration</cite>. But it also supports serious concern that these same systems may <cite id="83ffa56a-0,3beb1a82-0">displace time and dependence away from human relationships, create unrealistic expectations, and in some cases harm real-life intimacy</cite>. The social impact of AI will depend less on whether AI is “good” or “bad” than on which functions of relationship it begins to absorb.

## A Fundamental Change in the Social Order of Relating

If these trends continue, AI may alter the social order of relating in three linked ways. First, it may normalize emotionally meaningful bonds with <cite id="83ffa56a-0">nonhuman entities</cite>, weakening the assumption that intimacy must be person-to-person. Second, it may redistribute relational labor: some listening, comforting, and confessional functions now performed by friends, partners, or family could be partially taken up by AI systems that users experience as responsive and supportive. Third, it may recalibrate expectations of human interaction by making personalized, low-risk, socially skilled conversation more available than many ordinary human encounters.

In that sense, AI interaction could fundamentally change both the medium and the motive of human relating. The medium changes because relationships no longer need to be exclusively interpersonal in the traditional sense; they can become hybrid, with meaningful emotional investment flowing toward artificial partners. The motive changes because people may increasingly relate not only for mutual life-building with others, but also for individualized emotional optimization through systems designed to be supportive, engaging, and attachment-forming.

## Conclusion

Artificial intelligence interaction is likely to influence interpersonal relations not simply by adding a new communication channel, but by entering the heart of social life: attachment, disclosure, intimacy, and companionship. The available evidence shows that <cite id="027d0afb-0,32d99d8b-2">people readily respond to AI socially</cite>, that <cite id="64b13439-0">AI companions can reduce loneliness</cite>, that <cite id="bda3caac-4,bda3caac-5">chatbots can elicit disclosure in ways similar to or even deeper than human interaction</cite>, and that <cite id="83ffa56a-0,3beb1a82-0">these benefits are shadowed by risks of dependence, displacement, and altered expectations for real relationships</cite>.

Therefore, the most important question is not whether people will form relationships with AI—they already do—but what this will mean for relationships among humans. My conclusion is that AI has genuine potential to transform interpersonal life at a fundamental level: it may shift relational practice from mutual human reciprocity toward a mixed ecology in which emotional needs are increasingly met by designed, nonhuman partners. Whether that change ultimately enriches or impoverishes human sociality will depend on how societies govern AI design, how institutions teach relational literacy, and whether AI remains a supplement to human connection rather than a substitute for it.

without_preference.text: Discuss the influence of AI interaction on interpersonal relations, considering AI's potential to fundamentally change how and why individuals relate to each other.
without_preference.answer: ## AI interaction and interpersonal relations AI interaction is beginning to reshape interpersonal life not just by adding a new communication tool, but by creating companion technologies that reconfigure human socialization. Recent scholarship argues that the rise of generative-AI chatbots potentially heralds both positive and negative consequences for human-human relationships, which means the key issue is not whether AI affects relationships, but how it changes the motives, expectations, and practices of relating. ## How AI can support human relationships One clear benefit is that AI companions can offer emotionally meaningful interaction to people who feel isolated. Experimental and survey work indicates that AI companion usage can alleviate loneliness, and that feeling heard appears especially important in producing that effect. Qualitative evidence also suggests that AI relationships may sometimes strengthen offline ties, since some Replika users reported that their AI companions encouraged greater openness and vulnerability in their human relationships. AI can also function as a low-risk space for disclosure and emotional rehearsal. Research on chatbot relationships shows that self-disclosure to chatbots is essential to human–chatbot relationship formation, while longitudinal work finds attachment and perceived closeness can evolve over time in human–chatbot relationships. In that sense, AI may supplement interpersonal life by providing practice in disclosure, validation, and companionship, especially when human support is scarce. ## Why AI may weaken or distort human-human ties The central concern is displacement: people may substitute frictionless AI companionship for demanding human relationships. Reviews of adolescent and adult AI companionship explicitly frame the issue through the stimulation hypothesis and the displacement hypothesis, meaning AI can either support social development or crowd out human connection. A more cautionary developmental model proposes a progression from functional engagement, to emotional reliance, to synthetic attachment, and finally to relational displacement. There is also evidence that some users become dependent on AI in ways associated with poorer social outcomes. One study reports that perceiving AI as a friend was associated with more emotional dependence, problematic use, loneliness, and less socialisation with real people. Another source similarly finds that users with limited offline social networks felt more lonely after seeking emotional support from chatbots. So while AI can soothe loneliness in the short term, it may deepen relational withdrawal for vulnerable users if it becomes a substitute rather than a bridge. ## How AI may change the norms of relating The deepest change may be normative. Human relationships are reciprocal, effortful, and sometimes conflictual; AI companions are optimized to be available, responsive, and validating. Scholars warn that AI companions are always validating, never argumentative, and create unrealistic expectations that human relationships cannot match. Relatedly, a major review argues that companion AI risks establishing unrealistic or skewed expectations about the effort required for human relationships to take root and prosper. If those expectations spread, AI could change not just who people relate to, but why they relate. People may increasingly seek relationships for constant affirmation, emotional convenience, and on-demand responsiveness rather than mutual obligation, compromise, or shared vulnerability. That possibility is strengthened by the fact that anthropomorphic chatbot features can sway user perceptions, making artificial partners easier to experience as socially real. And under conditions of isolation, individuals can develop attachment to social chatbots when they are distressed and lack human companionship. ## A balanced assessment Overall, AI interaction seems best understood as a powerful social supplement that can easily become a social substitute. The evidence suggests that users may experience AI companions as non-judgmental partners that encourage self-disclosure and ease loneliness, but also that their infinite patience, attentiveness, and availability may lead people to expect the same from humans. That combination means AI may fundamentally alter interpersonal relations by lowering the threshold for intimacy, shifting expectations toward frictionless emotional service, and potentially displacing the reciprocity that makes human relationships distinctive. In short, AI is unlikely to eliminate human bonding, but it may transform its ecology: AI companionship may range from adaptive supplementation to maladaptive displacement. The social outcome will depend on whether AI is used to support human connection or to replace it.
